The association expressed confidence that addressing the outstanding issues would consolidate the gains already made and strengthen the relationship between the FCT Administration and healthcare workers.

World.title: Yahyah: Nigeria, Others Need $3bn Settlement Fund to Unlock $3 Trillion Energy Market
World.content:
• RHG chair says region must build integrated energy market

Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja





West Africa needs a $3 billion regional settlement facility, harmonised regulations and deeper cross-border integration to unlock a potential $3 trillion cumulative energy market by 2035, the Chairman of RHG Advisory, Suleiman Yahyah, has said.

Yahyah, who spoke on the second day of the West African Refined Fuel Market (WARFM) conference in Abuja yesterday, said the region could no longer afford to approach energy development as a collection of individual national projects, arguing that a systems-based approach was needed to rapidly correct existing market imbalances.

The conference was organised by the West African Regulators Forum (WARF), the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority(NMDPRA) and S&P Global Energy.

According to Yahyah, West Africa has reached a critical point in the evolution of its energy market, driven by growing investments in refining, changing global market dynamics and the need to address widespread energy poverty.

He stated that thinking only in terms of individual projects would take many years to transform the region’s energy market, while a systems approach could accelerate the process.

Yahyah noted that Africa accounts for about 20 per cent of the global population but produces only 7.5 per cent of global hydrocarbons, while more than 600 million people remain in energy poverty.

The situation, he added, was also acute in West Africa, where he estimated that about 45 per cent of the population was in energy poverty, with more than 75 per cent lacking access to clean power.

To change the situation, Yahyah proposed the development of an integrated regional energy market in which individual countries would retain regulatory responsibilities while transactions increasingly took place across national borders.

“So, essentially, we regulate nationally and transact regionally,” he suggested.

He explained that this would require countries to harmonise their regulatory frameworks to enable operators licensed in one West African country to operate and trade in another without having to navigate fundamentally different market rules.

The proposed framework, he said, should include common product specifications, shared data standards, modern energy contracts, interconnected infrastructure and a regional dispute resolution mechanism.

“If we do that, it is possible that by 2035, we can have a market that is $3 trillion cumulative,” he said.

Yahyah identified liquidity as one of the most critical requirements for the proposed market, calling for central banks, the African Finance Corporation (AFC), the African Development Bank (AfDB), sovereign wealth funds and the African Energy Bank (AEB) to collaborate on establishing a regional settlement facility.

“We estimate that this settlement facility will be in the region of $3 billion, but anchored in Naira,” he said.

He suggested that the system could build on the existing Pan-African Payment and Settlement System rather than creating an entirely new platform, allowing transactions to be settled across the region while providing a mechanism for conversion into dollars.

He also said the eventual system would need to accommodate the proposed Eco currency as the monetary integration process evolves.

“Without liquidity, we can’t create an African or West African energy market that is going to be efficient,” Yahyah said.

Beyond finance, he identified talent as another critical component of the regional market, stressing that West Africa needed skilled professionals capable of regulating, trading, analysing and developing the legal and institutional frameworks required for a sophisticated energy market. “Talent is infrastructure,” he pointed out.

Yahyah also advocated strategic partnerships with established global market institutions, arguing that African countries should not attempt to recreate methodologies, technologies and market infrastructure that already exist internationally.

“We are not going to reinvent the wheel,” he said, urging partnerships with institutions such as S&P Global, Argus and Bloomberg.

He said such partnerships should nevertheless be structured around local content requirements and designed to ensure that international players operate as participants in an integrated regional market rather than as isolated entities.

Yahyah further proposed that countries outside West Africa, including Angola and Algeria, should initially participate as observers in the West African Regulators Forum, while the region conducts biannual assessments of its progress against agreed targets.

He said the success of the proposed market should ultimately not be measured only by the value of transactions or the number of projects completed, but by its impact on ordinary people.

He said the key indicators should include access to energy, affordability, reliability, transition to clean cooking, productive use of energy in agriculture and industry, poverty reduction and improvement in regional welfare.

He also called for greater participation by African investors, saying the region could combine local capital with international expertise through joint ventures and partnerships. “We have to do joint ventures. We have to do partnerships,” he said.

Yahyah argued that a more integrated regional market would create opportunities for young Africans and generate jobs and wealth, but stressed that regulatory harmonisation, funding and human capital would be essential to achieving the vision.

World.title: Orlando Pirates midfielder suffers another injury blow on return
World.content:
Orlando Pirates midfielder Sihle Nduli suffered another injury blow on his return against AmaZulu on Wednesday night.

Nduli was named in the Pirates starting line-up in a league match which ended in a 1-1 draw at Durban’s Hollywoodbets Kings Park Stadium.

However, he had to be substituted in the 53rd minute after being injured by Thandolwenkosi Ngwenya who escaped a straight red card.



The midfield anchor first suffered a long-term injury in November 2025 against Golden Arrows, and he was ruled out for the season.

At the time, Nduli injured his Achilles tendon and ankle, and he had to watch his teammates from home for five months.

And it is unclear, at least at this stage, as to how long this latest injury will sideline the former Stellenbosch FC midfielder for.

Nduli’s place was taken by newly-signed midfielder Thapelo Mokobodi who played alongside Camren Dansin for the remainder of the game.

World.title: Cyril Ramaphosa offers condolences after Lake Kariba ferry tragedy
World.content:
President Cyril Ramaphosa has expressed his condolences to Zimbabwe following the Lake Kariba ferry tragedy, which has claimed 44 lives. Image: SABC News

President Cyril Ramaphosa has expressed his condolences to Zimbabwe following the Lake Kariba ferry tragedy, which has claimed 44 lives.

Ramaphosa said South Africa stands in solidarity with the people of Zimbabwe during what has been a devastating tragedy.

He extended his sympathies to the families of those who lost their lives, survivors of the accident and relatives still waiting for news of loved ones.



The South African president also wished those who survived the tragedy a speedy recovery and paid tribute to the emergency teams involved in the response.

Cyril Ramaphosa commended those working to support affected families and communities while continuing efforts to recover people who remain missing.

On behalf of the Government and people of South Africa, President @CyrilRamaphosa extends his deep condolences to the Government and people of Zimbabwe following the extensive loss of life in a tragedy on Lake Kariba, Zimbabwe. https://t.co/BE4mvH5k1y — The Presidency 🇿🇦 (@PresidencyZA) August 13, 2026

Mnangagwa calls for urgent action

Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa also sent messages of condolence to the families of those who died in the accident on Wednesday.

Mnangagwa described the incident as a tragedy that had exposed serious deficiencies in Zimbabwe’s maritime capabilities.

He called on relevant government agencies to urgently address the shortcomings exposed by the disaster and take an active role in implementing remedial measures.



The Zimbabwean president said lessons must be learned from the tragedy and that steps should be taken to prevent similar disasters from occurring in the future.

The Lake Kariba disaster has prompted renewed scrutiny of safety measures and emergency preparedness on one of Africa’s largest artificial lakes, as authorities continue supporting affected families and dealing with the aftermath of the tragedy.

World.title: Permanent residents in SA and Smart IDs: What the LAW says
World.content:
Permanent residents in SA are fully entitled to apply for Smart ID cards, as of a law change in May 2025. For years, naturalised citizens and permanent residents had no path to the Smart ID. The Department of Home Affairs’ excuse was plausible. It said its IT systems had no way of linking the citizen’s database to a non-citizen one.

Therefore, previously, the only option was the green barcoded ID book. However, the old ‘green mamba’ is easier to forge and becoming increasingly unwelcome as proof of identification as a result. It’s no wonder that for the millions who had built a life in South Africa, the lack of a Smart ID card became a daily reminder of their second-tier status in the country.

PERMANENT RESIDENTS IN SA & SMART IDS

However, back in May 2025, Home Affairs Minister Leon Schreiber ended that exclusion. All naturalised citizens and lawful permanent residents in SA became eligible for the Smart ID for the first time in the country’s history. Roughly 1.4-million people qualified overnight. It was framed by the department as the biggest milestone yet in its digital overhaul. Nevertheless, due to eHomeAffairs IT challenges, the rollout still has to happen in phases. And this is where portions of lawful permanent residents in SA are still tetchy:



Phase 1 covers naturalised citizens and permanent residents from visa-exempt countries only. Only if your country of origin appears on South Africa’s visa-exempt list, can a candidate apply for Smart IDs.

covers naturalised citizens and permanent residents from visa-exempt countries only. Only if your country of origin appears on South Africa’s visa-exempt list, can a candidate apply for Smart IDs. Phase 2 is for applicants from visa-required countries. This phase has yet to be announced and no date has been confirmed by the department at the time of writing. So, it’s still green ID booklet for you.

is for applicants from visa-required countries. This phase has yet to be announced and no date has been confirmed by the department at the time of writing. So, it’s still green ID booklet for you. All applicants can go through the eHomeAffairs portal, DHA Live Capture office, or one of the new participating banks in SA when applying.

CITIZENS VERSUS PERMANENT RESIDENTS

The mistreatment of naturalised citizens and permanent residents in SA was largely overlooked until Dr. Leon Schreiber took over office. Image: File

According to reports, even once issued, the card does not erase the legal distinction of permanent residents in SA. A South African ID number carries an eleventh digit that flags the status:

1 for a permanent resident.

0 for a citizen.

If a permanent resident later naturalises, that digit changes from 1 to 0 and a new Smart ID is issued to match.

Moreover, until that time, permanent residence does not open every door full citizenship does. A South African passport remains reserved exclusively for citizens only. Permanent residents travel on their foreign passport and use their South African ID to prove status inside the country.

HOW TO APPLY FOR AN ID IN SOUTH AFRICA

First-time permanent resident applicants need to complete a BI-9 form.

They must supply an original and certified copy of their Permanent Residence Permit.

Produce a certified copy of their original passport.

Unabridged birth certificate authenticated or apostilled.

Applicable proof of residential address.

The fee is R140, the same for any other South African citizen.

The All Blacks have endured a series of injury problems since starting their tour to South Africa, and it’s now been confirmed that Billy Proctor will return home to New Zealand after fracturing his shoulder blade in the game against the Stormers.

That has now opened the door for the All Blacks selectors to bring in superstar flyhalf Richie Mo’unga as a replacement in the Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry squad.

Mo’unga has not played for the All Blacks since the 2023 World Cup final against the Springboks, having decided to ply his trade in Japan after that tournament.



New Zealand Rugby have a strict policy whereby overseas-based players will not be eligible for the All Blacks, but Mo’unga recently became available for selection again after playing for Canterbury against Auckland in the NPC on 1 August.

Interesting selection for All Blacks

The 32-year-old joins a talented group of flyhalves and playmakers in South Africa, which includes Ruben Love, Beauden Barrett, Damian McKenzie and Josh Jacomb.

“Richie is the obvious choice as a replacement. His job now is to get in and learn our systems, get his head around the detail and earn the right to play,” coach Dave Rennie commented.



“We really feel for Billy. He has had a great season so this is frustrating for him. It is the harsh reality of our game. We wish him all the best with his recovery and hope to see him fit and well in time for the end of year tour selection.”

Mo’unga will arrive in Johannesburg on Friday.

World.title: Five things that happen when Zimbabweans return from South Africa
World.content:
More than 115 000 Zimbabweans have returned home from South Africa since the repatriation exercise began in May 2026, according to figures released by Zimbabwean authorities.

The returns have taken place amid anti-immigrant protests, attacks and a crackdown on undocumented migration.

The figure includes Zimbabweans who returned through Government-assisted arrangements as well as those who made their own way home.



The scale of the movement has created a major challenge for Zimbabwe, with authorities now focusing not only on getting citizens home but also on helping them settle back into communities.

So, what happens to Zimbabweans when they return from South Africa?

Here are five things to know.

1. Returnees are transported to Zimbabwe

For those using assisted repatriation arrangements, the journey home begins with registration and transport from South Africa.



Zimbabwean officials have been working with South African authorities and other stakeholders to facilitate through border points, with Beitbridge serving as a major entry point.

The Government has also arranged transport for returnees once they cross into Zimbabwe.

In some areas, buses have been used to take returnees from Beitbridge and other arrival points towards their home districts.



Authorities have also established holding centres to assist people who require urgent support after arriving in the country.

2. They can receive basic assistance after arrival

Returning home does not necessarily mean that a person immediately has somewhere to stay, money or access to essential services.

Some Zimbabweans left South Africa suddenly after losing accommodation, employment or belongings.



The Government and humanitarian organisations have therefore been providing assistance to vulnerable returnees, including transport and medical support.

The humanitarian situation has been particularly concerning for people who left South Africa without medication or medical records.

The Associated Press reported that aid groups had raised concerns about interruptions to treatment for people with chronic conditions, including HIV, after they returned to Zimbabwe.



This means the repatriation process is about more than simply crossing the border.

3. Their skills can be registered for opportunities in Zimbabwe

One of the biggest questions facing Zimbabwe is what happens to people who have spent years working in South Africa.

Many returnees have acquired skills and experience in sectors such as construction, manufacturing, hospitality and other trades.



Zimbabwe has responded by creating a system to identify and register the skills of returning citizens.

By July, the Ministry of Skills Audit and Development said it had registered 15 000 skilled Zimbabweans who had returned home, mainly from South Africa.

The Government has presented the initiative as a way of connecting returnees’ skills and experience with opportunities in Zimbabwe.



More recently, Government figures indicated that 38 057 returnees had registered through the Skills Registration Process, showing that the programme has continued to expand as more Zimbabweans arrive home.

4. Some returnees can be connected to employment opportunities

Returning from South Africa does not automatically mean that a person will receive a job.

However, the skills-registration programme is intended to help Government identify people who could contribute to Zimbabwe’s economy.



There have already been efforts by private companies to recruit returning Zimbabweans.

For example, a Harare-based construction company advertised employment opportunities specifically targeting Zimbabweans returning from South Africa.

The challenge is significant because many returnees had established their livelihoods in South Africa and now have to find ways of earning an income back home.



The success of the reintegration programme will therefore depend heavily on whether returnees can translate their skills and experience into sustainable employment or business opportunities.

5. They are expected to rebuild their lives in Zimbabwe

The final stage is perhaps the most difficult: settling back into life in Zimbabwe.

For some returnees, this means going back to their rural homes or reconnecting with relatives.



For others, it means finding accommodation, enrolling children in schools, looking for work or starting a business.

The Zimbabwean Government has said its approach is not simply to bring citizens home but to support their reintegration.

President Emmerson Mnangagwa has directed authorities to ensure that returning citizens are welcomed with dignity and supported through programmes designed to help them contribute to the local economy.



The scale of the return movement means that this process could take months.

World.title: Time is of the essence: Ford Ranger 2.3 EcoBoost Sport review
World.content:
You may recall our first drive of the Ford Ranger 2.3 EcoBoost Sport in May took place during the Southern Cape floods! It was a baptism this 4×2-only bakkie didn’t ask for, with dozens of water crossings, a flooded Swartberg Pass and Oudtshoorn cut off on one side. Nevertheless, this is the long-awaited follow-up. Dry tar, open road, no rivers to ford in the Ford. How does the new petrol derivative fair in the real world?

FORD RANGER 2.3 ECOBOOST SPORT

The 2.3-litre EcoBoost 4×2 is also available in Wildtrak spec. This Sport fits between that and the XL. Image: Ray Leathern

By far and away the best-selling double cab in South Africa, Rangers have always announced themselves with a characteristic diesel clatter on start-up. That’s not judgement, it’s a soundtrack that owners learn to love and respect for all the open-road efficiency and low-down grunt it signifies. However, the Ford Ranger 2.3 EcoBoost Sport skips all of that. And in the real world, it’s really rather pleasant. Hit the starter button and there’s, well, near-silence and minimal vibration.

On the move, the smooth linearity continues. Throttle response builds from the first squeeze, with none of the turbodiesel’s characteristic lag-then-shove. It’s quick rather than fast, delivering its 222 kW and 452 Nm without unnecessary theatre. The 10-speed automatic, sharpened for 2026, shuffles through gears decisively. Only occasionally do you hear a subtle turbo flutter when overtaking, which is a totally fuss-free affair. If you’ve only known a diesel bakkie, the refinement and ease of use of the Ford Ranger 2.3 EcoBoost Sport is a literal breath of fresh air.



WHAT ABOUT THE FUEL ECONOMY TRADE-OFF?

The Ford Ranger 2.3 EcoBoost Sport’s semi-autonomous driving tech is some of the best we’ve tested, across all segments. Image: File

Of course, a still relatively heavy double cab (even though its only 4×2) with a turbo petrol engine is going to use more juice between visits to the fuel station. Ford’s claimed/combined figure for the 2.3 EcoBoost sits at 9.3 l/100 km. We took it for a leisurely drive over the Women’s Day long weekend and, in isolation, returned in the 10 l/100 km range. However, with a heavier right foot dictated by the mixed-use driving week that followed, we finally settled in the 11 l/100 km range. So, yes, in the real world the petrol drinks more, somewhere between one and a half and two litres more every 100 km.

However, given the smoothness, refinement and cheaper petrol price, that perceived gap starts to look mighty small. Timing appears ideal for uptake of the Ford Ranger 2.3 EcoBoost Sport in a diesel crisis nobody saw coming. May 2026 delivered the worst diesel shock in decades. The Strait of Hormuz disruption pushed Brent crude past $100 a barrel. Diesel jumped R6.19 a litre, more than double petrol’s R3.27 increase. Now in August 2026, at the time of writing, petrol prices have decreased by 52 cents per litre, while wholesale diesel prices increased by R1.23 to R1.38 per litre, respectively.

FORD RANGER 2.3 ECOBOOST SPORT VERDICT

Subtle refinements made at the Silverton factory improve every element of the Ford Ranger experience. Image: Ray Leathern

So, strip away the launch-day floodwater theatrics, and the Ford Ranger 2.3 EcoBoost Sport does actually deliver something rare. It’s got everything that makes a Ford Ranger the defacto best-selling double cab in South Africa. We’re talking affordability at R839 600. We’re talking about all the brilliant semi-autonomous driving tech you’d expect in a high-end premium vehicle.

Then you combine it with a top-notch cabin and petrol-powered road manners, and there are remarkably few compromises to be had here. Time will only tell whether buyers are ready to vote with their wallets and adopt a petrol-powered double cab into their everyday lives. However, all we can report is that it is smooth, quiet and refined beyond measure. Fortune favours the brave and early adopters will be rewarded handsomely.

THE FIGURES

World.title: Kaizer Chiefs v Mamelodi Sundowns: Date, venue, kickoff time, TV channel
World.content:
Kaizer Chiefs will host Mamelodi Sundowns in their third Betway Premiership match of the season this weekend.

Amakhosi have made a strong start to their league campaign, winning both of their opening matches and currently sitting at the top of the log.

Chiefs secured a 2-0 victory over Sekhukhune United in midweek, with Luke Baartman and Mduduzi Shabalala finding the back of the net in the second half to secure all three points.



It is the second successive season that Chiefs have won their opening two league matches, and they will now face a much tougher test against Sundowns.

All attention turns to Sunday as Amakhosi look to extend their unbeaten run against their rivals to four matches across all competitions.

Kaizer Chiefs and Sundowns meet early

The two sides met twice last season, with both encounters ending in draws.

Sundowns, meanwhile, will be looking to bounce back after a difficult start to their league campaign. The defending champions, who missed out on a ninth consecutive league title last season, opened their Betway Premiership campaign with a scrappy 3-2 victory over TS Galaxy on Tuesday.

Masandawana will now be hoping to claim maximum points away from home against Chiefs, but they face an Amakhosi side that appears to have gained confidence from their impressive start.

Although Sundowns have traditionally dominated this fixture and have been favourites in many of their recent meetings, this weekend’s encounter could be a much closer contest.



Sundowns have shown some defensive vulnerability, while Chiefs have looked particularly strong in the league so far.

When do Kaizer Chiefs play Sundowns?

Kaizer Chiefs host Mamelodi Sundowns at FNB Stadium on Saturday, 15 August, with kick-off scheduled for 15:00. The match will be televised on SABC 1 as well as SuperSport 2.
