World.title: Nick Reiner indicted on murder charges in parents' killings at their LA home
World.content:
Nick Reiner has been indicted on murder charges in the killings of his parents, Rob and Michele Reiner, inside their Brentwood home last year.

On Wednesday, Nick Reiner pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder with the special circumstance allegations of multiple murders and murder by means of lying in wait, the Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office said. He also faces a special allegation that he personally used a dangerous and deadly weapon, a knife.

The grand jury, which had been meeting in secret, returned the indictment on July 20. The grand jury indictment is a major step toward trial and allows prosecutors to skip California's preliminary hearing process, where evidence is publicly aired.

CBS LA has reached out to Nick Reiner's public defender, Kimberly Greene, and a representative for the family.

Rob, 78, and Michele, 70, were found dead inside their Brentwood home on Dec. 14 by their daughter, Romy Reiner, according to multiple sources. The LA County Medical Examiner's Office said the couple died of "multiple sharp force injuries."

"This was a profound betrayal by someone who was loved and trusted by the very people he is accused of killing," District Attorney Nathan Hochman said. "The indictment unsealed today also adds a special circumstance allegation that the defendant committed the murders by means of lying in wait. We hope that by having a grand jury return an indictment in this case it will bring us one step closer to a trial and achieving justice."

The couple married in 1989 and had three children: sons Nick and Jake and daughter Romy.

Rob Reiner rose to fame for his role as Archie Bunker's son-in-law, Michael Stivic, better known as "Meathead" on CBS' "All in the Family." He won two Emmy Awards for the role.

He also made a name for himself in the film world, directing some of Hollywood's biggest movies such as "The Princess Bride," "When Harry Met Sally…," "A Few Good Men," "Stand by Me" and "This is Spinal Tap."

Michele Reiner was a successful photographer who took the photo of President Trump used on the cover of his book "The Art of the Deal," according to Variety.

The night before the killings, the Reiners attended a party at Conan O'Brien's, where Rob and Nick Reiner had a brief but loud argument, sources who were at the party told CBS News.

On the day the couple was found dead, they had plans with their longtime friends Michelle Obama and former President Barack Obama, according to the former first lady.

If convicted on the charges, Nick Reiner faces death or life in state prison without the possibility of parole, the DA's Office said. The decision on whether the prosecutors will seek the death penalty will be made at a later date.

He remains in custody with no bail. His pretrial hearing is scheduled for Sept. 15.

The Associated Press contributed to his report.

World.title: New indictment alleges Nick Reiner was lying in wait before killing his parents
World.content:
New indictment alleges Nick Reiner was lying in wait before killing his parents

toggle caption Evan Agostini/Invision via AP

LOS ANGELES — A Los Angeles County grand jury has indicted Nick Reiner on murder charges in the killings of his parents, Rob Reiner and Michele Singer Reiner, and adds the allegation that he was lying in wait before attacking them.

The grand jury, which had been meeting in secret, returned the indictment on July 20, and it was unsealed Wednesday, when 32-year-old Nick Reiner entered a not guilty plea.

Rob Reiner, a director, actor and Hollywood luminary, and his wife, a photographer and producer, were stabbed to death in their home in the upscale Brentwood section of Los Angeles on Dec. 14. Nick Reiner was arrested within hours and charged two days later.

The grand jury indictment is a major step toward trial and allows prosecutors to skip California's preliminary hearing process, where evidence is publicly aired.

Lying in wait means a suspect waited for or hid from victims in order to ambush them, and as an allegation it's meant to show premeditation. A finding that he was lying in wait along with a murder conviction would make Reiner eligible for the death penalty, but prosecutors said they haven't decided whether to seek it.

Sponsor Message

"This was a profound betrayal by someone who was loved and trusted by the very people he is accused of killing," Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said in a statement. "We hope that by having a grand jury return an indictment in this case it will bring us one step closer to a trial and achieving justice."

Unsealed indictment gives few new details in secrecy-shrouded case

Prosecutors have said nothing about possible motives, and leaks in the case have been virtually nonexistent on both sides.

The Los Angeles County chief medical examiner told The Associated Press he would like to make their autopsy reports public, but a court order has prevented him from doing so.

The unsealed indictment reveals few new details in a case that has been shrouded in secrecy. It does not explain how or why Reiner was lying in wait. Without elaborating, prosecutors have said since December that the parents were stabbed. The indictment includes a special allegation of use of a deadly weapon — a knife — that could also contribute to a stiffer sentence.

Indictment released as Nick Reiner seeks trust funds

The indictment comes as Reiner is seeking unpaid money from a trust his parents established for him, saying he needs it to help in his defense.

Sponsor Message

Reiner said in a court petition that the trustees who oversee the funds have denied them to him without legal justification. The money was to have gone to Nick Reiner even if his parents were alive, legal filings say. The petition says the trust has at least $1.5 million in assets, but trustees would not share the exact amount.

"Nick loved his parents, and he is devastated by their deaths. But the facts about what did and did not happen to them are not at issue," the petition says.

He is seeking to hire back high-profile criminal defense attorney Alan Jackson, who initially represented him before Reiner's siblings would no longer agree to fund his defense and a public defender took over.

A hearing on the petition is set for next week.

The LA County Public Defender's Office, which is representing Reiner, declined to comment on the indictment.

Grand jury process happens in secret

California prosecutors can charge a defendant and take the case through a preliminary hearing — a sort of trial in miniature where evidence is publicly aired and a judge decides whether it should be sent to trial — as recently happened with singer D4vd.

Or they can use a grand jury to go through the process in secret. They can also publicly file charges and later seek a secret grand jury indictment, essentially creating a new version of the case, as happened here and in the Los Angeles prosecution of Harvey Weinstein.

Rob Reiner had prolific career as actor and director

Rob Reiner began as an actor, starring in the TV sitcom, "All in the Family," as Michael "Meathead" Stivic, the liberal son-in-law to a much more conservative and bigoted Archie Bunker, played by Carroll O'Connor. Reiner won two Emmy Awards for the role, and last month got a posthumous Emmy nomination for his work as a guest star on "The Bear."

Sponsor Message

He became a prolific director whose work included some of the most memorable and endlessly watchable movies of the 1980s and '90s. His credits included "This is Spinal Tap," "Stand By Me," "A Few Good Men," and "When Harry Met Sally…" during the production of which he met photographer Michele Singer. They wed soon after and were married for 36 years.

Nick Reiner was the second of the three children they had together. He and his father co-wrote the script for the 2015 film "Being Charlie," which was partly based on the son's teenage struggles with addiction and homelessness.

His older brother Jake Reiner wrote in April that the experience of losing his parents and having his brother at the center of it was "a living nightmare" that is "too devastating to comprehend."

World.title: Controversial group wins $158M-contract to represent unaccompanied immigrant children
World.content:
Controversial group wins $158M-contract to represent unaccompanied immigrant children

toggle caption Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images North America

The Trump administration has awarded a controversial anti-human trafficking organization a no-bid $158 million contract to provide legal services to unaccompanied migrant children, according to a notice posted Friday by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.

Utah-based Our Rescue, previously known as Operation Underground Railroad, says it helps law enforcement perform sting operations to catch human traffickers and rescue survivors. It's unclear if it has immigration lawyers on its staff, although its website says it offers "legal support to help prosecute offenders." Our Rescue did not immediately return NPR's request for comment.

The group was founded by activist Tim Ballard, who was the subject of the 2023 film Sound of Freedom . The movie starring Jim Caviezel was heavily promoted in conservative media as QAnon conspiracies flourished.

Sponsor Message

Within months of the film's release, however, Ballard faced accusations of sexual exploitation himself. He has repeatedly denied them, but was quietly removed from the group. It's now headed by CEO Derek Benner , who previously worked for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement .

toggle caption Fred Hayes/Getty Images for Angel Studios

In a statement to NPR, the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR) said the contract will run for six months, from Aug. 7 to February 6, 2027. The agency said it is working with other providers besides Our Rescue, including the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants.

"ORR is committed to ensuring every (unaccompanied immigrant child) has legal representation in immigration court," an ORR spokesperson told NPR Wednesday.

Michael Lukens, the executive director of the nonprofit organization Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, on Wednesday blasted HHS's decision to award Our Rescue the contract.

His organization provided legal services to unaccompanied immigrant children under the previous contract.

"HHS is trying to give a contract to a nonprofit that is highly problematic in their history and has no expertise in providing legal services to unaccompanied children," Lukens told NPR. "This all to me boils down to children are going to be harmed and that seems to be the point of a lot of these actions."

There are currently about 24,000 immigrant children in the U.S. who are classified by the federal government as unaccompanied, but only 1,800 are in custody of HHS . The agency defines them as minors who have no lawful immigration status in the U.S. and who have "no parent or legal guardian in the U.S. available to provide care and physical custody."

Sponsor Message

The contract with Our Rescue was granted a week after a contract with a group of nearly 100 legal nonprofits to do similar work expired on July 31 . The expiration left attorneys scrambling to figure out how to ensure the minors continued to have legal representation.

In a statement to NPR, ORR said it has been using the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants (USCRI) to provide legal representation to all unaccompanied immigrant children in ORR care since Aug. 5. That organization will provide legal services until Dec. 31.

But that's not a solution, Lukens said.

"HHS is causing chaos in the system, and that may be on purpose," Lukens said. "They let a contract expire. They don't have any long term contract in place. They're trying to do these sort of gap-fillers while also reaching out to unqualified organizations about serving the children."

Lukens said Amica Center for Immigrant Rights and other nonprofits continue providing legal representation for their unaccompanied minor clients despite not being paid. He said it is the only way to ensure continuity in legal representation for the minors.

The Trump administration had stopped paying the legal nonprofits — including Lukens' back in November, when lawyers refused to turn over confidential information about the children they represented.

Lukens said that information was covered by attorney-client privilege, and that the nonprofits decided to not apply for a new contract because of those concerns.

Trump administration chooses organizations with GOP ties

This latest development builds on a pattern of granting contracts to people with administration ties.

Our Rescue's current CEO Derek Benner served as executive director of the Department of Homeland Security's Homeland Security Investigations during the first Trump administration.

Last week, the administration posted a notice on the federal registry announcing its intent to give Burke Law Group, a small Texas law firm, up to $150 million to represent unaccompanied immigrant children in government custody.

Sponsor Message

However, Burke Law Group withdrew from the process and will no longer get the contact after NPR and other news outlets reported on its ties to the Trump administration and lack of experience in immigration matters.

A co-founder of Burke Law Group, Marcella Burke, served in the first Trump administration in both the Interior Department and the Environmental Protection Agency. Jeffrey Hall, a founding partner, currently serves as an assistant administrator at the EPA.

In a post on X Tuesday, Burke Law Group said they "were approached by the Trump administration to fill a gap in legal services and we were considering how we might help." But, the firm said it had "decided not to apply for a grant or a contract" with the U.S. Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR).

A spokesperson with ORR confirmed Burke Law Group's decision. The agency told NPR it had intended to enter into a cooperative agreement with the law firm, which the agency said had "a strong geographic presence in Texas."

But the Houston-based company specializes in advising "companies on complex environmental, regulatory, and enforcement matters," according to its website. Only two of the firm's 24 attorneys specialize in immigration and asylum cases.

World.title: White House press secretary leaving
World.content:
White House press secretary leaving

toggle caption SAUL LOEB/AFP via Getty Images

White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt is leaving her role at the end of the month to spend more time with family, President Trump said Wednesday.

She will continue to be an outside adviser, he added.

"Our wonderful White House Press Secretary, and one of my most trusted aides, Karoline Leavitt, will be departing her role at the end of the month so she can spend more time with her beautiful young children and family, a decision I totally understand and respect!," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Leavitt, 28, was the youngest ever White House press secretary. She recently returned from parental leave after the birth of her second child in May.

Sponsor Message

"The truth is since returning to the White House after the birth of my daughter, I have felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy, and attention required of the White House Press Secretary — and that is why I have ultimately made the bittersweet decision to depart the White House and embark on a new chapter in my life," she said on social media.

Leavitt's departure comes as the president, and his party, are struggling with voters who disapprove of his handling of the economy and high prices amid the Iran war.

In his post, Trump said Leavitt would still be an "influential voice" for the GOP.

Leavitt first started working for Trump in his first administration in 2020 and left shortly before his term ended. She later made an unsuccessful run for Congress in her home state of New Hampshire. Later, she went on to work for Trump's super PAC before working for Trump's 2024 campaign.

It's not yet clear who will replace her; several Cabinet secretaries filled in for Leavitt while she was on parental leave.

At the podium, Leavitt was often confrontational with the press corps, criticizing some outlets for what she described as bias. She was a staunch defender of Trump's policies even on issues such as denying the results of the 2020 election, which Trump continues to falsely say he won.

Sponsor Message

The start of her tenure also came with mounting tensions with the press corps. After The Associated Press refused to call the Gulf of Mexico the "Gulf of America," their reporters lost access to White House events and inclusion in travel with the president as part of the traveling press corps. New media outlets, many with coverage that supports the president's agenda, were included in the briefing room and on Air Force One.

Press access to Leavitt and other senior communication officials were also cut last October. Journalists used to be able to walk into the area called "upper press" but now an appointment is required.

Trump would often compliment Leavitt at events at the White House, calling her a "superstar."

During a meeting at the White House with Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán in November, Trump joked that the prime minister wanted Leavitt to work for him in Hungary.

"That's a very good decision you just made," Trump said to Orbán, before turning to Leavitt. "Please don't leave us, Karoline."

World.title: Inflation eases in July as gasoline and grocery prices fall
World.content:
Inflation eases in July as gasoline and grocery prices fall

toggle caption Justin Sullivan/Getty Images North America

Inflation cooled a bit last month as gasoline and grocery prices fell.

Consumer prices in July were up 3.4% from a year ago, according to a report Wednesday from the Labor Department. That's a smaller annual increase than in May or June.

Loading...

Prices rose just 0.1% between June and July, after falling 0.4% between May and June. Rising rents and airfares last month were partially offset by falling prices for gasoline and groceries.

Lettuce prices plunged more than 16% in July after an outbreak of food-borne illness prompted a recall of iceberg lettuce from Mexico. Retailers offered deep discounts on other lettuce varieties in hopes of wooing anxious shoppers.

Gasoline prices also dropped in July, although the average price of regular gas is still more than a dollar a gallon higher than before the war with Iran snarled tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, according to AAA.

Stripping out volatile food and energy prices, "core inflation" was 2.5% for the 12 months ending in July. That's down from 2.6% in June. Easing inflation will be welcome news for the Federal Reserve, which has promised to bring price hikes under control.

Investors think the relatively tame inflation report will make it less likely the central bank feels the need to raise interest rates when policymakers meet next month.

Sponsor Message

Market odds of a September rate hike fell to about 40% after Wednesday's cost-of-living report, although there will be another inflation report before policymakers gather again next month.

World.title: Woman behind petition to oust U.S ambassador says response is 'beyond what I expected'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The woman behind a petition calling for U.S. President Donald Trump's representative in Ottawa to be kicked out of the country says it's grown beyond her expectations.

The online petition, which is set to be presented in the House of Commons in the fall, says Pete Hoekstra should be declared persona non grata and the Canadian government should request his removal as U.S. ambassador to Canada.

More than 70,000 people had signed the petition as of Wednesday evening, approximately double the number of signatures 24 hours earlier.

"It's beyond what I expected out of this," said Lee Walker, the Calgary-based woman behind the petition, in an email to CBC News.

"It tells me that it's not a fringe issue, and that a lot of Canadians are uncomfortable with how Hoekstra has been repeating Trump talking points about our sovereignty and Canada as a whole."

Walker's petition accuses Hoekstra of making statements that undermine the Canada-U.S. diplomatic relationship and of "making repeated interventions in Canadian political discourse inconsistent with diplomatic protocol."

The petition also says Hoekstra has normalized the Trump administration's threats to annex Canada. The ambassador made headlines in June after saying that Canada's annexation by the United States would be a great topic of discussion for Prime Minister Mark Carney and U.S. President Donald Trump.

Walker said comments like that from an ambassador aren't appropriate.

"Words from someone in his position carry immense weight, and normalizing that kind of rhetoric can have real consequences," she said.

Hoekstra has also said it's dangerous for Canadian political leaders to describe the Trump administration's ongoing tariff campaign as a trade war and has criticized Canadian politicians who have responded to the tariffs by discouraging travel to the U.S. and for pulling American liquor off of shelves.

'Turmoil already exists'

The petition also calls on the Liberal government to direct a parliamentary committee to review U.S. diplomatic interference in Canadian affairs.

A spokesperson for the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa declined to comment on the petition except to say the embassy is aware of it.

When asked about the potential impact the petition could have amid sensitive trade talks between the U.S. and Canada, Walker said there's already tension between the two countries.

"The turmoil already exists. It's just one-sided right now," she said.

Walker said her intention is to make clear " that respect for Canada and its sovereignty isn't optional or up for negotiation."

Canadian and American negotiators have been going back and forth in recent weeks in an effort to reach some sort of deal before Aug. 19, which is when Trump has promised a 50 per cent levy on hundreds of Canadian goods in addition to the sectoral tariffs already in place.

WATCH | More about the petition: Canadian petition calls to expel U.S. ambassador | Duration 0:34 Nearly 30,000 Canadians have signed a petition calling for U.S. President Donald Trump's representative in Ottawa to be kicked out of the country. The online petition accuses Ambassador Pete Hoekstra of making statements that undermine the Canada-U.S. diplomatic relationship.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc has been in Washington to meet with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer three times in as many weeks. CBC News previously reported that the two are aiming to present Trump with a path to a potential trade deal as early as Monday.

The petition will be presented in Parliament by Green Party Leader Elizabeth May in the fall. Members of Parliament can table petitions in the House of Commons without endorsing their contents.

As for what she wants to happen once it's presented, Walker said she's not sure the government will take steps to declare Hoekstra persona non grata, but hopes the petition will send a message.

"This sort of conduct from a sitting ambassador isn't something we'll just shrug off," she said.

World.title: 4 ex-Western University students accused in London, Ont., explosives-making scheme face 19 new charges
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The four people accused in a London, Ont., explosives and firearms-manufacturing investigation now face 19 new charges, according to court documents filed Tuesday.

Jerry Tong, Zekun (Alex) Wang, Fei (Frank) Han and Feiyang (Astrid) Ji were charged in January. All four were students or recent graduates of Western University, with the three men having studied in the engineering department.

The amended list of charges filed with the Ontario Court of Justice brings the total to 31 separate counts. Some of the charges are joint counts against all four, while others pertain to the specific accused.

The newest charges include possession of five specific explosive substances, possession of stolen property and access to computer data related to making firearms.

The lengthy investigation dates back to Jan. 24, when police responded to an overnight trespassing call at Western after two men entered one of the school's engineering buildings.

One person was arrested just outside the building. An investigation led police to a house in the nearby University Heights neighbourhood, where the other three were taken into custody.

Police spent days investigating inside the residence at 212 Chesham Place in London. (Alessio Donnini/CBC)

Police completed a multi-day search of the residence at 212 Chesham Place, where Wang, Han and Ji lived, as well as two additional homes in Orléans, in suburban Ottawa, and Gatineau, Que.

Firearms charges in other cities

When they were first arrested, the four faced multiple firearms charges, including the manufacturing of a handgun and possession of a loaded restricted handgun.

New charges against Tong, Wang and Ji include the possession of magazines and suppression devices, as well as possession of another prohibited firearm. Tong and Wang are also now accused of handing and carelessly storing a rifle.

Tong, who faces the majority of charges, also has new counts related to events in other cities. He's been charged with storing rifles at a home in Orleans, manufacturing a prohibited firearm in Ottawa and possessing a rifle at an unauthorized location in Quebec.

Court documents show that Tong held a firearms licence, but some of his charges relate to possessing a firearm at a place not indicated on his licence.

WATCH | How this Ontario home became the centre of a national security probe: How this Ontario home became the centre of a national security probe | Duration 2:14 Four people are in custody after police discovered chemicals they say could be used to create explosives at a home in London, Ont. But, new information shows the suspects were working on developing an anti-drone weapon system. Here’s what we know so far.

Tong and Wang also face new charges related to events that happened months before they were arrested.

Wang is now charged with manufacturing a weapon between Sept. 1, 2025, and Jan. 24, 2026, while the pair are charged with breaking into a Western building on Oct. 9, 2025.

Explosive substances revealed

Court documents also show that Tong, Wang, Han and Ji face a new list of charges for possessing explosive substances, and names them for the first time.

They are accused of possessing pentaerythritol tetranitrate (PETN), trinitrotoluene (TNT), dinitrophenol (DNP), hexamethylene triperoxide diamine (HMTD) and lead azide.

Originally, all four were charged with possession of precursor substances and finished high explosives.

London police are seen outside the home at 212 Chesham Place on Feb. 2. (Alessio Donnini/CBC)

All four also face a new count of possessing property of Western University valued at less than $5,000.

Wang faces a solo charge of accessing computer data that pertains to a firearm or a prohibited device, specifically, design files capable of being used with a 3D printer, metal milling machine or similar computer system for the purpose of manufacturing a device.

2 out on bail, 2 in custody

In total, these are the number of charges each accused faces:

Tong: 28.

Wang: 20.

Han: 11.

Ji: 13.

The four are still making their way through the courts, with two out on bail and two still in custody.

Tong did not request bail and remains in custody. Han was denied bail and remanded back into custody in February.

Wang was granted bail in March under strict conditions, including 24-hour house arrest and constant supervision from two sureties, who each posted $200,000. Ji is also out on bail with no sureties.

World.title: Canada, U.S. not yet ready to make tariff deal, Canada unsatisfied with latest U.S. offer: sources
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As the clock ticks toward U.S. President Donald Trump's latest tariff deadline, Canada and the U.S. aren't at a point where a tariff deal can be reached — and Canadian officials are not satisfied with the latest U.S. offer, according to two sources with knowledge of the trade talks.

According to sources on both sides of the border, the Americans offered a new proposal on Tuesday which would lower some of the sectoral tariffs but not to the degree that the Canadian side would like to see. CBC News is not naming the sources because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

Negotiators have been going back and forth in recent weeks in an effort to reach some sort of deal before Aug. 19, which is when Trump has promised a 50 per cent levy on hundreds of Canadian goods in addition to the sectoral tariffs already in place.

The Americans are seeking a deal that would see preferential access to Canadian critical minerals and cover security and energy, the sources said.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc has been in Washington to meet with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer three times in as many weeks. CBC News previously reported that the two are aiming to present Trump with a path to a potential trade deal as early as Monday.

Sources told CBC News last week that the Canadian side has aggressively argued to the Americans that there would be no political appetite among Canadians to keep talks going if the Aug. 19 tariffs come into place.

Both sides have agreed to hold daily meetings at various levels up until that deadline, the sources said.

WATCH | New pitch for Trump in the works: Canada-U.S. trade reps working on new pitch for Trump | Duration 2:22 CBC News has learned Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer are working on a proposal to pitch to U.S. President Donald Trump before a tariff deadline that could see hundreds of Canadian goods hit with a 50 per cent levy.

Neither LeBlanc nor Canada's chief trade negotiator, Janice Charette, answered reporters' questions after they were seen leaving Greer's office on Tuesday afternoon.

LeBlanc later posted to X saying that discussions are "ongoing" and he and Charette will "continue to engage at the negotiation table."

LeBlanc's office told CBC News he and Charette remain in Washington as of Wednesday night.

In addition to trying to dissuade Americans from levying new tariffs, LeBlanc and Charette are looking for relief on tariffs the U.S. has slapped on Canadian steel, aluminum, lumber and autos.

Canada is also hoping the ongoing trade talks between the two countries will result in a renewal of the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) after the Trump administration last month declined to extend the deal past 2036.

WATCH | Canada not satisfied with latest U.S. trade offer, sources say: Canada rejects latest U.S. trade offer days before tariff deadline | Duration 1:48 One week before new 50 per cent tariffs on billions in Canadian goods are set to kick in, Canada has rejected the latest U.S. counter-offer on a trade deal, sources tell CBC News.

When announcing the Aug. 19 tariffs, the U.S. raised a number of trade irritants, including Canada's retaliation against U.S. trade policy with the removal of U.S. alcohol from provincial store shelves and alleged Canadian discrimination against U.S. motor vehicles and dairy.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre wrote to Carney on Sunday, calling on him to show some "backbone" as trade negotiations ramp up.

Poilievre said Canadians deserve a "good deal" that includes zero tariffs on softwood lumber, an end to sectoral tariffs on steel and aluminum, a tariff-free auto pact and full exemption to Buy America rules on infrastructure projects at all levels of government.

"No more pursuing policies of a managed decline at home. No more caving," Poilievre wrote.

Industry sources previously told CBC News that Canada is preparing to meet some U.S. demands — including ending the booze bans — in exchange for tariff relief.

World.title: Why this American doctor is leaving Utah to serve a remote community in B.C.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

American physician Leo Bay and his family are busy boxing up their belongings and getting ready to leave their home in Utah.

"It's a big move, but it's an exciting move," Bay said.

They've decided to move to Canada where Bay will work as a family doctor on the Sunshine Coast.

When he, his wife and their three children first got off the ferry to visit Pender Harbour, they knew instantly it was where they wanted to live.

"We fell in love with the Sunshine Coast," Bay said.

The Bay family has been living in a rural area of Utah and believes the transition to the Sunshine Coast should be smooth as they enjoy the outdoors. (Pender Harbour Health Centre)

Bay has been practising medicine for eight years and has worked with remote communities as the associate chief medical information officer for Wisconsin, Minnesota, and North Dakota.

At the end of August, he starts at the Pender Harbour Health Centre providing care to 1,000 people in the remote B.C. coastal community.

"The opportunity to be able to live and work in that community is so exciting and so meaningful," Bay said.

Why Canada?

Bay said he's looking forward to focusing on patient care.

"I think that there are lots of things within the U.S. health system that as a primary care doctor we struggle with," he said. "Insurances in the U.S. only cover very limited portions of things or have very strict restrictions."

The idea of coming to Canada five years ago would have been disruptive, he said, and felt impossible.

B.C.’s Ministry of Health said that more than 2,900 job applications have been received from U.S. health-care workers and physicians as of March 2026. (Pender Harbour Health Centre)

Back in July 2025, the College of Physicians and Surgeons of B.C. implemented bylaw changes that help U.S.-trained doctors become fully licensed in B.C. without the need for further assessment, examination or training if they hold certification from the American Board of Medical Specialties, American Board of Family Medicine or the American Osteopathic Board of Family Physicians.

B.C.'s Ministry of Health launched a $5-million digital advertising blitz in June 2025, targeting health workers in Washington state, Oregon and California. Ads have also been running in U.S. academic publications through September.

"Seeing the programs that were available, that really made a difference in making it feel like something that was feasible," Bay said.

Nick Gaskin, executive director at the Pender Harbour Health Centre, said a community member donated $105,000 to the clinic so renovations could be done, which he said helped bring in the new American doctors. (Pender Harbour Health Centre)

According to the Ministry of Health, more than 580 U.S. health-care workers, including 270 physicians, have accepted job offers in communities throughout B.C. as of March 2026.

"B.C. now has the most doctors per capita in Canada with more than 15,000 physicians, an increase of 23 per cent from 2017 to 2024," said the ministry.

4 new doctors to Sunshine Coast

At the Pender Harbour Health Centre, Bay will be in the company of a fellow American who also moved to Canada.

Dr. Derek Williams, who has been practising medicine for 25 years, moved from Montana earlier this year.

Nick Gaskin, executive director at the centre, said they only had one part-time physician serving 500 people before the two new physicians joined.

Pender Harbour Health Centre recently underwent a $300,000 renovation to the primary care wing that was made possible through donations from the community, according to Gaskin. (Pender Harbour Health Centre)

"To have 2,000 members of our community attached to physicians at this clinic is going to be fantastic," Gaskin said.

The remote nature of the community has posed a challenge to attract and retain physicians over the years, he said.

"I think the political landscape certainly makes a difference. I also think that we live in a different world right now where people are moving around," Gaskin said.

Two other doctors have also moved to the Sunshine Coast — one from Ohio and another from the U.K. — and a nurse practitioner will soon be arriving.

WATCH | 400 doctors, nurses have relocated from U.S. to B.C. in last year: 400 doctors, nurses have relocated from U.S. to B.C. in last year | Duration 2:05



Lyndsay Montina, the executive director of Sunshine Coast Division of Family Practice, said there has long been a doctor shortage in B.C.

"We've had some people that have been waiting for a family care provider for quite a long time, and so being able to have these new providers come, it's awesome," Montina said.

People who are looking for a family physician can visit the Health Connect registry.

World.title: B.C. premier promises review of emergency response to wildfire near Summerland, B.C.
World.content:
Eby says there are 'lessons to be learned' after fast-moving fire overwhelmed authorities

B.C. premier says lessons to be taken from how quickly wildfire spread | Duration 2:58

B.C. Premier David Eby offered condolences and praised the work of volunteers at a wildfire update on Wednesday in Penticton, B.C., where many evacuees have fled. He also pledged a review of the emergency response, saying there is 'an important set of lessons to take' about how fast the Bald Range fire blew up and that 'this may be our new normal.'

World.title: White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt to leave job at month's end, Trump says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt will step down at the end of the month, U.S. President Donald Trump announced Wednesday. The 28-year-old recently returned to the White House after taking leave following the birth of her second child.

White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt will leave her role at the end of the ‌month, U.S. President Donald Trump said Wednesday, leaving the president without one of his most trusted advisers ahead of November's midterm elections.

Leavitt will be an outside communications adviser and party operative shaping the future contours of Trump's "Make America Great Again" movement, she and Trump said in statements.

In a social media post, Leavitt, 28, said ​she aimed to spend more time with her young children. She gave ​birth to a daughter, her second child, in May and recently returned from maternity leave.

"Karoline has been a real leader in the White House, and has done a phenomenal job fighting for Justice, Liberty, and Freedom, ​since 2018, including our Historic Re-Election Campaign of 2024," Trump said in a social media post, ⁠calling Leavitt "one of the best ⁠White House Press Secretaries in the History of the Office."

Leavitt called ‌her role at the White House "the honor and adventure of a lifetime."

White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt and U.S. President Donald Trump are seen attending the White House Correspondents' Association dinner at the Waldorf Astoria in Washington, D.C., last month. (Mandel Ngan/AFP/Getty Images)

Leavitt joined Trump's 2024 ⁠campaign ⁠and ​served as transition spokesperson before Trump selected ​her to ⁠be White House press secretary. She was the youngest person to be appointed to the role.

Trump did not outline plans for who might replace her in the high-profile job.

Leavitt 'spoke Trump fluently'

"Few could or will ever compare to Karoline," said ⁠Harrison Fields, Trump's former principal deputy press secretary.

"She's someone who not only spoke Trump fluently, she knew how to feed the media beast in a cunning, audacious and successful way that, most importantly, played to her audience: the president."

Trump is seen speaking with reporters at Joint Base Andrews, in Maryland, on Tuesday, as Leavitt stands nearby. (Mark Schiefelbein/The Associated Press)

In her year and a half on the ‌job, Leavitt and White House communications director Steven Cheung transformed the administration's posture toward the media — in ways that some of Trump's allies cheered and free press advocates criticized.

The Trump administration began hand-picking which journalists receive access to the president, jettisoning the long-running system set up by the independent White House Correspondents' Association.

The press pool was traditionally a ​rotation chosen by the industry group to ensure media outlets had uniform access to the president and could relay his activities to the public and to other journalists who ⁠could not attend smaller gatherings.

As part of that process, the Trump administration press office created a special "new media" seat in the briefing ⁠room that gave podcasts, newsletters and fledgling digital outlets a more prominent role in covering the presidency.

Some press advocates hailed ⁠the move ⁠as a recognition of the changing media landscape. ​Others criticized it as a lever the administration could use to reward outlets whose coverage it saw as favourable.

World.title: McIntosh takes silver in women's 200m freestyle; Tierney wins 100m backstroke gold at Pan Pacs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Toronto's Summer McIntosh opened her race schedule at the Pan Pacific swimming championships Wednesday night with a second-place finish outdoors in the women's 200-metre freestyle in Irvine, Calif.

The 19-year-old, competing at the event for the first time, touched the wall in one minute 53.86 seconds, nearly 2-10ths behind Australia's Lani Pallister, who clocked a championship record 1:53.67. Erika Fairweather of New Zealand was third, covering four lengths of the pool at William Woollett Jr. Aquatics Center in 1:55.05.

"She hasn't raced the [200 free often] because she's been so busy breaking world records in all the other [events]. She's so good that you're not going to keep Summer McIntosh down," said CBC Sports analyst Byron MacDonald. "She's got the ability to get better and better. She'll learn from this."

Pallister led McIntosh by 4-100ths of a second after 50 metres but the Canadian grabbed the lead through 100 by 12-100ths. McIntosh tried to maintain the advantage through 150 metres but Pallister went ahead by 9-100ths.

"She tried to make a move on the third length but couldn't pull away. Pallister was having nothing to do with it," MacDonald said. "Summer hasn't raced [the 200] at a big meet since 2023 [and] didn't execute the way she wanted.

WATCH | McIntosh swims to silver in 200m freestyle final: Summer McIntosh wins silver in women’s 200m freestyle at Pan Pacs | Duration 5:44 Summer McIntosh captured the silver medal in the women’s 200-metre freestyle, finishing in 1:53.86, just behind Australia’s Lani Pallister, who won gold in 1:53.67, at the 2026 Pan Pacific Swimming Championships in Irvine, Calif.

"In 2023, she was expected to win at the world championships, was [dealt an upset loss by Australia's Mollie O'Callaghan and Ariarne Titmus] and that was a learning lesson, and she got better. Now, she's going to have to learn from this one."

Before Wednesday, McIntosh hadn't raced the 200 free on the international stage since the 2023 world championships.

"Training for 200 freestyle kind of naturally worked into my training schedule on a weekly basis because I'm a 400 freestyler," she told CBC Sports' Devin Heroux this week. "It just kind of matches with events perfectly, to be honest."

McIntosh, who opted not to race the 200 butterfly on Wednesday, will also swim the 200 individual medley, 400 free and 400 IM in Irvine.

She qualified for the 200 free final in 1:55.85 after mentioning this week she would like to stop the clock in 1:52. The retired Titmus has held the world record of 1:52.23 since the Australian Olympics trials on June 12, 2024.

WATCH | McIntosh breaks down silver-winning 200m free race: Summer McIntosh has 'more to give' after silver medal finish in 200m freestyle | Duration 0:51 Summer McIntosh touched the wall behind Lani Pallister of Australia for a silver medal in the 200m Free at the 2026 Pan Pacific Swimming Championships.

McIntosh holds four individual long-course (50m pool) world marks in the 200 butterfly, 200 IM, 400 free and 400 IM.

At the beginning of July, she took down the longest-standing women's world record at the Canadian trials in the 200 fly, dating to 2009. A day after that momentous swim in Montreal, McIntosh pulled out of the trials due to illness.

She has spent the past few weeks recovering and building toward Pan Pacs and says she's in full health.

In the women's 200 free consolation final, Brooklyn Douthwright of Riverview, N.B., was seventh in a field of eight in 1:58.86, one spot ahead of Edmonton's Emma O'Croinin (1:58.93).

Blake Tierney wins gold

In the men's 100m backstroke, it was Saskatoon's Blake Tierney who came out on top.

The 24-year-old leveraged a strong finish to take gold in a time of 53.18 seconds, edging out Will Modglin (53.37) and Jack Aikins (53.46).

WATCH | Tierney takes gold in men's 100m backstroke: Blake Tierney earns gold in the men’s 100m backstroke at Pan Pacs | Duration 5:00 Blake Tierney claimed Canada’s 1st gold medal of the 2026 Pan Pacific Swimming Championships, winning the men’s 100-metre backstroke in 53.18 seconds in Irvine, Calif.

"I don't know if I can really take it all in right now ... I think looking back I'll definitely be happy with it," Tierney told CBC Sports' Devin Heroux after the race.

"Not the best time or anything, but pretty close. I think I got the closing speed. I don't know what I split but still a lot of work I can do.

It is the first international gold medal of Tierney's career.

"I had a good year of training. Training pays off," Tierney said.

Tierney is the Canadian record holder in the event with a best-time of 52.95.

WATCH | Tierney discusses gold-medal winning race at Pan Pacs: Blake Tierney talks 'closing speed' after winning gold at 2026 Pan Pacific Swimming Championships | Duration 1:31 100m backstroke winner Tierney joins Devin Heroux to talk about his gold medal and what he learned about himself Wednesday in California at the 2026 Pan Pacific Swimming Championships.

Ruck races to 2 bronze

Taylor Ruck kicked off the Canadian medal count with a third-place finish in the women's 50m butterfly final.

The 26-year-old from Kelowna touched the wall in a time of 25.23 seconds to win bronze and set a Canadian record.

Ruck lowered her previous Canadian record, set in the prelims, taking off four tenths from her time of 25.61 on Thursday morning.

WATCH | Ruck earns 50m butterfly bronze: Taylor Ruck wins bronze in the women’s 50-metre butterfly at the Pan Pacific Swimming Championships | Duration 3:57 Taylor Ruck swam to a bronze medal in the women’s 50-metre butterfly, clocking 25.23 seconds to set another Canadian record and earn Canada’s first medal at the 2026 Pan Pacific Swimming Championships in Irvine, Calif.

She placed behind Americans Kate Douglass (25.06), who won silver, and Gretchen Walsh, whose 24.65 time was a championship record.

Later in the competition, the four-time Olympic medallist added another bronze in the 100m backstroke final.

Ruck swam to a time of 58.40, placing behind Americans Katharine Berkoff (57.93) and winner Regan Smith (58.11).

"I think the energy was just there. I had a good talk with my coach beforehand and yeah I just felt, felt like the energy was just getting channelled right," Ruck told CBC Sports after the backstroke final.

"I had a lot of fun with it too and uh found the competition to just yea, get things right."

WATCH | Ruck adds 2nd bronze of the day in 100m backstroke final: Taylor Ruck wins another bronze in women’s 100m backstroke at Pan Pacs | Duration 5:38 Taylor Ruck won her 2nd medal at the 2026 Pan Pacific Swimming Championships in Irvine, Calif., swimming to bronze in the women’s 100-metre backstroke in 58.40 seconds.

Canada wins 4x100 medley relay bronze

To cap the evening, the 4x100 medley relay team of Ruck, Ingrid Wilm, Oliver Dawson and Finlay Knox rounded out the podium with bronze.

The quartet finished with a final time of 3:43.22.

Winning gold in the event was the United States team of Will Modglin, Van Mathias, Gretchen Walsh and Kate Douglass, who raced to a world-record time of 3:36.70.

Australia's team of Iona Anderson, Samuel Williamson , Matthew Temple and Meg Harris came in second with a time of 3:39.30.

World.title: Hockey Canada suspensions remain for four 2018 world junior players acquitted in sex assault trial
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An independent appeal board has ruled that five players from Canada's 2018 world junior team acquitted last year of sexual assault breached the Hockey Canada code of conduct.

Hockey Canada said in a release Wednesday that it accepted the board's recommended continued suspensions and reinstatement dates for Alex Formenton, Cal Foote, Carter Hart, Dillon Dube and Michael McLeod.

The five were acquitted in July 2025 on sexual assault charges stemming from an encounter with a woman known as "E.M." at a 2018 Hockey Canada gala in London, Ont., celebrating the national junior team's world championship gold medal.

But the three-judge appeal board — John Laskin, Katherine Swinton and Thomas McEwen — recommended continued suspensions from Hockey Canada-sanctioned programs for four of the players.

Reinstatement dates vary

McLeod will not be eligible for reinstatement until Nov. 10, 2030. Foote will be eligible on Nov. 10, while Hart and Dube will be eligible on that day in 2027 and 2028, respectively.

Formenton is eligible for immediate reinstatement.

Hockey Canada says all other players from the 2018 team are eligible for consideration to participate in any Hockey Canada-sanctioned program, effective immediately.

The suspended players, who all had NHL careers before the charges were filed, have been eligible to sign with NHL teams since Oct. 15 and able to play since Dec. 1.

Where are the five players now?

Hart signed with the Vegas Golden Knights and helped them reach this year's Stanley Cup final.

Dube became the second of the five to find NHL work when he signed with St. Louis on July 1.

McLeod played last season with Omsk Avangard of the Kontinental Hockey League.

Foote played last season with the American Hockey League's Chicago Wolves and recently had a one-year contract with Farjestad BK rescinded when the Swedish club received criticism for the signing.

Formenton has spent the last three seasons playing in Switzerland.

When it became public in 2022 that Hockey Canada had settled a lawsuit with the woman out of court, Canada's sport minister at the time, Pascale St. Onge, ordered a forensic audit to ensure to public funds were not used in the settlement, and froze federal funding to the organization for almost a year.

Accountability remains a priority

Hockey Canada executives were grilled by MPs on Parliament Hill on how it handled the situation.

"We take note of the independent appeal board's findings today, including that all five players were in breach of the Hockey Canada Code of Conduct," Adam van Koeverden, Canada's current secretary of sport, said Wednesday in a statement. "This case started a national conversation about safe sport and the problematic culture in men's hockey. It is the voices of women and survivors, and the courage and bravery it takes to come forward, that have led to changes we are seeing in toxic culture."

"Since 2022, important progress has been made at Hockey Canada to address long-standing systemic failures. Hockey Canada has since become a full signatory to the Canadian Safe Sport Program, with continued commitments to a culture of change."

"Canada's sport system must prioritize the safety and well-being of everyone involved. National sport organizations must be held accountable as they progress on implementing measures to prevent and address maltreatment, because we know that when safeguards are weak or absent, real harm occurs."

"Our government continues to closely monitor national sport organizations and the systemic changes they are undertaking to ensure a culture of safety, respect, and integrity across all sports."

World.title: Colombia asked US to carry out joint military operations: Hegseth
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella asked the US Government for joint military operations “to destroy terrorists and terror networks,” said US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth Wednesday.

At an event of the so-called Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (ACCC) in Panama, Hegseth said that “Colombia will join the ACCC, becoming the 19th member.”

Through the newly inaugurated president, as our president likes to say “President El Tigre,” Colombia has already requested that our department of war join Colombia in its fight against narcoterrorism. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth

Hegseth’s announcement was rejected by leftist opposition party Historic Pact, whose Senate chief Ivan Cepeda said that “the US citizen Abelardo de la Espriella wants to surrender our government, our territory and our sovereignty to the strategic interests of the United States.

Cepeda stressed that Colombia’s constitution allows only the Senate to permit the entry of foreign troops to the country.

Colombia’s sovereignty is not up for negotiation, it is not to be surrendered, and it cannot be subordinated to the military interests of any foreign power. To defend it is to defend the dignity of the nation, the independence of the Republic, and the right of the Colombian people to freely decide on their territory and their destiny. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Ahead of taking office on Friday, De la Espriella said that he would join US-led alliances that allegedly seek to combat drug trafficking.

In his inaugural speech, the president said he intends to “defeat, without truce, narco-terrorism and all criminal organizations that threaten the freedom of Colombia.”

The State Department last week announced that it would seek to send a $1 billion military aid package to Colombia to “support the De la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten US, Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity.”

World.title: Controversy in Colombia over refusal to allow foreign search and rescue teams
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella has been criticized over its refusal to accept foreign search and rescue workers in the crucial hours after Monday’s earthquake.

One of the first to raise the alarm was China’s ambassador to Bogota, Zhu Jingyang, who called on the government on Tuesday to “release the name of the official and his or her designated contact person to coordinate international aid for the earthquake victims.”

El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele said that he was told that Colombia’s “rescue teams, medical personnel, and other emergency responders are on the scene and handling the situation” and “they do not require personnel support.”

Mexico’s President Caudia Sheinbaum said that her government was waiting for approval to send a team of 225 rescue workers to look for survivors, but was waiting for a “formal invitation” from Bogota.

In a response to growing pressure, newspaper El Tiempo said Colombia didn’t need foreign search and rescue teams because “the country has 23 teams with personnel that is part of the global elite.”

The Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday evening that it had “called on the international community to provide support in addressing the emergency, in order to tackle the most severely affected areas and mitigate the disaster.”

But social leader Leonard Renteria from Buenaventura said Wednesday that “as of yesterday, we still didn’t know anything about the arrival of rescue workers” in the partially destroyed port city.

“On the streets, we’ve seen people from the neighborhoods with the firefighters and civil defense personnel,” Renteria posted on social media platform X.

Fifty hours after Monday’s disaster, the US Department of State said it had “mobilized urban search-and-rescue (USAR) technical teams from Fairfax County, Virginia, and Los Angeles County, California to support Colombia’s search and rescue efforts.”

With chances of finding people alive rapidly decreasing, pressure on the government to respond increased online.

“I would really like to know the technical reason for rejecting assistance from teams that specialize in this type of disaster. There are many affected areas and plenty of evidence of technical inadequacies,” said civil engineer Gina Villalobos on X.

According to opposition congresswoman Maria Fernanda Carrascal, “it was an ideological decision, they only wanted rescue workers from Israel and the United States to enter while the Mexicans have been ready since Monday.”

On Wednesday afternoon, newly appointed disaster response chief David Tamayo said the government would also allow search and rescue workers from Ecuador and El Salvador “that can guarantee the provision of search and rescue teams and that are recognized by their own governments as meeting international search and rescue standards.”

These teams would come to search for hundreds of people who are feared to be under the rubble of buildings that collapsed in the worst earthquake in 10 years.

World.title: West Colombia earthquake killed more than 227 people, say local authorities
World.content:
Local and regional authorities have said that at least 227 people were confirmed killed in Monday’s earthquake while search and rescue teams continue to look for survivors.

So far, 120 people were confirmed dead in Valle del Cauca where locals said that entire towns in the north of the province were all but destroyed by the 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck the Choco province on Monday.

In Cali, the capital of Valle del Cauca, rescue workers continued to look for survivors under the rubble of apartment buildings that collapsed. Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder imposed a curfew in the city after locals chased him away from a search and rescue operation.

Choco Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said that mayors from the capital Quibdo and 22 affected towns reported 14 deaths and 140 injuries.

Multiple parts of the western province have yet to be contacted, however, as the local energy and telephone grid were destroyed by the earthquake, said Cordoba.

In Pereira, a city located at only 60 kilometers of the earthquake’s epicenter, and the surrounding Risaralda province, at least 88 people had died and dozens were still missing.

All major cities in the coffee region, Choco and Valle del Cauca declared an emergency to deal with the hundreds of injured that required medical attention at one of the cities’ hospitals.

President Abelardo de la Espriella said Tuesday morning that the earthquake destroyed more than 5,000 homes and that 188 people were missing.

The National Army and fire brigades from across Colombia sent teams to the cities in the disaster area to help with local search and rescue missions.

The US Department of State said it had committed $15.5 million “in funding for emergency shelter, food, protection, and earthquake assessments” for Colombia.

The Chinese embassy in Bogota said that Chinese companies that operate in Colombia were “sending heavy equipment to the most affected areas of the earthquake, participating in rescue efforts and the clearing of debris, in order to rescue the affected population using all available means.”

World.title: Colombia declares national disaster after devastating earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella declared a national disaster and sent his ministers to the west of Colombia to coordinate rescue operations in response to a 7.4M earthquake.

Following an emergency meeting at disaster management agency UNGRD, De la Espriella said he would travel to Pereira, one of the worst hit cities, to further coordinate the government response.

Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara would coordinate rescue operations for the rest of the coffee region, the health and defense ministers would travel to the Choco and Transport Minister Elsa Noguera would coordinate efforts in Valle del Cauca from Cali.

De la Espriella canceled plans he had to visit La Guajira, a northern province that wasn’t affected by the earthquake.

Throughout the morning, local and regional media reported dozens of collapsed buildings in multiple cities in Valle del Cauca, the coffee region and Choco.

More than 110 people were killed and dozens were injured because of the earthquake, De la Espriella said at a press conference.

The earthquake damaged more than 1,500 homes and destroyed 37. Sixty-one buildings collapsed and 18 healthcare centers suffered damage as well as 52 schools and 17 community centers.

The roof of the Pereira airport also came down and five other airports in western Colombia reported damages, said the president.

According to the National Police, road travel has been complicated because of landslides and fallen trees.

The government has yet to report on missing persons.

“Right now, the most important thing is to protect lives, rescue those who remain trapped, treat the injured, and bring aid to the hardest-hit communities,” said Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo.

“United we will overcome this emergency,” Restrepo added.

The vice-president, together with Foreign Minister Omar Bula, will coordinate foreign aid.

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade and the strongest in the west of the country since 1979.

World.title: 7.4M earthquake hits western Colombia: at least 110 killed, dozens of buildings collapsed
World.content:
An M7.4 earthquake hit western Colombia on Monday, killing at least 110 people and injuring hundreds.

The earthquake struck around 7:30 and had its epicenter in San Jose del Palmar, a municipality in the Choco province.

In the hour that followed, locals began reporting collapsed buildings in the cities of Cali, Pereira and Manizales, where a tower of the cathedral and a dozen other buildings fully or partially collapsed, according to Mayor Jorge Eduardo Rojas.

In a first report on fatalities, Risaralda Governor Juan Diego Patiño said that at least 40 people were killed in the capital Perira. Another three would have been killed in Manizales.

In Cali, an unknown number of people would be trapped under the rubble of multiple buildings. At least 27 people would be killed in the Valle del Cauca province.

Large parts of the roof of the Pereira airport came down, according to video shared on social media.

Flights to Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura were suspended while airport authorities check for damages to infrastructure

In Quibdo, the capital of Choco, at least four people were killed and another 69 were injured, Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said in her second report.

The earthquake was also felt strongly in the capital Bogota and in Medellin where no injuries were reported.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said on social media platform X that he had “personally taken charge of the emergency response in San José del Palmar.”

“I will also be in Pereira in person to stand with those affected and monitor the government’s response,” said De la Espriella, who took office on Friday and has yet to appoint his director of disaster response agency UNGRD.

The president later reported that he was on his way to Bogota to lead rescue efforts from the UNGRD’s main office.

I have established a Unified Command Post at the UNGRD, from where I will personally lead the efforts to assist the communities in Chocó, the Coffee Region, and all affected areas. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade.

World.title: US seeks $1B aid package for Colombia’s new government
World.content:
Th US State Department said it will ask Congress for $1 billion for “deepening our shared and economic partnership” with the government of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

The funding boost, which resembles that of the first year of Plan Colombia in 2000, seeks to “support the De la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten US, Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity.”

In preliminary talks, De la Espriella had already agreed to join the “Shield of the Americas,” a regional initiative of far-right governments to jointly fight crime.

According to a fact sheet, the funds that would require congressional approval would be used to:

Strengthen Colombia’s security forces

Disrupt illegal armed groups and organized crime’s ability to launder money

Significantly expand coca eradication and cocaine interdiction operations

Halt migration

Increase State presence in conflict regions

Combat child recruitment and exploitation by illegal armed groups

The administration of President Donald Trump also seeks to “increase trade and deepen economic ties between our countries.”

In order to do this, nominated US ambassador Nate Morris told the Senate that De la Espriella would withdraw from a memorandum of understanding with the government of China that sought to improve ties with the Asian giant.

Trump’s aid package would help Colombian communities “recover from potential El Niño-related flooding, drought,” which is expected to cause emergencies between December and March.

The US would also support a Bilateral Prosperity Dialogue to “stabilize” Colombia’s economy, “strengthening its energy generation and distribution sectors, exploring critical mineral investments, and creating new opportunities for US investors.”

The aid package would additionally “strengthen Colombian small and medium enterprises in agribusiness, manufacturing, and tech services by connecting them to US buyers and linking them to U.S.-aligned supply chains.”

The two governments would additionally seek to modernize Colombia’s digital, port and energy infrastructure while “positioning Colombia as a trusted nearshoring partner for supply chain diversification.”

World.title: De la Espriella sworn in as Colombia’s new president
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in in Colombia’s third largest city, Cali, under extreme security precautions.

De la Espriella was sworn in by the president of Congress, Senator Honorio Henriquez of the far-right Democratic Center party in the theater of the private University of Santiago de Cali.

The first part of the ceremony was attended by the Spanish King Felipe VI, multiple heads of state from Latin America and more than 60 ambassadors.

After being sworn in, De la Espriella went to the nearby Pichincha Battalion to assume the supreme command of the armed forces and hold his first speech as president.

The president vowed the security forces that he would be “an essential part of the miracle country” and vowed that at the end of his four-year mandate “authority will be felt in every corner of the country.”

De la Espriella also promised that “nobody will be persecuted for his opinions” and warned members of the “regime” of former President Gustavo Petro he would cooperate with “other States,” suggesting they could be extradited.

Both ceremonies were boycotted by Petro’s leftist political party, the Historic Pact, which organized political rallies elsewhere in Cali, and in the cities of Bogota and Barranquilla.

In Barranquilla, Senator Ivan Cepeda stressed the left does not recognize the incoming government because of De la Espriella’s US citizenship and his alleged debts with the US Department of Justice.

“De la Espriella, who once acted as an intermediary for drug traffickers and paramilitaries—from whose ill-gotten gains he has profited—has now become a figure who will be pressured by the United States, by his own government, and by its federal agencies to allow all kinds of foreign intervention in Colombia,” said Cepeda.

The leftist senator lost the elections to De la Espriella with a razor-thin margin of less than one percent. His supporters continue to seek a court order to nullify the election.

World.title: Colombia investigating governors, mayors over $941M corruption racket
World.content:
Prosecutors arrested 13 suspects and asked Colombia’s Supreme Court to investigate seven (former) governors over their alleged involvement in the embezzlement of COP3 trillion ($941 million).

The arrests and the investigation requests are related to the public-private partnership Sierra Nevada Mixed Fund, which was created by Martin Zuleta (U Party) and his family when he was mayor of La Paz, Cesar, in early 2021.

While supposedly serving the interests of La Paz, the Sierra Nevada Mixed Fund allegedly used forged documents to illegally appropriate funds from the General Royalties System with the help of governors from at least five provinces.

“So far, we’ve tracked 3 trillion pesos, of which it has been established that some were misappropriated through irregular contracts,” anti-corruption prosecutor Madeleyne Perez said at a press conference.

Among those whose cases were forwarded to the Supreme Court were the governors of Magdalena, Vichada, Amazonas Guaviare an Vaupes.

Former Governors Rafael Martinez of Magdalena and Alvaro Leon of Vichada will also be investigated by the Supreme Court.

Among those who were arrested is the mayor of Maria la Baja, a contractor and multiple (former) directors of the mixed fund.

The non-profit has been investigated since 2024 when authorities found irregularities in the construction of a high school in the Huila province, funds for school transport in Casanare and funds meant for indigenous reserves in La Guajira.

A report by the now-defunct radio station W from that year showed that Sierra Nevada had been hired by authorities from throughout Colombia for a wide variety of projects, avoiding any open bidding procedure.

W found more than 100 contracts between mainly local and regional government authorities and the non-profit.

According to Caracol, Zuleta was taken to hospital after his home was raided by prosecution officials and would be available to cooperate with the prosecutors investigating his alleged involvement in corruption.

World.title: The main land crossing between Argentina and Chile passes its winter closure record
World.content:
The main land crossing between Argentina and Chile passes its winter closure record

13th Thursday, August 2026 - 06:55 UTC Full article

The corridor was closed as a precaution on July 14 in anticipation of the forecasts

The Cristo Redentor international crossing, which links the Argentine province of Mendoza with Chile's Valparaíso Region through the Andes, has now been closed for close to a month because of a snow and wind storm, surpassing the winter closure record set in 2023. Authorities on both sides estimate it could reopen next week, depending on weather conditions.

The corridor was closed as a precaution on July 14 in anticipation of the forecasts. Snowfall extended between the settlements of Punta de Vacas and Las Cuevas, reached accumulations of up to four meters in some sections and affected 80 kilometers of Route 7, the largest such record in the area since 2008, according to the national roads agency. Winds blew at between 110 and 160 kilometers per hour, with zero visibility.

Official counts put the number of international freight trucks held at various points in Mendoza at around 1,550, although transport sector estimates raise the figure above 2,000. Drivers from Argentina, Brazil, Uruguay, Paraguay and Chile are among those stranded. Each immobilized vehicle represents losses of close to 600 dollars a day, according to the sector's own calculations.

The delay has drawn criticism. The Mendoza truck owners' association toured the corridor and said the road was in good condition at least as far as Puente del Inca, and called for the tunnel to be opened. The national roads agency replied that clearing work reached the mouth of the international tunnel on August 9, but that winds prevent traffic being allowed through to Las Cuevas and that precautions are being intensified given the risk of avalanches.

In Chile, the head of the Border Crossings Unit, Sergio Salazar, rejected the idea that opportunities had been missed. “There really were no such windows,” he said, explaining that work on the Chilean side was completed the previous Friday and on the Argentine side this week. He said the only opening was brief and risky, and the decision was not to expose a small number of trucks.

Reopening will not restore normal traffic immediately. Authorities calculate between five and six days to clear the accumulated backlog, constrained by the winter timetable, which limits operations to around twelve hours a day. Under normal conditions the corridor handles between 500 and 600 trucks daily.

The storm has also kept the Pehuenche, Agua Negra, Pircas Negras, Pino Hachado and San Francisco crossings closed. Alternative routes to the Pacific involve travelling around 2,000 additional kilometers.
