Chile · Business

Key Facts Profit swing Arauco posted net income of about US$71–72 million in H1 2026, reversing a US$10 million loss in H1 2025.

Arauco posted net income of about US$71–72 million in H1 2026, reversing a US$10 million loss in H1 2025. Revenue uptick Cumulative revenue rose 0.7% in H1 2026, while Q2 sales climbed 5.2% year on year on higher volumes.

Cumulative revenue rose 0.7% in H1 2026, while Q2 sales climbed 5.2% year on year on higher volumes. Copec pledge Empresas Copec approved an irrevocable, unconditional commitment of up to US$450 million for Arauco from 1 January 2027 to 31 December 2028, subject to trigger events.

Empresas Copec approved an irrevocable, unconditional commitment of up to US$450 million for Arauco from 1 January 2027 to 31 December 2028, subject to trigger events. Megaproject The Arauco Sucuriú project in Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil, carries a total investment of about US$4.6 billion.

The Arauco Sucuriú project in Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil, carries a total investment of about US$4.6 billion. Capacity target The pulp mill is planned for 3.5 million tonnes of pulp per year, with startup targeted for late 2027.

The pulp mill is planned for 3.5 million tonnes of pulp per year, with startup targeted for late 2027. Volume driver Arauco attributed the quarterly sales gain mainly to higher pulp and wood sales volumes, not price increases.

The turnaround is real, but the bigger story is the capital commitment behind Sucuriú — a bet that Brazil’s pulp demand will justify a US$4.6 billion plant just as global prices start to recover.

If you track Latin America’s commodity giants, you already know the name Arauco — but the numbers from the first half of 2026 give you a clearer picture of where the company stands and where it’s heading. The Chilean pulp and forestry firm swung back to profit, posting net income of about US$71–72 million for January–June 2026, versus a loss of about US$10 million in the same period last year. That recovery came on the back of a stronger second quarter and higher sales volumes in both pulp and wood. And while the profit figure is modest, the real signal is in the parent company’s wallet: Empresas Copec has now committed up to US$450 million to the Arauco Sucuriú project in Brazil, a US$4.6 billion pulp mill that could reshape supply dynamics in the region. For anyone living in or invested in Latin America, this is not just a Chilean story — it’s a continental one.

Arauco’s US$4.6 billion Sucuriú mill is rising in Mato Grosso do Sul. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

The H1 2026 Numbers: A Modest but Meaningful Turnaround

Arauco’s return to profit in the first half of 2026 was not a dramatic leap, but it was a clear directional change. Net income of about US$71–72 million compares with a loss of about US$10 million in H1 2025 (the two main Chilean market outlets round the figure slightly differently). The improvement was helped by a better second quarter, when sales rose 5.2% year on year, mainly due to higher volumes in both the pulp and wood businesses. Cumulative revenue for the six-month period rose about 0.7% — a small gain, but one that suggests demand is stabilizing rather than collapsing.

What’s notable is that the growth came from volume, not pricing. That tells you something about the market environment: buyers are active, but they’re not yet paying a premium. For Arauco, that means operational efficiency and scale are doing the heavy lifting. The company didn’t break out segment-level earnings in the summary, but the tone is consistent with a firm that has cut costs, kept mills running, and is now waiting for the price cycle to turn in its favor.

The US$450 Million Commitment: What Copec Is Really Saying

Empresas Copec’s decision to approve an irrevocable, unconditional commitment of up to US$450 million to Arauco is the kind of move that gets attention in boardrooms across Santiago and São Paulo. The funds will be available between 1 January 2027 and 31 December 2028, but only if certain trigger events occur. That conditional structure gives Copec flexibility while signaling to the market that it stands behind the project.

The commitment is tied directly to the Arauco Sucuriú project in Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil. With a total investment of about US$4.6 billion and planned capacity of 3.5 million tonnes of pulp per year, Sucuriú is one of the largest industrial projects in the region. Startup is targeted for late 2027, and while that timeline is ambitious for a project of this scale, the fact that Copec is willing to back it with hard cash — not just promises — says a lot about its confidence in the pulp market’s long-term trajectory.

Why the Arauco Sucuriú Project Matters for Latin America

For a reader living in or invested in Latin America, the Arauco Sucuriú project is more than a corporate headline. A pulp mill of this size creates thousands of construction jobs, then hundreds of permanent positions, plus indirect work in forestry, logistics, and services. Mato Grosso do Sul is already a forestry hub, and Sucuriú would cement that status. It also means export revenue — pulp is a dollar-earning commodity, and Brazil is already the world’s largest producer of hardwood pulp.

But there’s a strategic angle too. Arauco is a Chilean company, and its decision to build in Brazil rather than at home reflects where the trees grow fastest and where infrastructure is most favorable. That cross-border investment is a reminder that Latin America’s commodity chains are deeply integrated — Chilean capital, Brazilian land, and global markets. For investors, the Sucuriú project is a long-term bet on pulp demand from packaging, tissue, and textiles. For residents, it’s about jobs and regional development. Both perspectives matter.

What to Watch Between Now and 2028

The trigger events for Copec’s US$450 million commitment are not specified in the public summary, but in practice they usually relate to construction milestones, cost overruns, or working capital needs. That means the money is there as a safety net, not a daily funding line. Arauco’s own cash flow, plus project financing, will likely cover most of the US$4.6 billion bill. The Copec pledge is a backstop — and a signal to lenders that the parent company won’t walk away.

For the next 18 months, the key indicators are pulp prices, Brazilian real exchange rates, and construction progress. If the mill starts up in 2027 as planned, it will add 3.5 million tonnes of supply to a market that is already well supplied. That could pressure prices in the short term, but it also positions Arauco to capture cost advantages in a region where eucalyptus grows fast and logistics are improving. The H1 2026 profit is a good sign, but the real test comes when Sucuriú starts producing.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was Arauco’s net income in H1 2026? Arauco reported net income of about US$71–72 million for January–June 2026, compared with a loss of about US$10 million in the same period of 2025. The improvement was helped by a stronger second quarter and higher sales volumes in pulp and wood. How much is Empresas Copec committing to the Arauco Sucuriú project? Empresas Copec approved an irrevocable, unconditional commitment of up to US$450 million to be available to Arauco between 1 January 2027 and 31 December 2028, if certain trigger events occur. It is a capital backstop to Arauco tied to the US$4.6 billion Sucuriú pulp mill in Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil, callable only if certain trigger events occur. When will the Sucuriú pulp mill start operating? The planned startup for the Arauco Sucuriú project is late 2027. The mill is designed for 3.5 million tonnes of pulp per year. Construction timelines for projects of this scale can shift, so treat 2027 as a target rather than a guarantee.

Sources: Celulosa Arauco and Empresas Copec disclosures; Diario Financiero; La Tercera.

World.title: IRSA Pushes Ahead With Ramblas del Plata, Buenos Aires’s US$1.8 Billion Riverfront District
World.content:
Argentina · Real Estate

Key Facts Project scale Ramblas del Plata spans 71 hectares on Buenos Aires’s southern waterfront, with up to 895,000 square metres of buildable area.

Ramblas del Plata spans 71 hectares on Buenos Aires’s southern waterfront, with up to 895,000 square metres of buildable area. Housing units More than 10,000 homes are planned, alongside a 27.5-hectare public park, a school of more than 10,000 square metres, a health center, hotels, offices, coworking spaces, and about 36,000 square metres of commercial space.

More than 10,000 homes are planned, alongside a 27.5-hectare public park, a school of more than 10,000 square metres, a health center, hotels, offices, coworking spaces, and about 36,000 square metres of commercial space. Investment size La Nación reported on 12 August 2026 that the project involves close to US$1.8 billion in planned investment.

La Nación reported on 12 August 2026 that the project involves close to US$1.8 billion in planned investment. Coastline recovery The scheme aims to reclaim nearly 4 kilometres of riverfront along the Río de la Plata.

The scheme aims to reclaim nearly 4 kilometres of riverfront along the Río de la Plata. Barter deal On 30 July 2026, IRSA announced a US$4 million barter exchange for a 2,360-square-metre lot, with roughly 4,500 square metres of saleable area.

On 30 July 2026, IRSA announced a US$4 million barter exchange for a 2,360-square-metre lot, with roughly 4,500 square metres of saleable area. Land use Private development covers about 29% of the site, leaving the rest for public space, streets, and amenities.

Private development covers about 29% of the site, leaving the rest for public space, streets, and amenities. Previous name The project was formerly known as Costa Urbana, on the ex-Ciudad Deportiva de Boca Juniors land.

The real story here is not a ribbon-cutting — it’s the slow, deliberate machinery of land monetization and infrastructure work that will decide whether Buenos Aires’s southern edge becomes a livable neighborhood or just another speculative address.

If you’ve been tracking Buenos Aires real estate, you’ve probably heard the name Ramblas del Plata floating around. It’s the rebranded version of the old Costa Urbana project, sitting on 71 hectares of what used to be Boca Juniors’s sports club land along the southern waterfront. And while there’s no groundbreaking ceremony to report — despite what you might have seen elsewhere — the project is very much moving forward. IRSA is advancing Ramblas del Plata through infrastructure works and commercialization deals, and the latest numbers give you a clearer picture of what’s actually being built, and how much it will cost.

The southern waterfront is set for one of the city’s biggest redevelopments. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What’s Actually Happening on the Ground

Let’s be precise about the timeline. On 30 July 2026, IRSA announced a barter deal for a 2,360-square-metre lot within the first extended stage of the project. The deal was valued at about US$4 million, and it gives the buyer roughly 4,500 square metres of saleable area. IRSA said the deal fits its strategy of continuing infrastructure works and advancing the commercialization of the project. By the August reporting, IRSA had sold around 19 lots for more than US$100 million, committing about 170,000 square metres. That is not a construction kickoff — it’s a land transaction that helps fund and de-risk the urbanization phase.

Then, on 12 August 2026, La Nación published a detailed report on the project’s scope. The headline numbers: close to US$1.8 billion in planned investment, and nearly 4 kilometres of recovered coastline. The project will include more than 10,000 homes, a 27.5-hectare public park — one of the largest in the city — a school of more than 10,000 square metres, a health center, hotels, corporate offices, coworking spaces, and about 36,000 square metres of commercial premises. The buildable area tops out at 895,000 square metres of floor space. Private development occupies about 29% of the land; the rest, more than 70%, is ceded to the city for parks, public space, and streets.

Why This Matters for Buenos Aires

This is one of the largest riverfront transformations the city has seen in decades. For years, that stretch of the Río de la Plata shoreline was closed-off club land — a blank spot on the map between La Boca and Puerto Madero. Now it’s being turned into a mixed-use district that could house tens of thousands of residents. If you live in or invest in Latin America, this matters because it’s a test case for how a major city handles waterfront redevelopment: who gets access to the river, how much housing actually gets built, and whether the public realm survives contact with private capital.

The political groundwork goes back to a 2021 rezoning approved by the Buenos Aires city Legislature (Law 6476), which cleared the way for the current development concept after a contested, court-challenged vote. The effect is clear: this land is no longer zoned for sports or docks. It’s zoned for a new neighborhood. That shift took years of negotiation between the city, the club, and developers, and it sets a precedent for other underused waterfront parcels across Latin America.

The Business Model: Phased, Not Flashy

IRSA isn’t building this all at once. The barter deal in July is a good example of their approach: swap a lot for value, use that to fund infrastructure, then sell or develop the next phase. It’s a slow, deliberate strategy that prioritizes cash flow and risk management over dramatic announcements. If you’re watching from an investor’s perspective, the key metric isn’t a groundbreaking date — it’s how many of these barter and pre-sale deals get done, and at what prices per square metre.

One thing to keep in mind: the US$1.8 billion figure is the total planned investment, not what’s been spent so far. And the US$4 million barter deal is a small piece of that puzzle. The project is still in its early stages, with infrastructure and urbanization work happening on the ground, but the main building construction hasn’t been formally announced. So if you see headlines about a “groundbreaking,” treat them with caution. What’s confirmed is that IRSA is moving dirt, signing deals, and preparing the land for the next decade of development.

Ramblas del Plata and the Future of the Southern Shoreline

The southern edge of Buenos Aires has always been the working-class side of the river — docks, factories, and the gritty charm of La Boca. Ramblas del Plata is an attempt to graft a modern, mixed-use district onto that history. The project includes a health center, hotels, and offices, which suggests the developers are aiming for a 24-hour neighborhood, not just a bedroom community. The 36,000 square metres of commercial space will need tenants, and the 10,000 homes will need buyers or renters. That’s a lot of supply coming into a market that’s still recovering from years of economic instability.

For anyone living in or invested in Latin America, the lesson is simple: this is how large-scale urban redevelopment actually happens in the region. It’s not a single dramatic event. It’s a series of land swaps, infrastructure contracts, and phased sales that stretch over years. The 2021 Legislature rezoning gave it its legal footing. The 2026 barter deals give it financial momentum. And the La Nación report gives it public visibility. Whether it succeeds will depend on execution, market demand, and the city’s ability to keep the waterfront public. For now, Ramblas del Plata is advancing — one lot at a time.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is IRSA building homes right now at Ramblas del Plata? No. The confirmed activity is infrastructure and urbanization work, plus commercialization deals like the July 2026 barter. No main construction start or groundbreaking ceremony has been officially announced. How much will the whole project cost? La Nación reported on 12 August 2026 that planned investment is close to US$1.8 billion. That’s the full-project figure, not what’s been spent so far. What happened to the old Boca Juniors sports club land? The 71-hectare site was formerly the Ciudad Deportiva de Boca Juniors. After a 2021 rezoning process, it was cleared for mixed-use development. IRSA’s project, formerly called Costa Urbana, is now branded as Ramblas del Plata.

Sources: La Nación (12 August 2026); IRSA regulatory disclosures (barter deal, 30 July 2026); Buenos Aires City Legislature (Law 6476, 2021).

World.title: Antofagasta Minerals Bets Over US$7 Billion on Copper Without Continental Water
World.content:
Chile · Mining

Key Facts Total package Antofagasta Minerals is investing more than US$7 billion across Centinela, Los Pelambres, and Zaldívar to keep producing copper without continental freshwater.

Antofagasta Minerals is investing more than US$7 billion across Centinela, Los Pelambres, and Zaldívar to keep producing copper without continental freshwater. Centinela build A US$4.4 billion second concentrator with 95,000 tonnes/day capacity will add more than 170,000 tonnes of copper-equivalent output.

A US$4.4 billion second concentrator with 95,000 tonnes/day capacity will add more than 170,000 tonnes of copper-equivalent output. Pelambres shift A roughly US$2 billion adaptation doubles desalination to 800 litres/second, letting the mine drop continental water use in 2027.

A roughly US$2 billion adaptation doubles desalination to 800 litres/second, letting the mine drop continental water use in 2027. Pipeline route Los Pelambres adds a new 125 km concentrate pipeline between its Chacay plant and the Punta Chungo port.

Los Pelambres adds a new 125 km concentrate pipeline between its Chacay plant and the Punta Chungo port. Zaldívar switch A US$900 million water project, part of a life-extension due in the second half of 2028, will use treated wastewater (supplied by Econssa) via a 163 km, roughly 200 litres/second system.

A US$900 million water project, part of a life-extension due in the second half of 2028, will use treated wastewater (supplied by Econssa) via a 163 km, roughly 200 litres/second system. Board move Juan Claro resigns from Antofagasta plc’s board effective 31 August 2026, after about 21 years as a non-executive director, with no severance payment.

The real story here isn’t just copper at record prices — it’s how one of Chile’s biggest miners is betting billions on water infrastructure to stay relevant for another quarter-century. For anyone living in or watching Latin America’s mining economies, this is the template for survival in a drier, costlier world.

If you’ve been following copper prices lately, you’ll know they’ve been hitting records. But the bigger news for anyone invested in or living near Latin America’s mining heartland is what Antofagasta Minerals is doing with that momentum. The Luksic group’s copper arm — the mining business of London-listed Antofagasta plc — is committing more than US$7 billion across its three flagship mines to keep producing copper without continental fresh water. That’s not a small tweak. It’s a structural bet that the future of Chilean copper is seawater, treated wastewater, and pipelines, not rivers and aquifers.

Desalinated seawater is becoming the backbone of Chilean copper. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Why Antofagasta Minerals is spending big on water

The logic is simple: copper doesn’t get mined without water, and Chile’s north is one of the driest places on Earth. Antofagasta Minerals is building a US$4.4 billion second concentrator at Centinela, with capacity of 95,000 tonnes per day. That alone adds more than 170,000 tonnes of copper-equivalent output. But the concentrator only works if water is available, so the company is pairing that expansion with a near-US$2 billion adaptation at Los Pelambres that doubles desalination capacity to 800 litres per second.

Once that system is operational in 2027, Los Pelambres stops using continental water entirely. The plan also includes a new 125 km concentrate pipeline between the Chacay plant and the Punta Chungo port, routed away from populated areas. This isn’t about being green for the sake of it — it’s about securing the resource that keeps the mine running.

Zaldívar’s wastewater solution

The third piece of the puzzle is Zaldívar, where Antofagasta Minerals is spending about US$900 million on the water component of a life-extension project due in the second half of 2028. That mine will stop consuming continental water and instead use treated wastewater supplied by Econssa from the Antofagasta area, delivered via a 163 km pumping system with a capacity of around 200 litres per second. It’s a longer pipeline, a different water source, and a clear sign that the company is willing to pay for infrastructure that others might consider too complex or too costly.

Together, these three projects form a coherent strategy: sustain output beyond 2050 without relying on the continent’s shrinking freshwater supplies. For a region where water rights are increasingly contested — between cities, agriculture, and mining — this is a way to de-risk operations before the conflict gets worse. It’s also a message to investors that Antofagasta Minerals is thinking in decades, not quarters.

What this means for anyone in Latin America

If you live in or invest in Latin America, this matters beyond the copper price. Mining is a cornerstone of Chile’s economy, and how it adapts to water scarcity will shape everything from local employment to export revenues. The shift to desalinated seawater and treated wastewater is expensive, but it’s also a moat: smaller miners may not afford it, while larger players like Antofagasta Minerals can consolidate their position. For expats and nomads in Chile’s coastal cities, the visible side is new pipelines and plants; the less visible side is a mining sector that can keep paying taxes, wages, and dividends even as the climate dries out.

There’s also a governance angle. Juan Claro is resigning from the board of Antofagasta plc effective 31 August 2026, after serving as a non-executive director since 2005 — about 21 years. The company says he will not receive any severance payment, only pay accrued through that date. He’ll also step down from the Sustainability and Stakeholder Management Committee. It’s a clean exit, and it happens as the company is making its biggest water-related commitments in years. Whether that’s coincidence or part of a broader refresh, it’s worth watching.

The bottom line on Antofagasta Minerals’ water bet

Copper prices at records make big investments easier to justify, but the logic here isn’t just cyclical. Antofagasta Minerals is positioning itself for a world where freshwater is scarcer, regulations are tighter, and communities are more vocal. The more than US$7 billion package is a hedge against all three. It’s also a reminder that the mining industry’s biggest challenges aren’t always underground — sometimes they’re about what flows above ground.

For investors, the key number isn’t just the copper-equivalent output or the desalination capacity. It’s the date: beyond 2050. That’s the horizon Antofagasta Minerals is planning for, and it’s the horizon that will determine whether Chile remains a copper powerhouse or slowly fades as water runs out. The company is betting billions that it can stay ahead of that curve. So far, the pieces are in place.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Antofagasta Minerals using only desalinated water now? Not yet. Los Pelambres will stop using continental water in 2027 once its desalination capacity doubles to 800 litres per second. Zaldívar will switch to treated wastewater from Antofagasta city by the third quarter of 2028. Centinela’s new concentrator is part of the same broader shift, but the full transition is phased over the next few years. What does “sin agua continental” mean exactly? It means operating without continental freshwater — that is, without drawing from rivers, lakes, or aquifers. Instead, the mines will use desalinated seawater from the Pacific, treated wastewater from nearby cities, and recycled water from tailings deposits like El Mauro. It’s a deliberate move to reduce dependence on increasingly scarce inland water sources. Will Juan Claro’s departure affect the company’s strategy? There’s no indication it will. Claro is leaving the board of Antofagasta plc after about 21 years as a non-executive director, with no severance payment. The water investment package was announced separately and is tied to sustaining output beyond 2050. Board changes at this level rarely reverse major capital commitments, especially ones this large.

Sources: Antofagasta plc and Antofagasta Minerals disclosures; Diario Financiero; La Tercera; Mining.com; BNamericas.

World.title: Vale Copper Bet Accelerates as Salobo Expansion Is Pulled Forward to 2028
World.content:
Brazil · Business

Key Facts — The decision Vale is speeding up a copper expansion at its Salobo complex in Para, moving startup to the first half of 2028.

— The head start That is about one year earlier than the miner had originally planned for the project.

— The price A simpler design cut the estimated cost to about US$215 million, from an earlier US$225-275 million range.

— The payoff The project adds around 30 kt a year of copper and about 15,000 ounces of gold, lifting processing capacity to 42 Mtpa.

— The context Vale wants copper output near 500 kt a year by 2028, betting on demand from the energy transition.

The extra ore the miner will squeeze out of tailings is small next to its iron business. Yet it lands exactly where the world is short: copper for grids, cars and the energy transition.

An open-pit copper mine in Brazil, seen from above. Vale is speeding up a copper expansion at its Salobo complex in Para, targeting startup in the first half of 2028. (Photo: Coordenacao-Geral de Observacao da Terra/INPE, CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Vale copper production is set to grow sooner than planned. After the miner decided to speed up an expansion at its huge Salobo complex in the northern Brazilian state of Para.

The new project will now start up in the first half of 2028, about a year ahead of the original timetable. And a simpler design has trimmed its estimated cost to around US$215 million.

What Vale just decided

On August 12. Vale Base Metals said it would go ahead with a new project at the Salobo mine and bring it online faster.

The plan is to have it running in the first half of 2028. Roughly one year earlier than the company had first mapped out.

It is a modest project by Vale’s standards, but the timing tells you where the miner sees the smart money going. Management framed it as a chance to add copper sooner, at a moment when the metal is in short supply worldwide.

What is actually being brought forward

This is not the big Salobo III phase, which is already finished and lifted the mine’s throughput to 36 Mtpa. The new piece is a coarse particle flotation project, a technique that pulls more copper out of ore the plant already handles.

In plain terms, it squeezes extra metal from material that would otherwise pass through with too little copper recovered. It should add about 6 Mtpa of processing capacity, taking the complex to roughly 42 Mtpa.

Plus around 30 kt of copper a year. It also brings a useful byproduct, about 15,000 ounces of gold each year, which helps pay for the whole thing.

The company operates in two segments, Iron Ore Solutions and Vale Base Metals. It extracts, produces, and distributes iron ore, iron ore pellets, briquettes, nickel, copper, other ferrous…

Why the price tag got smaller

Vale did not just speed the project up; it also made it cheaper by simplifying the design. The estimated cost fell to about US$215 million, down from an earlier range of US$225-275 million, or roughly R$1.16 billion.

Vale’s own share of the bill is expected to be near US$175 million, because partner Wheaton is helping fund part of it. That kind of cost discipline has become a theme for Vale, which has been trimming and streamlining projects across its base-metals arm.

What Salobo is

Salobo sits in the Carajas region of Para, in the eastern Amazon, and is Vale’s flagship copper operation. For years it ran at about 24 Mtpa.

Until the Salobo III expansion raised throughput to 36 Mtpa after a build that cost around US$1.1 billion. The complex produces copper in concentrate along with gold, and it is central to Vale’s ambition to become a bigger copper name.

This latest project is a lighter. Faster add-on that stretches what the existing plant can do rather than digging a whole new mine.

The bigger Vale copper strategy

Salobo is one leg of a wider push; the other main pillar is the Sossego mine, also in Carajas. Vale has laid out a plan to lift copper output toward 500 kt a year by 2028.

Up from a target near 400 kt in 2026. It has also floated a broader spending program of around US$3.3 billion to grow copper and nickel in Brazil and Canada.

The thread is simple: Vale wants to be far more than an iron ore company a decade from now.

Why copper matters now

Copper is the quiet workhorse of the energy transition, needed for wiring, motors and the machinery of electrification. Electric cars use far more of it than petrol ones.

And every new power line and wind farm pulls on the same supply. Analysts have long warned of looming copper deficits, as demand climbs faster than new mines can be built.

That is the bet behind Vale’s move: get more copper flowing before the squeeze on supply gets tighter.

How the copper business is doing

Vale is not waiting on 2028 to show progress; its copper unit is already running strongly. In the second quarter of 2026 the company produced 98.4 kt of copper.

Up 6.3% from a year earlier and its best second quarter since 2017. Salobo led the way with 52.4 kt in the quarter, while Sossego added 25.9 kt to the total.

Copper sales reached 97.6 kt, up 9.7% year on year, and Vale kept its full-year guidance at 350-380 kt.

An iron ore giant leaning on copper

Vale is still, first and foremost, one of the world’s largest iron ore miners, and that business pays the bills today. But iron ore is tied to steel and to China’s building cycle, which has cooled and looks unlikely to roar back.

Copper offers a different growth story, anchored to electrification rather than to construction and property. Adding copper capacity is how Vale hopes to steady its earnings against the swings of the iron ore market.

What it means for Para and the Amazon

Carajas is one of the richest mineral districts on earth, and it sits inside the eastern reaches of the Amazon. More copper output means more activity and jobs around the mines, which matters for local economies in Para.

It also draws scrutiny, as expanding mining near protected Amazon areas raises real environmental questions. Reusing the existing Salobo plant, rather than opening new ground, is the kind of choice that eases some of that pressure.

What to watch next

The near-term test is simple: can Vale hold the 2028 start date and the leaner budget it just promised. Beyond that, watch copper prices and whether the wider push toward 500 kt a year stays on track.

If the metal stays scarce and the projects land on time, this small acceleration could look shrewd in hindsight.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Vale decide about Salobo?

Vale Base Metals approved a new coarse particle flotation project at its Salobo complex in Para. With startup in the first half of 2028, about a year earlier than planned.

How much will the Salobo project cost and add?

A simpler design cut the estimate to about US$215 million, with Vale’s share near US$175 million. It should add roughly 30 kt of copper and about 15,000 ounces of gold a year.

Why is Vale focusing so much on copper?

Copper is central to the energy transition, powering electric cars, grids and renewables. Vale wants output near 500 kt a year by 2028 to grow beyond its iron ore roots.

How is Vale’s copper output doing now?

In the second quarter of 2026 Vale produced 98.4 kt of copper. Up 6.3% year on year and its best second quarter since 2017, led by record output at Salobo.

Sources: Vale Base Metals, Infomoney, The Globe and Mail, Investing.com, company filings.

World.title: Taesa Closes US$300 Million Buy of Energisa Transmission Lines
World.content:
Brazil · Business

Key Facts — The price R$1.638 billion, about US$303 million, at completion, up from R$1.545 billion, about US$286 million, at signing.

— What was bought 100% of five Energisa transmission companies in Goiás, Bahia, Pará and Tocantins.

— The network About 1,305 km of lines, 12 substations and 4,494 MVA of transformation capacity.

— The income Roughly R$291 million, about US$54 million, in annual permitted revenue for the 2025-2026 cycle.

— The timing Signed on 21 May 2026 and completed on Wednesday, 12 August 2026, after ANEEL approval.

The deal folds five power-line concessions across four states into an already vast grid. Adding the kind of regulated, inflation-linked income that draws income investors to transmission.

High-voltage power line towers carry electricity across long distances. Taesa completed a R$1.638 billion, about US$303 million, purchase of five Energisa transmission companies. Photo: Rsparks3, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.
