World.title: Lasha Bugadze becomes first modern Georgian writer whose book was barred from being sent to prison
World.content:
Precedent for literary censorship in Georgia

The administration of Rustavi Prison refused to allow Lasha Bugadze’s new novel, The Observer, to be delivered to the prison. The book was intended for Nana Sander, who was convicted over her participation in a protest on 4 October 2025.

Notably, the penitentiary code contains no provision explicitly banning fiction from being brought into prisons.

The book’s synopsis describes a fictional political reality involving the long rule of a “despot”, the “division of the country into zones” and a “cult of the leader”. It also mentions the scheduling of elections and a decision by the country’s population on whether they should take place.

According to Bugadze, a prison official refused to allow the book in, saying the novel contained “political content”.

The writer says it is unclear to him who determined that the book contained political content and what criteria they used. He suspects the decision may have been prompted by words and phrases in the novel, such as “despot” and “cult of the leader”.

“The employee told me directly that the book could not be delivered because it was political in nature. I don’t think he sat down and read the book. I doubt he even read the synopsis,” Bugadze said.

In his view, someone appears to have judged the work to be political without giving any clear reason.

“Who put this label on the text? [Who decided] whether it was political or not? What does that even mean? And, excuse me, even if the content is political, why should a citizen – whether a prisoner or anyone else – not have the right to read such a book?” the writer said.

Bugadze sees the incident as a potential precedent for censoring literary works:

“It can be described as the first significant example of literary censorship in modern Georgian history. This is an extremely dangerous precedent, and under no circumstances should it be considered normal. The situation requires a response. No one has the right to stop someone from reading.”

The head of the human rights organisation Sapari, Baia Pataraia, announced that legal proceedings would begin over the incident:

“We are taking legal steps. <…> First, we will demand a written and reasoned refusal.”

The organisation PEN Georgia also responded to the case. It described the incident as an alarming precedent for censorship of a literary work, linked not only to the novel’s content but also to the author’s political and civic stance. The organisation stressed that censoring fiction and restricting freedom of expression are unacceptable in a democratic society.

Lasha Bugadze’s The Observer

Precedent for literary censorship in Georgia

World.title: Armenia seeks alternatives amid concerns over possible Russian gas price hike
World.content:
Russian gas pressure on Armenia

If the issue of raising gas tariffs arises, the Armenian authorities will discuss it with their Russian counterparts in a friendly atmosphere, Sargis Khandanyan, an MP from the ruling Civil Contract faction, told journalists.

Khandanyan added that he had no information about any negotiations with Russia over gas tariffs. However, he expressed confidence that, if necessary, Armenia would be able to find alternatives to Russian gas. These could include supplies from Iran, although this is not the only option.

Yerevan and Tehran have already discussed the issue. Following talks held with Iranian partners by Armenia’s Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure, Davit Khudatyan, it emerged that the volume of Iranian gas supplies could potentially be doubled.

“This decision has nothing to do with any other country, Russia in particular. It is a profitable economic activity that both countries are interested in expanding,” the Armenian minister said.

Political analyst Robert Ghevondyan notes that there has recently been increasingly frequent talk of a possible revision of Russian gas prices. He views the issue in the context of the levers of pressure being used against Armenia. In his view, Moscow has already exhausted much of its arsenal and is now resorting to economic leverage, including in the energy sector.

“Political, cultural and terrorist levers, as well as the influence of the criminal subculture, are no longer working for various reasons. And Russia, in order to prevent Armenia from strengthening its independence, has decided to make full use of its last remaining lever,” Ghevondyan said.

‘This scenario cannot be ruled out’: On gas imports from Azerbaijan

Journalists asked MP Sargis Khandanyan how likely it was that the tariff on gas imports from Russia could change by the end of the year.

“I am not aware of when this issue was last discussed with Russia. Nor am I aware of any information that would give grounds to believe that the gas tariff could change,” he replied.

At the same time, the MP noted that the government attaches great importance to diversifying supplies. He recalled the agreements reached during the visit of Armenia’s Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure to Iran. According to him, the “Trump Route” could also be considered as one such opportunity:

“As part of the transit route that will connect Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan through Armenian territory, a gas pipeline will be built. This could provide another opportunity. We could consider this pipeline as an additional source. Of course, this is a very theoretical idea, but it would not be difficult to implement.”

Asked about the possibility of importing gas from Azerbaijan, Khandanyan said that Yerevan and Baku were discussing a broad range of issues:

“I do not know how far we have progressed on the issue of gas supplies, but this scenario cannot be ruled out.”

In late October 2025, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev announced that all restrictions on transit to Armenia would be lifted. Since then, Armenia has been receiving petroleum products from the neighbouring country by rail. According to official figures, Azerbaijan has already supplied Armenia with 20,000 tonnes of petroleum products.

Yerevan and Tehran agree to increase gas supplies. Can Moscow stand in the way?

Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure Davit Khudatyan paid a three-day visit to Iran. Upon returning from Tehran, he said that the volume of Iranian gas supplied under the “Gas for Electricity” programme could be at least doubled. He explained that the pipeline’s capacity exceeds the volume of gas currently being supplied.

Under the programme, Armenia has been receiving gas from Iran since 2009, converting it into electricity which is then supplied back to Iran.

To increase gas imports and export a corresponding volume of electricity to Iran, construction of the Iran-Armenia high-voltage power transmission line needs to be completed. The Armenian government hopes that the long-delayed project will be completed by the end of the year.

Meanwhile, since 2015, the Armenian section of the pipeline carrying gas from Iran has been controlled by Russian company Gazprom.

As a result, some experts doubt whether Iranian gas supplies can be increased without Moscow’s consent. The Armenian government, however, has assured that there will be no obstacles to expanding supplies under the “Gas for Electricity” programme.

Expert commentaty

Political commentator Artem Yerkanyan says:

“Russian Security Council Deputy Secretary Alexei Shevtsov threatened that unless Armenia revises its foreign policy course, it will have to pay $800 for Russian gas instead of the current $177. Compensating for that difference would cost at least $1bn. That is more than the €50m the European Union has promised Armenia as compensation for the impact of strained relations with Russia.

It is worth explaining what the figures of $177 and $800 actually mean. Russia’s Gazprom sells gas for $177 to Gazprom Armenia, which is owned by Gazprom itself. In other words, it also earns revenue from the distribution of the gas, and that revenue also goes to Gazprom. Therefore, I think it would be incorrect to say that Armenia buys gas for $177.

It is also unclear where the figure of $800 comes from, considering the following:

China buys Russian gas for $258;

Turkey for $280;

Hungary, Serbia and Slovakia for $400;

Spain, France and Belgium for $450.

Moreover, according to a forecast by Russia’s Ministry of Economic Development, by the end of this year the average price at which Russia will sell gas to countries outside the EAEU [an economic bloc led by Russia] will be $290.

If the average price is $290, why are they planning to sell it to Armenia for $800? That is unclear.”

Political analyst Robert Ghevondyan argues:

“Following the elections, the Armenian authorities have continued to pursue a multi-vector foreign policy. Dependence on Russia is steadily declining, with the economic dimension playing an increasingly important role in this process.

While Russia is trying to exert economic pressure, Armenia is opening up new markets that Armenian businesses previously ‘failed to notice’ because of their excessive focus on the Russian market. Although problems remain with some goods, economic diversification is advancing rapidly.

In the energy sector, Armenia has alternatives when it comes to building a new nuclear reactor, which in itself is a headache for Russia.

It is no coincidence that, alongside economic blackmail, Rosatom executives periodically make Armenia ‘attractive’ offers to build a new Russian nuclear reactor. However, the Armenian authorities are likely to opt for a different proposal.

A rise in gas prices could initially cause problems. But Armenia has alternatives here as well: Iranian, Turkmen and now Azerbaijani gas.

Consequently, in the near future, Russian gas may find itself merely competing on the market. This would limit the Kremlin’s ability to use gas prices to blackmail Armenia.

In conclusion, it should be noted that increased pressure from Russia is having the opposite effect. Armenia is steadily ‘freeing itself’ from excessive Russian influence and diversifying its economy. The Kremlin does not appear to recognise this yet, but that is its problem.”

World.title: Kobakhidze: Georgia does not publicly declare Russia an enemy because this would require follow-up steps
World.content:
Georgian prime minister on Russia

Georgian Dream Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze told journalists that the Georgian government does not publicly call Russia an “enemy” because such a political statement would require corresponding action.

A journalist asked Kobakhidze whether the Georgian government considers Russia an enemy. The prime minister replied:

“Your questions are shameful, you look ridiculous. Let me explain in simple terms why this question is shameful: you want to get a sensational headline, even in the Russian media, saying that I have declared the Russian Federation an enemy. This is a specific political statement that would have to be followed by specific steps – roughly the same, or exactly the same, as those your party” (referring to the United National Movement – JAMnews) “took in 2008 and before.”

The journalist asked whether this was precisely why the government was reluctant to openly call Russia an enemy.

“Of course. What, should I repeat it again?!” Kobakhidze replied.

Kobakhidze also addressed Russia’s occupation of Georgian territories and reiterated that the Russian Federation occupies 20% of Georgia’s territory.

“Of course, the Russian Federation is the only state and party that has occupied Georgian territories. This is an absolutely clear fact. Numerous statements have been made about this, and there is no doubt about it,” Kobakhidze stressed.

He said Russia’s occupation of Georgian territory was a “crime against the Georgian state and the Georgian people”:

“This is an egregious crime: first the occupation, and then the so-called recognition.”

Georgian prime minister on Russia

World.title: Breaking: One of Australia's most senior Catholics guilty of sexually abusing young men
World.content:
The former Bishop of Broome, who at the peak of his powers was one of the most senior and long-serving Catholic clerics in the country, has been found guilty of sexually abusing multiple young men.

Christopher Alan Saunders, 76, has been on trial accused of sex offences against three young men when he was the Bishop of a remote area of Western Australia three times larger than England.

After a trial that ran for more than three weeks, a District Court jury took almost seven hours to find him guilty of abusing two of those men.

He was convicted of one count of sexual penetration and 12 counts of indecent assault.

Saunders was found not guilty of six other charges.

There was no reaction from the former bishop after the verdicts were read out.

Vulnerable victims

The victims were young Aboriginal men who lived in the Kimberley, where Indigenous people make up more than 40 per cent of the population.

The assaults happened at various places, including at the Bishop's Catholic church-owned residence in the popular tourist haven of Broome, and at a retreat known as the beach house.

The court had been told of "shirts off" gatherings that Saunders held, supplying alcohol and food to young men wearing only boxer shorts.

Christopher Saunders served as the Catholic Bishop of Broome for 25 years. (Supplied)

The then-bishop would occasionally engage in wrestling and boxing with the men, the court heard.

The court had heard Mr Saunders had used his feet to touch young men sexually, grabbed their "privates" and in one instance, engaged in oral sex without consent.

As he chose not to give evidence in his defence, the playing of police interview recordings were the only occasions when the jurors could hear denials from Mr Saunders himself.

The prosecution told the jury Mr Saunders had a sexual interest in young Aboriginal men and a "tendency" to act on that interest.

Prosecutor Adam Ebell encouraged the jury to focus on the testimony of the men. (ABC News: David Weber)

In closing submissions, prosecutor Adam Ebell said while the victims did have criminal histories, the jurors should focus on what they said happened to them at the hands of Saunders, a trusted figure at least one of the men referred to as 'Brother B'.

Defence lawyer Tony Hager said his client's behaviour might have been unusual, "boozy" and "sleazy".

But Mr Hager said Saunders wasn't on trial for inviting young Aboriginal men over to have a drink, or for using church funds to buy alcohol, or for taking alcohol to a dry community.

Defence lawyer Tony Hager described the behaviour as "sleazy". (ABC News: David Weber )

He told the jury his client "wasn't on trial in Rome" for not adhering to a code of conduct, or "standing before the Pope" trying to justify his pastoral care as he was not on trial "as a representative of the Catholic Church".

Mr Hager suggested the memories of the three complainants may have been affected by alcohol use, especially given the passage of time since the alleged events.

The former bishop is due to be sentenced at a later date.

World.title: Logan mayor says region can't handle proposed Cowboys' leagues club
World.content:
North Queensland Cowboys are proposing to build a leagues club south of Brisbane but the Logan City Mayor warns the club "can't pick our pocket".

The project, which is in its preliminary stages, would see 100 gaming machines built in Holmview, Logan.

It is part of the Cowboys' plan to expand their reach to support junior and senior local rugby league across the state.

Logan City Mayor Jon Raven said he only found out about the plans for 100 machines a few weeks ago when the Liquor and Gaming Office wrote to the council.

The proposed location of the club near Holmview Shopping Centre in Logan. (ABC News)

"We'd never heard from the Cowboys until they put in this pokie palace application," he said.

"I would have thought, if you were going to try and take money out of Logan, come and talk to the community first."

Mr Raven said the area wouldn't be able to handle 100 poker machines.

"All of the other pubs that have pokies machines in that area have less than half the number of machines that the Cowboys are proposing to land in Logan," he said.

Logan City Mayor Jon Raven has voiced concern over the plans. (ABC News: Tobi Loftus)

In the community impact statement, the club said it would provide local sponsorships, donations and support to sport and community of $1,650,000 over the first five years, commencing from $100,000 in the first year of operation.

"That's just not good enough," Mr Raven said.

"When you think about how far away Townsville is from Logan, Parramatta is closer to Logan than Townsville.

"They are so far out of catchment," he said.

The proposed leagues club would include 100 gaming machines, or pokies. (ABC Gold Coast: Kimberley Bernard)

Large support base

Cowboys Group Chief Executive Tim Follett said there was a significant and passionate support base in the state's south east with the region home to one of their largest supporter communities outside North Queensland.

"For many years we've heard from members and fans who would love a place they can call their own," he said.

In the community impact statement, it said 59 current financial members lived in the local community area but noted there "would most likely" be more supporters there.

The club says it has a significant support base in south-east Queensland. (ABC News: Chloe Chomicki)

Mr Follett said the Cowboys were committed to engaging openly and collaboratively with key stakeholders at appropriate times during the planning process.

"As part of our early consultation, we have reached out to the mayor's office to commence discussions and understand how we can work constructively with Logan City Council throughout the process."

Mr Follett said any future venue would be developed with a strong focus on community connection and local impact.

He said should the project progress, the venue would contribute to local employment, support community initiatives and build partnerships with grassroots sporting organisations and charities across the region.

Logan Mayor Jon Raven said he only found out about the plans for 100 gaming machines recently. (ABC News)

"While this opportunity remains in its early stages, we believe there is potential to create a venue that brings Cowboys supporters together, whilst also delivering meaningful benefits for the local community," Mr Follett said.

Queensland Sport Minister Tim Mander said the Office of Liquor and Gaming Regulation Commission was looking into the issue.

When asked if he thought it would be beneficial for the venue to be in the state's south east, Mr Mander said he didn't know the area well enough.

Cowboys Group chief executive Tim Follet said the region is home to large contingent of Cowboys supporters. (Supplied: Cowboys Group/Facebook)

"Let's just let the process take place and let's make sure that the public get their right to say something as well," he said.

'Big decision' for Logan

Shadow Treasurer Shannon Fentiman said she encouraged local community members to have their say on the proposal before she said, "anything about that".

"This is a big decision for Logan City, and I want locals to have their say," the Waterford MP said.

Mr Raven said the venue's approval was up to the Liquor and Gaming Office.

"They have overturned or reduced licences before," he said.

How much do pokie clubs really give back to the community? In some cases, poker machine venues are donating less than 1 per cent of their gambling earnings to the community.

"We'd love to see them either reduce the number of licences for machines significantly or increase the amount of return to the community," he said.

But Mr Raven said Logan was open to having their own NRL team.

"If the Cowboys aren't sustainable in North Queensland… the Logan Cowboys sounds like a pretty good name for our new team," he said.

Community consultation on the proposed project closes in September.

World.title: Taylor's tetchy press conference, Bragg's big day out
World.content:
Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where Courtney Gould gets you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.

Anthony Albanese and Angus Taylor are both leaders under pressure trying to control the narrative in different ways.

While the prime minister was cutting off a press conference to avoid answering questions over what's become a melee over melons, back in Canberra the opposition leader's staffer was caught on camera letting loose at a journalist.

Channel 10 journalist Ashleigh Raper was grilling Taylor about his links to Dallas McInerney, who has been named in the NSW ICAC inquiry into illegal donations to the NSW Liberals.

The opposition leader has previously denied he gave money to the Liberal faction at the centre of the corruption probe into branch stacking. He repeated on Thursday that no payment had been made, while avoiding questions about discussions (after allegations surfaced in the inquiry members of the group had asked him for money).

After Taylor walked away, his senior adviser Kane Silom took aim at the Channel 10 reporter. "Are your ratings that bad? Seriously, that's a fricken disgrace," he said. "No wonder 10+ got cut," he said, referring to the current affairs program that was recently wound back.

Anthony Albanese faced questions over a gesture he made during a podcast interview. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Albanese prefers to avoid the question all together. Like Taylor, he also made himself available to the media. The press conference in Newcastle, to mark a deal to keep the Tomago smelter running, was only the fourth in the past month. None of the press conferences were held in Canberra where he faced questions from political reporters.

The government had been running the line that the prime minister's gesturing in front of his chest, while he discussed the two melons gifted to him by his Japanese counterpart, had been misinterpreted.

So, the press conference was the first chance to ask the prime minister: so what DID you mean?

Albanese began answering the question (he uses his hands all the time and the relationship with Japan is great), before NSW Premier Chris Minns intervened to demand the topic return to the smelter.

A carefully timed cut off by a staffer ensured journalists not from the local area had no further opportunity.

When life gives you melons

The prime minister's decision to appear on the Bush Deep podcast last month has become a game of whack-a-mole for the government. When it was originally published, Albanese copped it for remarks he made about Kylie Minogue. He swiftly apologised for that.

But after a former Japanese ambassador, Shingo Yamagami (who is no fan of the Labor government as my colleague Stephen Dziedzic reported), claimed the joke was disrespectful, the podcast returned to the headlines.

Albanese could have done the same thing he did last time, swiftly conceding his mistake before moving on but he didn't.

Instead, a diplomatic note in which Japan said it saw no ill-intent in the remarks found its way into the media. The Coalition referred the apparent leak to the federal police as it took up the issue in parliament.

As David Speers wrote, the full-throated pursuit of the saga by the Coalition might, in time, prove to be the right choice. Slowly chipping away at the paint of Albanese's character, much like Labor did to Scott Morrison.

Albanese is fortunate that none of the women involved, Sanae Takaichi, Kylie Minogue, nor his wife Jodie, have publicly commented on the jokes he made about them.

Japan's PM gifted the Australian PM two crown melons, which can be worth hundreds of dollars each. (X: @takaichi_sanae)

Getting grilled at press conferences isn't the only common ground Albanese and Taylor have shared this week. The pair met several times behind the scenes in a bid to hash out deals on gambling advertising, the National Disability Insurance Scheme and the news media bargaining incentive.

The government wants all three bills ticked off before parliament rises next week. Albanese told the caucus he expected the NDIS overhaul to pass with the Coalition's support.

He was also projecting confidence that the government's planned changes to gambling advertising would pass once an agreement was reached on winding back inducements to entice people to punt.

A targeted crackdown on inducements offered to high rollers and a simplified option to curb ads on streaming services may be where this lands, as Clare Armstrong reported this week.

Crossbench MPs conceded they had "lost the battle" on tougher gambling advertising restrictions, as some within the Coalition began calling for an automatic review to be baked into the legislation.

Loading

Bragg's big day out

Meanwhile, a curious appearance at the National Press Club by Liberal moderate Andrew Bragg also ruffled some feathers within the opposition.

The NSW frontbencher was there to outline the plan to slash the National Construction Code to just 80 pages. Gone would be things like energy efficiency standards in favour of a "simple" house with "basic" amenities to get more people into more dwellings.

Andrew Bragg strayed far from his policy area in his address to the National Press Club. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

But the speech took a turn before he even got to that point. Bragg's wide-ranging address freelanced well beyond his housing portfolio, taking aim at "indolent" leaders over the past 20 years, apologising for failing to "do more to stop the madness" during the Morrison-era.

The tax scales should be rebalanced, he argued, while also wading into the GST, fiscal management, energy and superannuation. He was later counselled by the opposition leader and urged to stick to sharing opposition policy rather than his personal opinions.

ABC Politics in your inbox Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Courtney Gould

"Andrew expressed some of his personal views yesterday. I've made clear to him that his job is to express … the views of the Coalition and the senior team of which he is a member when it comes to immigration policy," Taylor said.

Nationals leader Matt Canavan also took issue with Bragg's assessment that backpacker visas could be on the list to be wound back under a Coalition crackdown on migration.

One of his colleagues would later describe the speech to Tom Crowley as "for Bragg by Bragg".

"Well, who said that?" he asked ABC's Radio National Breakfast host Sally Sara, who declined to tell him.

World.title: Platforms failed to stop death threats against activists, report says
World.content:
WARNING: This story contains graphic depictions of gender-based violence.

A year ago, Coralie Alison woke to find her personal phone number, date of birth and passwords had been posted online.

In the hours that followed, she received horrific deepfake images of herself.

"Images of my throat slit, my body burned alive, decapitated, stripped of my clothing and minced alive," she said.

Ms Alison was one of five members of the women's rights group Collective Shout who found themselves the target of violent abuse after the group successfully campaigned to remove video games depicting rape, incest and violence towards women and girls from online platforms.

The women at Collective Shout were subjected to online abuse. (Supplied: Collective Shout)

The United Nations' special rapporteur on violence against women, Reem Alsalem, described the backlash that followed as "the most serious form of online violence against women human rights defenders" she had seen "in a long time".

The women detailed the abuse they received in a report released on Wednesday, while the Online Hate Prevention Institute (OHPI) was also commissioned to write a report on their experience.

The report found the targeted abuse was fuelled by misogyny and disinformation that tech platforms were unwilling or unable to stop.

Online terror begins

The furore started when payment processors including PayPal, Visa and Mastercard introduced new rules that compelled video game content to adhere to payment policies.

"Thousands of perpetrators across multiple platforms and countries mobilised to punish us for our 'crime' of successfully persuading gaming platforms, through their payment providers, to halt the sale of games featuring rape, sexual torture and child sexual abuse and incest," said Collective Shout director Melinda Tankard Reist.

Elon Musk re-tweeted an petition against Collective Shout and his platform X was used to harass the women. (Supplied)

Elon Musk, the owner of X, weighed in on the Collective Shout debate, endorsing a petition calling on the payment platforms to reverse their decision by reposting it on X along with the statement, "bravo".

X has no discernible Australian or global press office for the ABC to contact for comment.

Melinda Tankard Reist says her group was "punished" for stopping gaming platforms using rape and sexual torture as entertainment. (Supplied)

Ms Tankard Reist said the coordinated abuse was intended to "humiliate, threaten and endanger our safety."

" The system [that was] supposed to protect us did not. "

The women said their families were also targeted and their home addresses published on the internet.

Toxic masculinity

Patrick Scolyer-Gray, author of the OHPI report, told supporters gathered at Australia's Parliament House on Wednesday that the case of Collective Shout was internationally significant.

He said the abuse was dressed up to appear as a defence of free speech and anti-censorship concerns.

"It was never about video games, and it was never about free speech, and the backlash can't be understood without recognising the central role of misogyny," he said.

"Nearly every institution that should or could have interrupted this campaign failed to do so.

"Platform moderation systems proved inadequate, disinformation spread faster than corrections, abusive material remained online long enough to create the appearance of public consensus."

The OHPI report made 47 recommendations, the first being that harmful and sexist content specific to women should be identified immediately.

The report suggested the content should be"classified as misogynistic and a form of gender-based hate speech" before being removed by online platforms.

The authors also called on media organisations to act quickly to debunk misinformation.

Hopeful future

E-Safety Commissioner Julie Inman Grant has been calling for more safeguards ot protect women online.

She said the technology industry needed to step up to stop these platforms from being weaponised.

Collective Shout member Caitlin Roper said she was surprised by the profiles of the abusers.

Caitlin Roper says some who participated in the campaign of abuse were "regular men", judging by their online profiles. (ABC NEWS)

"Some might [think] that the abuse was perpetrated by a very specific subset of misogynistic men in the dark corners of the internet," she said.

" The reality is that many of our abusers are 'regular men', who threatened to rape us, hunt us down and kill us from their actual social media accounts, showing them smiling alongside their wives and sometimes daughters. "

Ms Roper said Collective Shout aimed to bring positive change that would "create a different world for our daughters".

"My greatest hope for this report is that the next woman who speaks out against male violence is protected, not punished for refusing to be silenced," said group member Renee Chopping.

World.title: Cult leader 'Little Pebble' found not guilty of grooming 7yo girl
World.content:
A doomsday cult leader has been cleared of allegations he groomed a seven-year-old girl for more than a decade.

William Kamm, who calls himself Little Pebble, faced a five-week trial at Sydney's Downing Centre District Court alongside his wife Sandra Susan Mathison.

They were both charged with grooming a child for unlawful sexual activity and grooming a child under 14 for unlawful sexual activity.

Mr Kamm, 76, and Ms Mathison, 60, were acquitted of all counts. The cult leader said "God bless the judge" outside the court.

William Kamm in 1988. (Supplied)

Judge Nicole Noman handed down her verdict after hearing evidence from the complainant, her relatives, corrections officers and police throughout the judge-alone trial last month.

Mr Kamm had pleaded not guilty to two counts of breaching an extended supervision order and inciting a person to do a sexual act with them in circumstances of aggravation. He was also cleared of those charges.

The convicted paedophile has a compound known as the Order of St Charbel in Bangalee on the NSW South Coast.

Court orders resulting from prior offending against a young girl have restricted him from returning there for years.

Judge Noman accepted the account that Kamm and Mathison had a plan for the complainant to become Kamm's spouse, but the evidence was not strong enough to prove beyond a reasonable doubt whether this would occur before she was 16.

Mr Kamm has been on bail for the duration of the trial.

The allegations

The complainant, now in her 20s, gave evidence throughout the trial and alleged she had been subjected to grooming and manipulation by Mr Kamm, beginning when she was seven.

William Kamm is the self-proclaimed leader of a cult that continues to operate on the NSW South Coast. (ABC Illawarra: Ainslie Drewitt Smith)

She alleged Mr Kamm whispered in code in a hoarse voice through recorded calls from Long Bay prison that she would be his "main queen" and begin a "new era" for their cult.

The court had heard Ms Mathison, who joined Mr Kamm's cult in 1984, facilitated the calls between Mr Kamm and the child by taking her into a room and putting the phone on loudspeaker.

William Kamm arrives at the Downing Centre in Sydney on June 23. (ABC News: Julia Andre)

The judge noted the complainant had the unenviable position of recounting more than a decade's worth of events, but found her evidence was truthful, although she was "mistaken" about some details.

Leaving the cult

Sandra Mathison and William Kamm being arrested in 2024. (ABC Illawarra: Supplied NSW Police)

As the complainant got older, she testified that she began experiencing panic attacks and suicidal thoughts as Mr Kamm's grooming allegedly escalated to forcing her to perform sexual acts during phone calls.

The judge found that while Mr Kamm was in a position of power over the complainant, the evidence was not strong enough to prove that he knew she was not consenting to masturbating over the phone with him.

Mr Kamm and the girl never met due to COVID-19 lockdown restrictions, which prevented him from leaving Sydney.

World.title: Ballarat man accused of raping teenager at neighbour's home
World.content:
Prosecutors say a Ballarat man raped a 16-year-old and later denied the accusation when she asked what his girlfriend would think about it.

Lachlan Young has pleaded not guilty to one count of rape, with his defence team telling a County Court jury he refuted allegations that any sexual intercourse occurred.

Prosecutor Andrew Buckland read a transcript of Snapchat messages between the pair, which occurred weeks after the alleged rape at Mr Young's neighbour's property on February 5, 2024.

"How's ya Missus, how would she feel about u f***ing an underage and cheating on her," the girl wrote on February 11.

In a message on February 29, she wrote, "Did you tell [your neighbour] about the night u f***ed me".

The next day, Young replied: "what are you on about?"

"Ur pathetic Lachie u literally f***ed me even though I said no at [the neighbour's] house," the girl responded.

Mr Young then blocked her, preventing further communication.

Alleged attack occurred in neighbour's backyard

Earlier on Thursday, Mr Young sat in the court dock in a charcoal suit and dark tie as 10 men and two women were selected for the jury.

The prosecutor said Mr Young first met the complainant, who cannot be identified for legal reasons, at his neighbour's Sebastopol house on February 4, 2024.

Mr Buckland said Mr Young, then aged 21, was socialising with teenagers, some of whom were visiting from another Victorian town.

Mr Young's trial is taking place in the County Court in Melbourne. ( ABC News: Danielle Bonica )

The prosecutor said in the early hours of February 5, Mr Young sent a Snapchat message to the girl saying he wanted to "do things".

"Come on please, just 5 minutes and I'll make it worth it," Mr Young is alleged to have said, when she told him she was 16.

The girl agreed to meet Mr Young in the backyard where the pair engaged in consensual sexual touching, Mr Buckland said.

However, the prosecutor said, Mr Young then forced the teenager to have sexual intercourse against her will.

"[The complainant] states that when this occurred she just kind of froze and didn't know what to do," Mr Buckland said.

"When the accused stopped he looked at [the complainant] and said, 'You should probably go back inside before people start looking for you'."

Later on February 5, Mr Young is alleged to have messaged the girl, "We didn't do much anyway".

Mr Buckland said the girl later disclosed allegations of the rape to a school counsellor and participated in a police interview on April 2, 2024.

Defence questions complainant's honesty

Defence barrister Glenn Casement said consensual sexual touching did occur between his client and the teenager, but denied it went any further.

He said the complainant's credibility and reliability would be the key issue for the jury to assess.

"Will you find her in this trial to be a witness of truth or someone telling unfortunate untruths and someone whose word you will only come to question and mistrust?" he said.

Mr Casement told the jury to listen out for changes in the complainant's story, which he said may play out in pre-recorded evidence played in court.

The defence barrister said the complainant found out about the existence of Mr Young's girlfriend and was "confronting him" about his honesty when she messaged him on February 11, 2024.

"At the end of this trial are you going to be left with troubling concerns on your hands about the role that this has played in the case?"

The trial, before Judge Caitlin English, continues.

World.title: 'I'll remember the people': Sidebottom among retiring AFL premiership duo
World.content:
Collingwood great Steele Sidebottom has officially told Magpies teammates he will be retiring at season's end.

The dual Magpies premiership hero's announcement on Thursday comes just hours after Richmond midfielder Dion Prestia also called it quits.

Debuting in 2009, Sidebottom has played 373 AFL games — the second most in Collingwood's storied history, only behind Scott Pendlebury.

A member of the Magpies' 2010 premiership side as a 19-year-old, Sidebottom then kicked a famous goal late in the 2023 grand final to help seal the club's next flag 13 years later.

Sidebottom (left) and Scott Pendlebury (right) have played the most matches together as teammates in VFL/AFL history. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

With Collingwood guaranteed to be in the wildcard round of the finals, at least, Sidebottom will be hoping for a fairytale farewell.

The versatile midfielder won Collingwood's Copeland Trophy in 2017 and 2018, also earning All-Australian honours once.

"As a young kid from 'Tally' [Tallygaroopna], I could never imagine I'd finish my AFL career with over 370 games, two premierships and 18 years of memories," Sidebottom said.

"When I look back on my time at Collingwood, I'll remember the people.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"So many teammates, coaches, staff and volunteers have invested their time and energy into helping me along the way."

Sidebottom might not be the only senior Collingwood player to retire this year, with Pendlebury also weighing up his future after breaking the VFL/AFL games record in May.

The Magpies have the oldest list in the AFL and are attempting to stay in premiership contention with a group in transition.

At Richmond, Prestia has joined premiership teammate Nathan Broad in ending his career.

After starting his career with Gold Coast, Prestia enjoyed instant success after making the switch to the Tigers in 2017.

Prestia won three premierships in his first four seasons with Richmond after joining at the end of 2016. (Getty Images: Mackenzie Sweetnam)

The midfielder played in three premierships (2017, 2019, 2020) in his first four seasons at Richmond.

Despite being riddled by injury in 2020 and restricted to just five games during the pandemic season, Prestia returned to play an important role in all four of the Tigers' finals.

"I felt like a Richmond man from the very beginning," Prestia said.

"My decision to come to Richmond was not to prove what I could do, but to be a part of a club that I saw potential for greatness, and didn't we prove that right?"

Prestia and Broad will be given a farewell in front of the Richmond army this Saturday when the Tigers host St Kilda at the MCG.

AAP

World.title: Three Sydney boys charged with gang sexual assault of 14yo girl
World.content:
Three boys have been charged over the alleged sexual assault of a 14-year-old girl in Sydney's eastern suburbs.

Police said it was alleged the girl was sexually assaulted by three boys in an alleyway on July 22.

Officers executed search warrants at several homes in the city's east on Thursday and three boys, one aged 13 and two aged 14 who attend The Scots College private school in Bellevue Hill, were arrested and taken to Surry Hills Police Station.

A 13-year-old and 14-year-old boy were later charged with aggravated sexual assault in the company of others and two counts of aggravated sexual touching of another person.

The other 14-year-old has been charged with a single count of the same offences.

Electronic devices were seized in the searches and would be forensically examined, police said.

Two replica firearms, a Glock-style BB gun, three laser pointers and a number plate, which is believed to have been stolen, were also seized.

The three boys have been granted bail.

School vows to cooperate with police

The Scots College in a statement confirmed the three boys under investigation by police over the alleged gang attack were students.

"The college takes this matter seriously and has cooperated, and will continue to cooperate, with police as required," the school said. "We believe it is important that the police investigation is allowed to take its course and it would not be appropriate for the college to comment further on the matter."

The boys are scheduled to face children's court later this month.

World.title: Australia v Bangladesh LIVE: Starc claims early scalp after Australia rolled; Ash Gardner apologises to her ex
World.content:
Australian women’s vice captain Ash Gardner has taken to social media on Thursday afternoon to publicly apologise to her ex, Monica.

Australian vice captain Ash Gardner’s Instagram story. Instagram

After Cricket Australia CEO Todd Greenberg told this masthead earlier that Gardner would have to recuse herself from any leadership meetings about the selection of her current partner, teammate Georgia Voll, Gardner said she was “grateful that the CA board has chosen to support my continued leadership”.

“While my separation from my wife is a personal matter, I understand my current relationship status needed to be addressed by Cricket Australia given my position as vice captain,” she posted to her Instagram story.

“I am grateful for the time Monica and I shared and sorry for the pain this has caused. I wish her nothing but happiness and success in the future.”

Gardner said she looks forward to continuing her leadership role.

“I won’t be making any further public comment on this matter at this time and ask that the privacy of those involved is respected,” she added.

World.title: Bold, crunch-topped pork noodles to rival your local
World.content:
Step 1 Preheat oven to 200C fan-forced (220C conventional) and line a baking tray with aluminium foil.

Step 2 Combine the sesame oil, garlic, sesame seeds and chilli flakes in a small frying pan. Cook gently for 6 minutes, or until garlic turns golden – keep an eye on it so it doesn’t burn. Set aside.

Step 3 Meanwhile, cook the noodles in salted boiling water for 3-4 minutes, or until tender. Drain and set aside.

Step 4 Heat half the oil in a large frying pan over high heat. Add the pork and cook, turning for 3-4 minutes, or until golden on all sides. Place on the prepared tray, brush with half the kecap manis and place the tray in the oven. Roast for 10-12 minutes, or until caramelised. Transfer to a plate and leave to rest, loosely covered.

Step 5 Place the large frying pan back over high heat with the remaining oil. Add the sugar snap peas, wombok, remaining kecap manis, and Shaoxing wine. Stir-fry for 3-4 minutes, or until tender and lightly charred.

World.title: Dominic Perrottet ‘favourable’ to Reformers-linked firm run by his ex-staffer
World.content:
ICAC’s Operation Rosny is investigating property developer Jean Nassif’s links to political powerbrokers, councils and Catholic schools. See all stories .

The then-treasurer Dominic Perrottet backed the Reformers-linked company Beckington when he was asked for advice on Catholic Schools NSW signing a contract with the fledgling government relations firm. Catholic Schools NSW boss Dallas McInerney told the Independent Commission Against Corruption on Thursday that he had sought Perrottet’s views before signing a contract with Beckington as the firm’s first client. Catholic Schools NSW chief executive Dallas McInerney is chaperoned from the ICAC after giving evidence on Thursday. Sam Mooy Liberal powerbroker and Reformers member Christian Ellis, who worked for Perrottet in his electorate office between 2012 and 2015, set up Beckington with another party operative, Jeremy Greenwood. The commission is investigating whether Beckington issued sham invoices to Catholic Schools NSW, which were approved by McInerney, to disguise political donations, among other allegations.



McInerney also told the commission that he never asked federal Liberal Leader Angus Taylor to fund the Reformers, after earlier claims emerged that Taylor had agreed to bankroll the conservative religious faction. The commission heard sensational evidence that in 2021 Taylor committed to a $15,000 “injection” to the Reformers with regular $3000 donations. Taylor has repeatedly denied any payments to the Reformers. Federal Opposition Leader Angus Taylor at a retirement village in Canberra on Thursday. Alex Ellinghausen McInerney told the commission that Reformers member Dylan Whitelaw may have lied when he told factional allies in a text message about the alleged money from Taylor. Ellis established Beckington after he was sacked in October 2019 from the office of Damien Tudehope, who was then a senior Liberal minister. His employment was terminated because Tudehope was concerned he was carrying out factional work during work hours.



Ellis first approached McInerney to pitch his services in April 2019, before Beckington was registered in July. McInerney said he knew this because he had received a draft introductory letter at that time. McInerney told the commission that he asked Perrottet for advice while he was considering a contract with Beckington to ensure Ellis and Greenwood had the respect and “entrée” into the then Coalition government. “I thought it was important to check in with a senior member of the government whether or not there was any reasons why this consultancy shouldn’t be taken on,” McInerney told the commission. Perrottet was “favourable”, McInerney said. He did not discuss the work of the Reformers during this conversation, he said.



“He knew both of the individuals concerned. He was aware that they were setting up their own shop, if you like, and there was no advice to give concern or pause,” McInerney said. Counsel assisting Juliet Curtin asked McInerney why he had not also sought the views of Tudehope, given Ellis had recently worked in his office. He said Perrottet was the treasurer at the time and a more senior member of the government. Loading Earlier in his evidence, McInerney described the Reformers as “spectacularly unsuccessful” in their mission to push conservative values within the Liberal Party. The schools’ body chief, who has stood aside from his role pending this inquiry, told the commission he was “mostly” supportive of the work of the Reformers, but their model was not right.



Curtin asked McInerney whether fellow Liberals Ellis, Robert Assaf and Jean-Claude Perrottet were fervent or passionate Reformers. He instead described their factional work as “a calling for them, a duty”. McInerney was also asked whether he had harboured political ambitions to run for parliament. He said he was interested in public office at different stages and had believed there was a deal in place with the late senator Jim Molan, which would have seen McInerney replace him. However, Molan ultimately did not retire. Curtin put to McInerney: “You backed Mr Molan on the mutual expectation that he would retire partway through the Senate term and help facilitate you taking over a Senate seat, is that correct?”



“That’s what Molan put to me,” McInerney said. Asked whether he was disappointed Molan did not retire and make way for him, McInerney said he was not sure how he felt at the time. In a message shown to the ICAC, it was revealed that McInerney told Greenwood: “I know I’ve been f---ed. I could have won the preselection there. [Matt] Camenzuli and [Lou] Amato ... and Connie [Concetta Fierravanti-Wells] have been doing anyone but Dallas campaign for months.” Lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood departs the ICAC Operation Rosny hearings on Wednesday. George Chan “Yeah, it’s f---ed. It’s f---ed. It’s f---ed,” McInerney’s message to Greenwood said. Meanwhile, NSW Liberal leader Kellie Sloane has replaced opposition planning spokesman Chris Rath as her representative on the party’s powerful state executive after it emerged the senior frontbencher helped fellow party members avoid providing evidence to a key parliamentary inquiry.



On Wednesday, the ICAC heard Rath was integral in helping Greenwood, as well as Jean-Claude Perrottet and his brother Charles, avoid attending the 2023 inquiry by keeping them abreast of the committee’s deliberations. Rath was a member of the committee. Related Article Live

Operation Rosny ICAC Operation Rosny as it happened: Catholic Schools NSW CEO Dallas McInerney denies claims over Angus Taylor funding commitment, says Reformer Dylan Whitelaw may have ‘lied’ That parliamentary inquiry into illegal donations and the Hills Shire Council was one of the catalysts for this ICAC inquiry, which is also investigating Nassif’s links to Liberal operatives and payments from Catholic Schools NSW to the Reformers. Sloane has declined to take any further action against Rath, who also took a photograph of a committee document and forwarded it to key witnesses involved in the parliamentary inquiry. He remains on her frontbench. Tudehope stood aside from her shadow cabinet because of his links to several persons of interest to the ICAC.

World.title: ‘We’re in some difficult territory’: Gardner sidelined from Voll selection talks
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket ‘We’re in some difficult territory’: Gardner sidelined from Voll selection talks Daniel Brettig August 13, 2026 — 5:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Darwin: Ash Gardner has been endorsed to continue as Australia’s vice captain by the Cricket Australia board, but will have to leave any leadership meeting when the selection of her partner Georgia Voll is discussed. The relationship between Gardner and Voll, which commenced at last year’s ODI World Cup in India and led to the breakup of Gardner’s marriage, has been tabloid fodder in recent weeks, leading to further CA conversations around her role as Sophie Molineux’s deputy. Ash Gardner with the T20 World Cup trophy at Lord’s. AP Photo CA chief executive Todd Greenberg said it was important that any conflict of interest, either perceived or actual, was handled transparently for the sakes of Gardner, Voll and the team, which recently won the Twenty20 World Cup in the UK. As vice captain, Gardner is not a selector either at home or on overseas tours, but she is part of leadership meetings and may be consulted about team selection from time to time.



“It wasn’t debated, but it was discussed yesterday at the board level,” Greenberg told this masthead on Thursday. “The board asked for an update on it, which we provided, and the outcome of that is the board are very supportive of Ash in the vice captaincy, [with a] huge and high regard for Ash. Editor's pick Exclusive

Australian cricket Cricket Australia parts ways with betting sponsor in 15-year first “We’ve got a respect at work policy, which we’ve now put some additional measures in place because we want to make sure that either the perception or the real conflict of [interest in] selections, even though a vice captain doesn’t have a say in selections in the team, the leadership role and the influence that that person might have, to put guardrails in about how the policy works. Outside of that, we’ve deemed it a personal matter.” Asked directly whether Gardner would have to recuse herself from any discussions of Voll with Molineux, coach Shelley Nitschke or the national selectors, Greenberg confirmed she would.



“We think that’s important,” he said. “Even if there’s not a conflict, even if there’s a perceived level of conflict, not just from the outside, but from other teammates or from staff. We’re in some difficult territory here because, like all sports, we’re all learning a little bit about how these high-performance environments can operate. “So we want to be making sure that our policies are keeping up with the realities, and I think that’s exactly what we’ve done. So the board was super supportive of Ash, and have been since the start.” Greenberg also confirmed CA was in the market for another betting sponsor following the end of its long-term deal with Bet365, but acknowledged that imminent changes to government legislation around gambling advertising would likely reduce the next partner’s visibility and the dollar value of the deal. Toyota has replaced Bet365 on the boundary rope signage at Test matches, and Greenberg said that conversations had evolved to how to communicate with existing customers of wagering companies without advertising aggressively to the wider public. “We’re in active conversations with partners, and you know we’re not shying away from that,” Greenberg said. “We’ve purposely kept it out of the Big Bash for obvious reasons. But [it’s] highly probable we’ll have a wagering partner for the summer.



Georgia Voll hits a boundary last summer. Getty Images “But there’s no doubt that the legislative changes will make that slightly more difficult in order to execute a deal, because it may not be as lucrative for them. So we understand the realities of that, but that’s the reality we have to deal with as part of the changes that have been made by government. “If it’s at a certain level now, it’s only going to get lower, not higher. The wagering partnerships are less about above-the-line activity, and it’s more about how do they talk to people who want to bet? Because betting is a pastime for lots of people in this country, and so there’s lots of people who like to bet on cricket. We’ve got to figure out how we talk to those people and not talk to our broader audience.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: From petri dish to patient:biotech’s formidable obstacle course
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears From petri dish to patient:biotech’s formidable obstacle course Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward August 13, 2026 — 5:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In biotech, discovering something that can change medicine might just be the easy part. Getting it from a laboratory bench into a hospital, or pathology clinic can actually present as many, if not more challenges than uncovering the discovery itself. Imagine a hypothetical ASX junior we’ll call XYZ Bio. Its scientists have discovered a molecule they believe could treat an aggressive cancer. Laboratory results look terrific, management understandably gets excited and investors start reaching for their calculators. A simple rejigging of the pit shell and cut-off grades against today’s much higher gold price could potentially add fresh ounces that were previously considered uneconomic, essentially hiding in plain sight. Microbial growth growing inside a petri dish Well, maybe. XYZ Bio doesn’t have a medicine yet. What it has is a promising scientific proposition.



Between that discovery and the first commercial sale sits one of the toughest obstacle courses in business. Laboratory research, pre-clinical testing, human trials, manufacturing, regulators, intellectual property, mountains of capital, and eventually, convincing doctors and patients the product is actually worth using. And there is no single course through this heady maze. Drugs, vaccines, diagnostics, medical devices, cell and gene therapies and medical software can all take different routes to market. What they all share however, is the need to progressively turn scientific promise into hard evidence. For investors, knowing exactly where a biotech sits on that journey can be every bit as important as understanding the science itself. XYZ Bio starts in the laboratory. Scientists identify a biological target, develop something designed to influence it and begin testing whether the theory stacks up. That can progress into pre-clinical studies examining activity, dosing, toxicity and how a potential treatment behaves inside a biological system. On paper, the road from there looks remarkably orderly. But biology frequently has other ideas.



Something can perform beautifully in a laboratory dish or animal model and behave very differently in a human being. That makes building the evidence required to bridge laboratory science and clinical development a critical early hurdle. NeuroScientific Biopharmaceuticals is currently negotiating that part of the journey through its work across immune-mediated inflammatory and neurological conditions, building the scientific and pre-clinical evidence required to advance its technologies towards clinical application.Interestingly, the company today announced that it was sitting down with the FDA at the end of August where the FDA will review the company’s clinical,scientific and product development plan for its StemSmart product for Crohn’s disease to make sure its up to scratch for a formal Investigational New Drug submission slated for the end of this year. To be clear, pre-clinical evidence isn’t second-rate evidence. It is answering an important earlier set of questions; whether the biology is sufficiently compelling, whether a potential treatment produces the intended effect and whether the evidence supports taking the next step. The considerably more expensive question of what happens in humans comes later. Perth-based Argenica Therapeutics has already crossed that divide with ARG-007, its neuroprotective peptide. After extensive pre-clinical work, ARG-007 moved into its first human safety study and then progressed into Phase II testing in acute ischaemic stroke patients. And the questions being asked are changing along the way.



First, is the scientific proposition worth pursuing? Then, can humans safely tolerate it? Only then can the clinical program start to address the question shareholders ultimately want answered; which is can the treatment improve outcomes in patients? For a conventional drug, that progression broadly runs through Phase I, Phase II and Phase III trials. Phase I generally concentrates on safety, tolerability and dosage. Phase II starts providing more meaningful evidence about efficacy while continuing to assess safety. Phase III typically tests the treatment across larger populations and provides pivotal evidence necessary for regulatory approval. And with every step, the stakes, and usually the bills, get bigger. Which is why “positive trial” should never be the endgame of anyone’s reading of an ASX announcement. What was the trial designed to prove? Was its primary endpoint met? How many patients were enrolled? Was there a control group? Was the improvement clinically meaningful and statistically convincing? An encouraging signal from a small group of patients and compelling evidence from a large, controlled study are very different beasts.



Amplia Therapeutics is negotiating that clinical-development hurdle with narmafotinib, its lead drug candidate for pancreatic cancer. Its Phase 1b/2a ACCENT study has generated high quality clinical evidence, including an outstanding objective response rate of 35.9 per cent among 64 patients receiving the 400mg dose showing a deep reduction in tumour size, along with a vanishingly rare five responses where the cancer completely disappeared. Median overall survival was reported at 11.1 months representing a significant 30 per cent improvement on chemotherapy alone. Those highly encouraging results have allowed Amplia to turn its attention to the next stage of development as it builds the further evidence required to potentially progress towards a registrational Phase III study. That is how biotech value can be built; one successful stage providing the evidence and confidence needed to attempt the next, usually more difficult and expensive, one. But then, somebody also has to pay for it. For a small ASX biotech without significant commercial revenue, cash runway can become almost as important as clinical runway. Capital raisings, licensing agreements and pharmaceutical partnerships can all form part of financing an expensive development program. Dilution isn’t necessarily a bad thing. The better question is what the new money can potentially achieve before the hat needs to be passed around again. And while the clinical trials are attracting the headlines, another question critical to the development puzzle is probably being asked behind the scenes - who is going to make the stuff?



Manufacturing doesn’t suddenly appear after Phase III. A developer needs suitable material for pre-clinical work and clinical trials, with manufacturing standards, consistency and quality requirements becoming progressively more demanding as the product moves closer towards market. That challenge becomes particularly complex with biologics and sophisticated DNA and RNA medicines. Perth-based Syngenis is building capability in precisely this part of the pathway, specialising in synthetic DNA and RNA molecules known as oligonucleotides used across therapeutic, diagnostic and research applications. For products destined for clinical use, Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) becomes crucial. Strip away the regulatory language and the principle is straightforward, you need to be able to make the right product, the same way, repeatedly and to the required quality. Syngenis is developing its manufacturing capability towards clinical-grade production, positioning the business to participate in a part of the biotech value chain that becomes increasingly important as DNA and RNA therapeutics advance. It is also developing a broader platform approach around oligonucleotide discovery and manufacture, potentially allowing it to participate across multiple products and development programs rather than staking everything on one drug. For XYZ Bio meanwhile, the clinical evidence is eventually assembled. Management might be eyeing the champagne fridge. Shareholders might be eyeing their calculators. But crucially, the regulator is eyeing another pile of evidence. Approval isn’t the end of regulatory oversight. Medicines continue to be monitored after reaching the market because rare safety issues can sometimes emerge only when much larger populations start using them.



That, broadly, is the conventional drug highway: discovery, pre- clinical evidence, human trials, increasingly demanding manufacturing and quality requirements, regulatory review and eventually, if all goes well, approval. But plenty of biotechs aren’t driving down that exact road. Vaccines travel through a broadly similar pre-clinical and clinical framework, although the equation changes because they can ultimately be administered to enormous numbers of otherwise healthy people. And because of this, the pathway vaccines have to tread can diverge quite significantly. Digital illustration of a DNA double helix strand. Safety becomes paramount and developers need to demonstrate immune response effectiveness and manufacturing consistency. Government procurement, public-health recommendations and competing products can then become important parts of the commercial equation. Head across to diagnostics and again, the road looks like a different proposition. Perth-based Proteomics International is negotiating that pathway through its Promarker platform, which uses protein biomarkers to develop diagnostic tests targeting diseases including diabetic kidney disease and endometriosis.



A diagnostic doesn’t necessarily march through conventional Phase I, II and III trials. Instead, developers need to prove that the test reliably does what it says on the tin. At this point, two numbers suddenly become very important; sensitivity and specificity. In simple terms, how good is the test at finding people who have the condition and how good is it at avoiding false alarms among those who don’t? Proteomics has progressively worked through that evidentiary pathway with clinical validation of its Promarker technology while also building intellectual-property protection around its diagnostic pipeline. PromarkerD has moved through to commercialisation, while PromarkerEndo has continued advancing towards commercial readiness and secured US patent protection, an important piece of the puzzle in the world’s largest healthcare market. Clearing those scientific and intellectual-property hurdles then brings a diagnostic developer to the commercial ones, getting pathology providers to offer the test, doctors to order it and healthcare systems to potentially reimburse it.



Medical devices and software take us down another branch. Perth-based Singular Health has been working its way through that pathway with 3DICOM, its technology for converting conventional medical images into advanced three-dimensional visualisations. Its desktop 3DICOM MD received US FDA 510(k) clearance, the official green light to sell a medical device, in 2022 and its cloud-based 3DICOM MD Cloud followed in January this year. Those clearances represent significant regulatory milestones and open opportunities in the enormous US healthcare market. There were no conventional Phase I, II and III drug trials because the regulatory hurdle was different. Medical devices are generally regulated according to the risks they pose, while software itself can qualify as a medical device depending on its intended purpose. Across Perth, Resonance Health offers a glimpse further down that road. Its medical-imaging technologies have progressed through development and regulatory clearances into international healthcare markets. For Resonance the challenge has shifted from getting technology approved to building commercial activity around it. Then there are technologies that make swallowing a tablet seem positively quaint. Cell therapies, gene therapies and gene editing can involve modifying cells, introducing genetic material or attacking disease through entirely different biological mechanisms.



Arovella Therapeutics has been negotiating that particularly complex pathway with its off-the-shelf CAR-iNKT cell-therapy platform targeting cancer. Advanced therapies can bring development, manufacturing and clinical delivery much closer together. Pre-clinical evidence has to be assembled, the therapy manufactured to the required standards, regulators satisfied, ethics approvals secured and clinical sites prepared before the first patient can be treated. This image is a close-up micrograph of human colorectal cancer cells captured using fluorescence microscopy Working through those steps is itself a major development exercise and demonstrates why an announcement saying biotech is “moving towards the clinic” can cover a considerable amount of territory. Different roads, then, but ultimately they all arrive at the same point being posed the same commercial question. Can somebody build a market for the product? Perth-based Orthocell provides a useful example of how a company tackles that transition. Its Remplir nerve-repair product received US FDA 510(k) clearance in April 2025, opening the door to the enormous American market. The company has since been putting the pieces required for commercialisation in place, including manufacturing, US warehousing, order processing and distribution, alongside engagement with the surgeons who ultimately use the product.



That is a different skill set from laboratory discovery or running a clinical trial, but no less important to the final outcome. FDA clearance opens the door. Manufacturing, distribution, reimbursement and clinician adoption help a company walk through it. Back at XYZ Bio, the same commercial reality eventually arrives. After years of research, trials, manufacturing work, regulatory scrutiny and capital raising, it finally has a cancer drug it is legally allowed to sell. Now it needs doctors to prescribe it, healthcare systems to pay for it and patients to benefit from it. And this is where biotech investors can sometimes get ahead of themselves. A company announces a breakthrough, the share price jumps and suddenly everyone is multiplying a gigantic addressable market by five per cent and buying a new boat on paper. The better question is much less exciting. What has actually been proven? Where is the company on the obstacle course? What hurdle has it just cleared? What other hurdles need to be jumped? What will getting there cost? And if everything works, who is going to pay for it? Taken together, the Australian companies scattered along our obstacle course show just how many different battles can sit between a bright idea and a commercial product. NeuroScientific is building the pre clinical evidence needed to move to Pre Investigational Drug status and from there to Phase 2 trials in humans. Argenica has crossed from clinical development into human Phase 2b trials and Amplia is at the clinical stage progressing to 1b/2b clinical trials to keep pushing narmafotinib forward. Syngenis, meanwhile, is tackling the manufacturing challenge behind increasingly sophisticated genetic medicines.



On different branches of the same journey, Proteomics is progressing diagnostics through validation, intellectual property and towards commercial adoption, while Singular has negotiated US medical-device clearance and Resonance shows what that pathway can look like once medical technology reaches international markets. Arovella is working through the complex steps required to bring an advanced cell therapy into patients, while Orthocell is tackling the job at the other end – converting regulatory clearance into manufacturing, distribution and clinical adoption. Different technologies. Different hurdles. Different stages. But together they provide a pretty good snapshot of what it takes to turn promising science into something that can actually reach a patient.And for punters every one of those hurdles successfully cleared can remove another layer of uncertainty and potentially another discount applied to what the science might ultimately be worth. That is the attraction of biotech. Successfully turning an idea conceived in a laboratory into a drug, vaccine, diagnostic, cell therapy or medical technology capable of improving patients’ lives can create enormous value. But a gigantic market at the end of the road doesn’t make the road any shorter. In biotech, the treasure at the end of the obstacle course can be enormous. There’s a reason for that. Getting there is bloody hard.

World.title: Alan Jones trial as it happened: Mother of complainant ‘J’ gives evidence after legal issue triggers adjournment
World.content:
Thank you for reading our live coverage of day seven of Alan Jones’ indecent assault and sexual touching trial in the NSW Local Court in Sydney.

A trio of witnesses related to the first complainant in the case, witness “J”, completed their evidence today and a new witness, complainant “C”, is expected to start giving evidence tomorrow morning.

Alan Jones outside the Downing Centre Local Court on Thursday. Oscar Colman

This was the key evidence today:

The mother of “J” told the court that she was in shock and told her son she should have protected him after he told her that Alan Jones had touched him inappropriately. She said “J” had initially denied that Jones had touched him after she asked him directly when allegations about the former broadcaster appeared in the media. However, she said that he told her a year later that he had lied.

She said Jones had given her gifts including a dishwasher, and that she had visited the then 2GB host’s Fitzroy Falls farm in the NSW Southern Highlands with her family.

A former coach of “J” told the court that Jones had helped the young athlete financially. The court has heard “J” did not raise any concerns about Jones with his then coach.

The former coach said that it appeared to him at the time that some of the complainant’s “most enjoyable experiences came from his association with Alan”, including meeting celebrities.

An ex-girlfriend of “J” who has given evidence that the then athlete confided in her 20 years ago that Jones touched him inappropriately was grilled by the veteran broadcaster’s barrister about text messages the complainant sent her after she gave a police statement. “J” promised to “look after” her, the court heard. She did not interpret this as a promise of financial support, the woman told the court.

The trial resumes at 10am tomorrow.

World.title: Australia v Bangladesh LIVE: Starc claims early scalp after Australia rolled; Ash Gardner apologises to her ex
World.content:
Australian women’s vice captain Ash Gardner has taken to social media on Thursday afternoon to publicly apologise to her ex, Monica.

Australian vice captain Ash Gardner’s Instagram story. Instagram

After Cricket Australia CEO Todd Greenberg told this masthead earlier that Gardner would have to recuse herself from any leadership meetings about the selection of her current partner, teammate Georgia Voll, Gardner said she was “grateful that the CA board has chosen to support my continued leadership”.

“While my separation from my wife is a personal matter, I understand my current relationship status needed to be addressed by Cricket Australia given my position as vice captain,” she posted to her Instagram story.

“I am grateful for the time Monica and I shared and sorry for the pain this has caused. I wish her nothing but happiness and success in the future.”

Gardner said she looks forward to continuing her leadership role.

“I won’t be making any further public comment on this matter at this time and ask that the privacy of those involved is respected,” she added.

World.title: Bold, crunch-topped pork noodles to rival your local
World.content:
Step 1 Preheat oven to 200C fan-forced (220C conventional) and line a baking tray with aluminium foil.

Step 2 Combine the sesame oil, garlic, sesame seeds and chilli flakes in a small frying pan. Cook gently for 6 minutes, or until garlic turns golden – keep an eye on it so it doesn’t burn. Set aside.

Step 3 Meanwhile, cook the noodles in salted boiling water for 3-4 minutes, or until tender. Drain and set aside.

Step 4 Heat half the oil in a large frying pan over high heat. Add the pork and cook, turning for 3-4 minutes, or until golden on all sides. Place on the prepared tray, brush with half the kecap manis and place the tray in the oven. Roast for 10-12 minutes, or until caramelised. Transfer to a plate and leave to rest, loosely covered.

Step 5 Place the large frying pan back over high heat with the remaining oil. Add the sugar snap peas, wombok, remaining kecap manis, and Shaoxing wine. Stir-fry for 3-4 minutes, or until tender and lightly charred.
