World.title: Dominic Perrottet ‘favourable’ to Reformers-linked firm run by his ex-staffer
World.content:
ICAC’s Operation Rosny is investigating property developer Jean Nassif’s links to political powerbrokers, councils and Catholic schools. See all stories .

The then-treasurer Dominic Perrottet backed the Reformers-linked company Beckington when he was asked for advice on Catholic Schools NSW signing a contract with the fledgling government relations firm. Catholic Schools NSW boss Dallas McInerney told the Independent Commission Against Corruption on Thursday that he had sought Perrottet’s views before signing a contract with Beckington as the firm’s first client. Catholic Schools NSW chief executive Dallas McInerney is chaperoned from the ICAC after giving evidence on Thursday. Sam Mooy Liberal powerbroker and Reformers member Christian Ellis, who worked for Perrottet in his electorate office between 2012 and 2015, set up Beckington with another party operative, Jeremy Greenwood. The commission is investigating whether Beckington issued sham invoices to Catholic Schools NSW, which were approved by McInerney, to disguise political donations, among other allegations.



McInerney also told the commission that he never asked federal Liberal Leader Angus Taylor to fund the Reformers, after earlier claims emerged that Taylor had agreed to bankroll the conservative religious faction. The commission heard sensational evidence that in 2021 Taylor committed to a $15,000 “injection” to the Reformers with regular $3000 donations. Taylor has repeatedly denied any payments to the Reformers. Federal Opposition Leader Angus Taylor at a retirement village in Canberra on Thursday. Alex Ellinghausen McInerney told the commission that Reformers member Dylan Whitelaw may have lied when he told factional allies in a text message about the alleged money from Taylor. Ellis established Beckington after he was sacked in October 2019 from the office of Damien Tudehope, who was then a senior Liberal minister. His employment was terminated because Tudehope was concerned he was carrying out factional work during work hours.



Ellis first approached McInerney to pitch his services in April 2019, before Beckington was registered in July. McInerney said he knew this because he had received a draft introductory letter at that time. McInerney told the commission that he asked Perrottet for advice while he was considering a contract with Beckington to ensure Ellis and Greenwood had the respect and “entrée” into the then Coalition government. “I thought it was important to check in with a senior member of the government whether or not there was any reasons why this consultancy shouldn’t be taken on,” McInerney told the commission. Perrottet was “favourable”, McInerney said. He did not discuss the work of the Reformers during this conversation, he said.



“He knew both of the individuals concerned. He was aware that they were setting up their own shop, if you like, and there was no advice to give concern or pause,” McInerney said. Counsel assisting Juliet Curtin asked McInerney why he had not also sought the views of Tudehope, given Ellis had recently worked in his office. He said Perrottet was the treasurer at the time and a more senior member of the government. Loading Earlier in his evidence, McInerney described the Reformers as “spectacularly unsuccessful” in their mission to push conservative values within the Liberal Party. The schools’ body chief, who has stood aside from his role pending this inquiry, told the commission he was “mostly” supportive of the work of the Reformers, but their model was not right.



Curtin asked McInerney whether fellow Liberals Ellis, Robert Assaf and Jean-Claude Perrottet were fervent or passionate Reformers. He instead described their factional work as “a calling for them, a duty”. McInerney was also asked whether he had harboured political ambitions to run for parliament. He said he was interested in public office at different stages and had believed there was a deal in place with the late senator Jim Molan, which would have seen McInerney replace him. However, Molan ultimately did not retire. Curtin put to McInerney: “You backed Mr Molan on the mutual expectation that he would retire partway through the Senate term and help facilitate you taking over a Senate seat, is that correct?”



“That’s what Molan put to me,” McInerney said. Asked whether he was disappointed Molan did not retire and make way for him, McInerney said he was not sure how he felt at the time. In a message shown to the ICAC, it was revealed that McInerney told Greenwood: “I know I’ve been f---ed. I could have won the preselection there. [Matt] Camenzuli and [Lou] Amato ... and Connie [Concetta Fierravanti-Wells] have been doing anyone but Dallas campaign for months.” Lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood departs the ICAC Operation Rosny hearings on Wednesday. George Chan “Yeah, it’s f---ed. It’s f---ed. It’s f---ed,” McInerney’s message to Greenwood said. Meanwhile, NSW Liberal leader Kellie Sloane has replaced opposition planning spokesman Chris Rath as her representative on the party’s powerful state executive after it emerged the senior frontbencher helped fellow party members avoid providing evidence to a key parliamentary inquiry.



On Wednesday, the ICAC heard Rath was integral in helping Greenwood, as well as Jean-Claude Perrottet and his brother Charles, avoid attending the 2023 inquiry by keeping them abreast of the committee’s deliberations. Rath was a member of the committee. Related Article Live

Operation Rosny ICAC Operation Rosny as it happened: Catholic Schools NSW CEO Dallas McInerney denies claims over Angus Taylor funding commitment, says Reformer Dylan Whitelaw may have ‘lied’ That parliamentary inquiry into illegal donations and the Hills Shire Council was one of the catalysts for this ICAC inquiry, which is also investigating Nassif’s links to Liberal operatives and payments from Catholic Schools NSW to the Reformers. Sloane has declined to take any further action against Rath, who also took a photograph of a committee document and forwarded it to key witnesses involved in the parliamentary inquiry. He remains on her frontbench. Tudehope stood aside from her shadow cabinet because of his links to several persons of interest to the ICAC.

World.title: ‘We’re in some difficult territory’: Gardner sidelined from Voll selection talks
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket ‘We’re in some difficult territory’: Gardner sidelined from Voll selection talks Daniel Brettig August 13, 2026 — 5:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Darwin: Ash Gardner has been endorsed to continue as Australia’s vice captain by the Cricket Australia board, but will have to leave any leadership meeting when the selection of her partner Georgia Voll is discussed. The relationship between Gardner and Voll, which commenced at last year’s ODI World Cup in India and led to the breakup of Gardner’s marriage, has been tabloid fodder in recent weeks, leading to further CA conversations around her role as Sophie Molineux’s deputy. Ash Gardner with the T20 World Cup trophy at Lord’s. AP Photo CA chief executive Todd Greenberg said it was important that any conflict of interest, either perceived or actual, was handled transparently for the sakes of Gardner, Voll and the team, which recently won the Twenty20 World Cup in the UK. As vice captain, Gardner is not a selector either at home or on overseas tours, but she is part of leadership meetings and may be consulted about team selection from time to time.



“It wasn’t debated, but it was discussed yesterday at the board level,” Greenberg told this masthead on Thursday. “The board asked for an update on it, which we provided, and the outcome of that is the board are very supportive of Ash in the vice captaincy, [with a] huge and high regard for Ash. Editor's pick Exclusive

Australian cricket Cricket Australia parts ways with betting sponsor in 15-year first “We’ve got a respect at work policy, which we’ve now put some additional measures in place because we want to make sure that either the perception or the real conflict of [interest in] selections, even though a vice captain doesn’t have a say in selections in the team, the leadership role and the influence that that person might have, to put guardrails in about how the policy works. Outside of that, we’ve deemed it a personal matter.” Asked directly whether Gardner would have to recuse herself from any discussions of Voll with Molineux, coach Shelley Nitschke or the national selectors, Greenberg confirmed she would.



“We think that’s important,” he said. “Even if there’s not a conflict, even if there’s a perceived level of conflict, not just from the outside, but from other teammates or from staff. We’re in some difficult territory here because, like all sports, we’re all learning a little bit about how these high-performance environments can operate. “So we want to be making sure that our policies are keeping up with the realities, and I think that’s exactly what we’ve done. So the board was super supportive of Ash, and have been since the start.” Greenberg also confirmed CA was in the market for another betting sponsor following the end of its long-term deal with Bet365, but acknowledged that imminent changes to government legislation around gambling advertising would likely reduce the next partner’s visibility and the dollar value of the deal. Toyota has replaced Bet365 on the boundary rope signage at Test matches, and Greenberg said that conversations had evolved to how to communicate with existing customers of wagering companies without advertising aggressively to the wider public. “We’re in active conversations with partners, and you know we’re not shying away from that,” Greenberg said. “We’ve purposely kept it out of the Big Bash for obvious reasons. But [it’s] highly probable we’ll have a wagering partner for the summer.



Georgia Voll hits a boundary last summer. Getty Images “But there’s no doubt that the legislative changes will make that slightly more difficult in order to execute a deal, because it may not be as lucrative for them. So we understand the realities of that, but that’s the reality we have to deal with as part of the changes that have been made by government. “If it’s at a certain level now, it’s only going to get lower, not higher. The wagering partnerships are less about above-the-line activity, and it’s more about how do they talk to people who want to bet? Because betting is a pastime for lots of people in this country, and so there’s lots of people who like to bet on cricket. We’ve got to figure out how we talk to those people and not talk to our broader audience.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Adam Liaw’s air-fryer roast vegetables with rosemary and feta
World.content:
Combine the garlic, broccoli, cauliflower, capsicum and onion together in a large bowl, then add the olive oil, smoked paprika and vegetable stock powder and season well with salt and pepper.

Step 2

Transfer to the basket of an air fryer, place the rosemary sprigs on top and cook for 15 minutes at 200C until the vegetables are very well browned. Transfer to a serving plate and scatter with the feta. Drizzle with a little extra olive oil and serve.

World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears From petri dish to patient:biotech’s formidable obstacle course Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward August 13, 2026 — 5:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In biotech, discovering something that can change medicine might just be the easy part. Getting it from a laboratory bench into a hospital, or pathology clinic can actually present as many, if not more challenges than uncovering the discovery itself. Imagine a hypothetical ASX junior we’ll call XYZ Bio. Its scientists have discovered a molecule they believe could treat an aggressive cancer. Laboratory results look terrific, management understandably gets excited and investors start reaching for their calculators. A simple rejigging of the pit shell and cut-off grades against today’s much higher gold price could potentially add fresh ounces that were previously considered uneconomic, essentially hiding in plain sight. Microbial growth growing inside a petri dish Well, maybe. XYZ Bio doesn’t have a medicine yet. What it has is a promising scientific proposition.



Between that discovery and the first commercial sale sits one of the toughest obstacle courses in business. Laboratory research, pre-clinical testing, human trials, manufacturing, regulators, intellectual property, mountains of capital, and eventually, convincing doctors and patients the product is actually worth using. And there is no single course through this heady maze. Drugs, vaccines, diagnostics, medical devices, cell and gene therapies and medical software can all take different routes to market. What they all share however, is the need to progressively turn scientific promise into hard evidence. For investors, knowing exactly where a biotech sits on that journey can be every bit as important as understanding the science itself. XYZ Bio starts in the laboratory. Scientists identify a biological target, develop something designed to influence it and begin testing whether the theory stacks up. That can progress into pre-clinical studies examining activity, dosing, toxicity and how a potential treatment behaves inside a biological system. On paper, the road from there looks remarkably orderly. But biology frequently has other ideas.

It is answering an important earlier set of questions; whether the biology is sufficiently compelling, whether a potential treatment produces the intended effect and whether the evidence supports taking the next step. The considerably more expensive question of what happens in humans comes later. Perth-based Argenica Therapeutics has already crossed that divide with ARG-007, its neuroprotective peptide. How many patients were enrolled? Was there a control group? Was the improvement clinically meaningful and statistically convincing? An encouraging signal from a small group of patients and compelling evidence from a large, controlled study are very different beasts.

Capital raisings, licensing agreements and pharmaceutical partnerships can all form part of financing an expensive development program. Dilution isn’t necessarily a bad thing. The better question is what the new money can potentially achieve before the hat needs to be passed around again. Perth-based Orthocell provides a useful example of how a company tackles that transition. Its Remplir nerve-repair product received US FDA 510(k) clearance in April 2025, opening the door to the enormous American market. The company has since been putting the pieces required for commercialisation in place, including manufacturing, US warehousing, order processing and distribution, alongside engagement with the surgeons who ultimately use the product.



That is a different skill set from laboratory discovery or running a clinical trial, but no less important to the final outcome. FDA clearance opens the door. Manufacturing, distribution, reimbursement and clinician adoption help a company walk through it. Back at XYZ Bio, the same commercial reality eventually arrives. After years of research, trials, manufacturing work, regulatory scrutiny and capital raising, it finally has a cancer drug it is legally allowed to sell. Now it needs doctors to prescribe it, healthcare systems to pay for it and patients to benefit from it. And this is where biotech investors can sometimes get ahead of themselves. A company announces a breakthrough, the share price jumps and suddenly everyone is multiplying a gigantic addressable market by five per cent and buying a new boat on paper. The better question is much less exciting. What has actually been proven? Where is the company on the obstacle course? What hurdle has it just cleared? What other hurdles need to be jumped? What will getting there cost? And if everything works, who is going to pay for it? Taken together, the Australian companies scattered along our obstacle course show just how many different battles can sit between a bright idea and a commercial product. NeuroScientific is building the pre clinical evidence needed to move to Pre Investigational Drug status and from there to Phase 2 trials in humans. Argenica has crossed from clinical development into human Phase 2b trials and Amplia is at the clinical stage progressing to 1b/2b clinical trials to keep pushing narmafotinib forward. Syngenis, meanwhile, is tackling the manufacturing challenge behind increasingly sophisticated genetic medicines.



On different branches of the same journey, Proteomics is progressing diagnostics through validation, intellectual property and towards commercial adoption, while Singular has negotiated US medical-device clearance and Resonance shows what that pathway can look like once medical technology reaches international markets. Arovella is working through the complex steps required to bring an advanced cell therapy into patients, while Orthocell is tackling the job at the other end – converting regulatory clearance into manufacturing, distribution and clinical adoption. Different technologies. Different hurdles. Different stages. But together they provide a pretty good snapshot of what it takes to turn promising science into something that can actually reach a patient.And for punters every one of those hurdles successfully cleared can remove another layer of uncertainty and potentially another discount applied to what the science might ultimately be worth. That is the attraction of biotech. Successfully turning an idea conceived in a laboratory into a drug, vaccine, diagnostic, cell therapy or medical technology capable of improving patients’ lives can create enormous value. But a gigantic market at the end of the road doesn’t make the road any shorter. In biotech, the treasure at the end of the obstacle course can be enormous. There’s a reason for that. Getting there is bloody hard.

World.title: Alan Jones trial as it happened: Mother of complainant ‘J’ gives evidence after legal issue triggers adjournment
World.content:
Thank you for reading our live coverage of day seven of Alan Jones’ indecent assault and sexual touching trial in the NSW Local Court in Sydney.

A trio of witnesses related to the first complainant in the case, witness “J”, completed their evidence today and a new witness, complainant “C”, is expected to start giving evidence tomorrow morning.

Alan Jones outside the Downing Centre Local Court on Thursday. Oscar Colman

This was the key evidence today:

The mother of “J” told the court that she was in shock and told her son she should have protected him after he told her that Alan Jones had touched him inappropriately. She said “J” had initially denied that Jones had touched him after she asked him directly when allegations about the former broadcaster appeared in the media. However, she said that he told her a year later that he had lied.

She said Jones had given her gifts including a dishwasher, and that she had visited the then 2GB host’s Fitzroy Falls farm in the NSW Southern Highlands with her family.

A former coach of “J” told the court that Jones had helped the young athlete financially. The court has heard “J” did not raise any concerns about Jones with his then coach.

The former coach said that it appeared to him at the time that some of the complainant’s “most enjoyable experiences came from his association with Alan”, including meeting celebrities.

An ex-girlfriend of “J” who has given evidence that the then athlete confided in her 20 years ago that Jones touched him inappropriately was grilled by the veteran broadcaster’s barrister about text messages the complainant sent her after she gave a police statement. “J” promised to “look after” her, the court heard. She did not interpret this as a promise of financial support, the woman told the court.

The trial resumes at 10am tomorrow.

World.title: Live: Man shot dead by police after allegedly stealing air rifle
World.content:
A man has been shot dead in Auckland, after leading police on a chase from Pakuranga to the Sylvia Park shopping mall in the suburb of Mt Wellington.

Police said the man was suspected of stealing an air rifle from a gun shop then drove erratically several kilometres across east Auckland. Police cars and the police helicopter were in pursuit.

His car got stuck at an intersection outside the mall and he fled towards the mall on foot, they said. Police tracked him down to an overpass, where they found him still with the rifle.

He was shot by police and died at the scene.

World.title: Dome Valley landfill proposal returns to court over river rules
World.content:
A controversial landfill proposal for north Auckland is back in court, with Forest and Bird challenging the development over its impact on rivers.

Waste Management New Zealand proposes building and operating the 80-hectare landfill in Wayby Valley, near Dome Valley and Wellsford.

In 2021, an Auckland Council independent commissioner panel granted conditional approval for the landfill. That would have seen 12km of streams destroyed within the footprint of the landfill.

The decision was appealed to the Environment Court by iwi, conservation, and community groups.

In 2023, the Environment Court issued a decision allowing the landfill to go ahead.

Forest and Bird appealed that decision, focusing on the relevance of river protections. That was heard at the Court of Appeal on Thursday.

Lawyer for Forest and Bird Martin Smith said it was agreed that the effect of the loss of 12.2km of streams could not be mitigated.

Waste Management New Zealand had proposed mitigating it through plantings alongside 50 to 60km of streams in the Hōteo River catchment and beside on-site streams, as well as through compensation.

Smith said the debate was about whether the significant effects could be offset or compensated.

He said the location of the landfill was also relevant, and that a landfill did not need to be located over a river to function: "It's not a hydro dam, it's not a port."

Forest and Bird did not accept statements that there was no better alternative site, Smith said.

Waste Management's lawyer Bal Matheson KC said the company had relied on offsets and compensation to reduce the level of impact to below material harm, and if there was no material harm then the rivers policy did not apply.

"We say it's entirely appropriate to offset and compensate."

Avoiding all effects was unreasonable and an inappropriate interpretation of the rules, he said.

As for the location of the landfill, Matheson said Waste Management took 10 years to select the site, avoiding places identified as high value ecological areas in the Auckland Unitary Plan.

Opponents of the proposed landfill protest in central Auckland in 2020. RNZ / Jogai Bhatt

He said he wasn't sure why the company was being criticised for building a landfill outside of a high value overlay.

Representing Ngāti Manuhiri, Jason Pou told the court the landfill proposal would allow hapū that had been historically dispossessed to rebuild their rohe and revitalise themselves by standing on their own land.

"There's a real impact on Ngāti Manuhiri in this in terms of their future generations," Pou said.

The new landfill was initially proposed to replace the company's Redvale landfill, which was consented to accept waste until December 2028.

Waste Management was seeking fast-track consent to expand Redvale Landfill and continue operations there to 2036. Minister for Infrastructure Chris Bishop granted the application for referral to the fast-track process in April.

Waste Management has also applied for referral to the fast-track process for its Wayby landfill. If referral is granted, the fast-track process would run alongside the court process.

The appeal was heard by Justices Jillian Mallon, Matthew Palmer and David Collins.

Justice Mallon said they were conscious of the need for a reasonably prompt decision.

They reserved their decision.

World.title: Pauline Hanna inquest: Unused Polkinghorne documentary footage shown at Coroner's Court
World.content:
Footage from the cutting room floor of a documentary about Philip Polkinghorne's criminal trial has been played at the inquest into Pauline Hanna's death.

Polkinghorne was found not guilty of murdering Hanna, his wife, in 2024.

Now, a coronial inquest is attempting to determine how she died and the circumstances surrounding her death.

Excerpts of interviews with Polkinghorne, filmed in 2022 inside the Remuera home where Hanna was found dead the year before, were included in a Blonde Razor Productions series. It aired in 2025.

At the time of the interviews Polkinghorne was charged with murder. He has since been acquitted.

In unused footage shown at the Coroner's Court in Auckland on Thursday, Polkinghorne told the documentary interviewer he did not use any electronic devices after watching TV with Hanna and going to sleep in separate bedrooms - the last time he says he saw his wife alive.

"She went to bed, and then I went to bed thereafter. I'd finished with a laptop and went to sleep. I didn't use any electronic devices that night to my recollection, didn't take my laptop to bed or anything like that."

Giving evidence at the inquest on Tuesday, Polkinghorne discussed evidence showing he was on his phone until about 2am the morning Hanna's body was found.

Polkinghorne at the inquest on Tuesday. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

He said he often stayed up late watching YouTube and it was a "bad habit" of his.

Polkinghorne also denied deleting WhatsApp messages between him and sex worker Madison Ashton.

"I discovered when I was in the police station, the day Pauline died, that my phone [messages] had been deleted. Who deleted it, how it was deleted, I don't know."

On Tuesday, Polkinghorne admitted to deleting the messages, saying they were embarrassing and unrelated to his wife's death.

Police counsel Alysha McClintock watched intently, having earlier accused Polkinghorne of changing his evidence several times since he was first interviewed by police, the details of which can't be reported on.

In another clip, Polkinghorne told the interviewer about his police interview the day Hanna was found, and what led him to walk out.

"I did not have a support person, I was freezing, I did not have access to a lawyer; I didn't know I needed one. I didn't have any access to anything, I wasn't given my rights.

"I was interrogated and videoed for five or six hours that day."

He got a call midway through from his friend, defence lawyer Tony Bouchier.

"He told me to walk out of the police station. I said 'no, I'm trying to help them Tony, I'm trying to help them discover what went wrong'."

He said police then accused him of lying about something which cannot be reported because of suppressions made by the Coroner.

"I thought this is enough and I just walked out."

World.title: The National Party's 92 political ads seen by only men
World.content:
An RNZ analysis of Facebook advertising by political parties in election year shows some seem to be chasing specific genders and age groups.

Out of more than 500 ads National has run on Facebook and Instagram this year, 92 were seen exclusively by men and only one solely by women.

National spent up to $21,000 on the male-only ads, which were seen up to 3.9 million times, compared with up to $99 on the female-only ad, which ran for just one day and was seen up to 999 times. National denies even placing that one ad which was briefly seen only by women.

ACT appears to be pursuing a similar strategy. Of the 63 ads it has placed, 14 were seen solely by men up to 518,000 times, and none were viewed solely by women. ACT spent up to $4000 for its male-only ads on the Meta platforms.

The Green Party appears to have the opposite approach. It seems to have targeted 13 of its 103 ads at women and none solely at men. It spent up to $5000 on female only ads, which were seen up to 768,000 times.

How the ads work

RNZ analysed Facebook and Instagram advertising data made public by Meta, from 1 January to 7 August this year, when the regulated advertising period began and spending caps kicked in.

Ads paid for by Parliamentary Service, which funds communications, rather than campaign spending, were excluded from the analysis.

Labour did not run any s funded by itself during this timeframe, and NZ First did not run any paid ads on Facebook or Instagram.

Political parties can target people by age, gender and region. Publicly available data on Meta doesn't allow people to see this targeting, but it does show who saw the ad. For an ad to be only seen by one gender it's highly likely this was a conscious targeting decision made by the party.

Left: National's only ad just seen by women ran on 12 June. It cost National less than $100 and Facebook estimates it was seen between 100 and 999 times by females 65 and older. Right: This ad, seen only by men, had up to $2000 spent on it and was seen up to 700,000 times. RNZ composite / Facebook screenshot

Why the parties target by gender

RNZ asked National, ACT and the Greens why they appeared to have targeted one gender over another, and what message this sent to voters of the neglected gender. No party directly answered the questions.

National's spokesperson said ads placed by the party were targeted to a range of demographics, with 80 percent seen by both men and women.

The spokesperson denied Meta's record of an ad aimed at women.

"We don't know what the $99 spend is you are referring to, but it was not placed by the National Party campaign."

Left: This ad from the Greens was only seen by females, it cost up to $2499 and was seen up to 449,999 times. Right: ACT's ad was only seen by men. It cost up to $999 and was seen up to 399,999 times. RNZ composite / Facebook screenshot

An ACT party spokesperson said the party doesn't share details of its digital strategy with the media.

"Our values and policies are for all New Zealanders - that is reflected in the range of candidates who have chosen to stand for ACT and unlock New Zealand's potential."

One quarter of the party's candidates currently listed on its website are women. NZ First and National have only marginally higher proportions of women on their lists than ACT.

Limited funding and resources were among the reasons a Green party spokesperson gave for the lack of male-only ads saying, "it's important we're strategic and intentional about where we put those resources and how to best cut through to certain audiences."

The spokesperson said online advertising allows the party to see what different groups care about.

Overall ad views

Viewership on ads that didn't appear to be targeted to a single gender also showed a skew for some parties, meaning they were seen more by one gender than another.

Two-thirds of the viewers of ACT's ads were male, while National and Opportunity had a male viewership of around 60 percent.

The Greens viewership was 54 percent female and Te Pāti Māori had a nearly even split between genders.

How gender voting patterns can swing results

A survey conducted after each recent general election showed more women voted for National in 2023 than men. The New Zealand Election Study surveyed almost 2000 people. It found 41 percent of the women surveyed voted for National compared to 37 percent of men.

Victoria University of Wellington political science researcher Sam Crawley said there's a generalisation that female voters often support left-leaning parties, but 2023 saw an upswing of women turning to National.

Crawley wonders if the cost of living was a factor in this change, causing swing voters to turn away from the incumbent party and give their support to National.

He was surprised at the percentage of ads National has run that appear to target men.

"Maybe they're focusing a bit more on their base and winning votes back off ACT and New Zealand First."

Social media and audience strategist Anna Rawhiti-Connell was puzzled that National ran the female only version for one day.

"You want to run it for maybe five to seven days, generally, because that is the ad's learning phase," she said.

The data from running an ad over a week can be used to fine-tune it to improve its performance.

She couldn't say if the ad was run as a mistake, but did describe it as a "funny one."

What they're spending

National has outspent all other parties on Meta this year, with up to $113,904 spent. They're followed by the Greens with an upper estimate of $42,883. ACT has spent up to $26,927, Opportunity up to $9342 and Te Pāti Māori up to $6285.

Labour has only run s funded by Parliamentary Service and NZ First has not run any advertising on Meta at all.

National's bigger spend meant its ads were seen more times than the ads of other parties, with Meta estimating close to 19 million views.

As well as gender differences, RNZ's analysis shows age differences in who has seen party messages.

s run by Te Pāti Māori and the Greens had the youngest audiences, while ACT appeared to have reached more people 65 and older.

The emergence of AI in campaign advertising

The days of manually targeting social media ads by demographic may be coming to an end, according to Rawhiti-Connell.

Meta's AI targeting tool called Andromeda focuses on what the company refers to as "creative diversification" rather than niche demographic targeting.

Rawhiti-Connell gave the example of an advertiser wanting to sell a sports drink to young, urban males. Traditionally, the advertiser would manually select an audience they wanted by selecting gender and an age range, and regions. They might also select interests, such as gyms, or protein.

Now, the advice is to leave the targeting broad and load several different versions of an ad.

"You might have an ad for this hypothetical sports drink brand where it's a guy looking happy, and then you might have one where it's a guy looking determined, and you might have one where it's a guy getting ready to go work out."

The way the audience reacts to different versions of an ad is then used by the AI to maximise the reach of the advertisers.

In some cases Meta's AI tools can even generate text in the ads tailored to different audiences, create image variations and resize video.

She's not sure political parties will be using all of Meta's AI tools due to possible audience backlash.

"Imagine if you have a video of Christopher Luxon and all the AI enhancements are running. You can see people reacting quite badly to that."

AI has been used by National to build a campaign microsite called 18 billion. The site has AI generated imagery of stacks of cash including $2 notes. It features a scale and allows users to attempt to balance proposed taxes against the pile of cash. No methodology is included in the site.

At the time of writing no paid Facebook advertising promoted the site.

World.title: Police disappointed some retailers still selling illegal meth pipes
World.content:
Police say it's disappointing there is still readily available access to illegal methamphetamine pipes across the country.

Last month a briefing paper warned the Health Minister that retailers were continuing to sell the pipes.

RNZ's Checkpoint visited five Auckland shops on Thursday and found the banned pipes in three of them, some costing under $10.

Illegal meth pipes still on sale Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

Police Assistant Commissioner Corrie Parnell told Checkpoint he was disappointed but not surprised it was so easy to find them still on sale.

"There is still readily available access to methamphetamine pipes across New Zealand. Cannabis is still our most readily and common used drug across New Zealand but more prevalent now and alongside that is use of methamphetamine," he said.

"We have had discussions with officials, we've been raising our awareness with our own front-line staff who are coming across not only methamphetamine pipes but all manner of sort of instruments that can be used with consumption of methamphetamine and other drug commodities."

Parnell said some retailers were deliberately flouting the rules and police were working to crack down on the problem.

"I think there is definitely an awareness you'd be naive to think there wasn't... my personal view is there is no excuse for not having an awareness of instruments able to be sold for illicit use of drugs," he said.

Penalties for anyone selling the pipes range from three months jail to a $5000 fine.

"Our community beat teams and our prevention teams day-to-day within their communities where they are able to take action they will," Parnell said.

"Often they'll have to make a decision around whether it's enforcement action or an alternate resolution pathway, but nonetheless there's an expectation certainly from police executive and police as a whole that where there's an offence we should be having an intervention there and then making a decision around charging or not."

Parnell said a whole systems level approach was needed to address the problem.

World.title: Ngāi Tahu unveils South Island council boundary plan
World.content:
Ngāi Tahu has unveiled a plan to reorganise the South Island's council boundaries, replacing the 24 councils within its rohe with five bigger ones aligned to major river catchments.

The iwi has lodged a Head Start proposal after the government asked councils to submit amalgamation plans by 9 August or have one imposed on them.

Ngāi Tahu was not invited to submit a proposal, but kaiwhakahaere Justin Tipa said the conversation was too important to sit on the sidelines.

"As an iwi whose takiwā spans most of Te Waipounamu, we have a unique perspective on the opportunities and challenges facing our communities. We've stepped back and looked at the South Island as a whole and asked what kind of local government would best serve future generations.

"A lot of the discussion to date has focused on where the lines should be drawn between urban and rural communities but council boundaries need to be at the right scale to deal with the challenges in front of us… planning around natural water catchments is simply a better way of managing systems and communities that are already connected."

The five councils would be supported by locally elected boards and a South Island-wide shared services entity, Ngāi Tahu said.

Ngāi Tahu has unveiled a plan to reorganise the South Island's council boundaries. Supplied

The iwi said the proposal would help counter the pressures of rising infrastructure costs, climate change, unequal population growth and high rates bills, while keeping a strong voice for local communities.

Tipa said smaller councils were being asked to tackle complex and expensive infrastructure challenges that were difficult to manage alone.

"Rather than every council trying to build that capability on its own, our proposal would create a takiwā wide shared services entity, giving councils access to specialist skills and expertise that would otherwise be difficult or expensive to maintain."

One of the most significant changes would be the creation of a large council encompassing Christchurch, Selwyn, Waimakariri, Hurunui and Kaikōura - areas which were experiencing similar growth and infrastructure pressures, Ngāi Tahu said.

Tipa said people would continue to elect representatives and make decisions about the future of their districts and cities, with democratic local government at the plan's core.

"We don't pretend to have all the answers. These ideas will need to be tested, refined, and strengthened as the conversation develops.

"But if local government reform is going to succeed, we need to be ambitious and prepared to seize the opportunities in front of us. Our focus is on what will best serve the people of Te Waipounamu, now and for generations to come."

Ten other Head Start proposals have been submitted by the South Island's 27 councils, including a vast new unitary authority spanning the central and eastern parts of the Mainland and two conflicting models for Southland.

Approved plans will be signed off in 2027, with changes expected to take effect from the 2028 local elections.

World.title: As it happened: Christopher Luxon won't release count of confidence vote after failed coup
World.content:
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon has survived a confidence vote - the second in just four months.

On Wednesday afternoon, Luxon confirmed speculation that MP Chris Penk had challenged him for the leadership - this is despite his earlier denial.

At a press conference after an urgent Caucus meeting, Luxon said it was united and determined to win the election.

"Our focus is on National's positive plan to fix the basics and to build the future, so that we realise the incredible potential that sits in this country, and that we set it up for our kids and our grandkids."

Luxon was flanked by senior MPs, including Nicola Willis, Mark Mitchell and Chris Bishop. Standing just behind them was Erica Stanford, who was rumoured to be gunning for the top job.

With Penk's failed challenge, Luxon said his position was now untenable and he was sacked from his ministerial portfolios. Penk later said he will not stand for re-election in November.

Speaking to Morning Report on Thursday morning, political commentator Janet Wilson said there were other senior ministers involved at the Bishop was "somewhere in there trying to manoeuvre".

"When you get that kind of manoeuvring, it's deeply decisive."

Fellow commentator Liam Hehir agreed, saying Penk was made to be the "scapegoat" and what happened was inevitable.

World.title: Pallister downs McIntosh to claim 200m gold medal at Pan Pacs
World.content:
Australia's freestyle star Lani Pallister has collected gold and silver medals in her arduous opening to the Pan Pacific championships in the United States.

Pallister triumphed in the women's 200m freestyle and then set a personal best when finishing behind American legend Katie Ledecky in the 1500m freestyle in Irvine, California on Wednesday (Thursday AEST).

Dolphins teammates Sam Short (men's 800m freestyle), Brittany Castelluzzo (women's 200m butterfly) and Ben Armbruster (men's 50m butterfly) also triumphed on the opening night of the Pan Pacs.

The Dolphins won four of 11 gold medals on offer, with Pallister's remarkable year continuing.

Sam Short claimed gold in the men's 800m freestyle. (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

Just weeks after winning four Commonwealth Games gold medals in Glasgow, Pallister pipped Canadian ace Summer McIntosh in the 200m final.

The Australian clocked one minute 53.67 seconds — just 0.02s outside her personal best in the event — with McIntosh second in 1:53.86.

About two hours later, Pallister then returned to the pool for the gruelling 1500m freestyle and set a her best time over the distance.

In what was essentially a match race against peerless American great Ledecky, who hasn't lost in the event in 16 years, Pallister put in a gallant effort.

Lani Pallister (left) and Moesha Johnson (right) were beaten out by Katie Ledecky (centre) in the 1500m freestyle. (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

The 26-year-old shadowed Ledecky, the winner of nine Olympic and 23 world championship gold medals, for the initial 500 metres.

The American great then produced her renowned burst to create a handy advantage en route to touching in 15:36.09.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Pallister's 15:38.62 eclipsed her previous best of 15:39.14 from June last year.

In the men's 800m freestyle, Short went close to a personal best as he edged American rival Bobby Finke.

Short clocked 7:37.02, just 0.71s shy of his best time in the event, with Finke finishing some five-and-a-half seconds behind in second.

Earlier, Armbruster claimed Australia's first gold medal of the pool meet, winning the men's 50m butterfly in 22.75 seconds, 0.02s outside the Australian record jointly held by Kyle Chalmers and Matt Targett.

And Castelluzzo took out the women's 200m 'fly in 2:06.24 from her Dolphins teammate Liz Dekkers (2:06.56).

AAP

World.title: Solomon rubbishes rumours of rifts with Essendon coaching candidates
World.content:
Interim Essendon coach Dean Solomon has described a rumoured falling-out with Mark McVeigh as like an "episode of Home and Away".

After Solomon chose not to put his hand up to be the Bombers' full-time coach, Essendon are closing in on announcing a leader as soon as next week.

McVeigh has been tipped to win the job, even ahead of Essendon icon James Hird.

It has led to suggestions of a rift among the trio, something Solomon has strenuously denied.

Solomon (centre) says there is no ill-feeling towards either Hird (left) or McVeigh (right) after pulling out of the Essendon coaching race. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

"We don't know where they've come from — they're rumours," Solomon said.

"[McVeigh's has been] one of my best mates since the age of 15.

"I've known Hirdy since the age of 17.

"The talks with me potentially not being here next year, whether that stimulated a bit of that conversation, we're unsure.

"But I feel like it's a bit of an episode of [long-running Australian TV soapie] Home and Away.

McVeigh, currently an assistant with Sydney, has been touted as the favourte to win the Essendon job. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

"There's nothing there. We all want to see this club heading in the right direction."

Solomon, McVeigh and Hird all played together at the Bombers, with Solomon and Hird playing in Essendon's most recent premiership side in 2000. McVeigh played with the pair in a losing grand final in 2001.

The trio also worked together briefly at GWS when McVeigh was the Giants' interim coach in 2022.

Solomon initially declared he would stay on at the Bombers next year, even if he wasn't senior coach.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

But his family remains living in northern NSW, complicating matters for him.

"Part of the process of thinking about going in the process for the senior coaching role was sitting down with my family and talking about that," Solomon said.

"My wife and kids live in northern NSW.

"I've had 10 to 11 months away from them at the moment.

"Is that sustainable long-term? It's probably not."

Solomon stressed the next coach didn't need to be an Essendon person, referencing the legendary Kevin Sheedy, who grew up supporting the Bombers but whose playing career was at Richmond.

"He just needs to be the right person," Solomon said.

"A lot of people surrounding our football club are really frustrated.

"We want to be great, and we want to be great really quickly.

"This is a big job and it's an exciting challenge."

AAP

World.title: Hulking prop set to be 1,000th Wallaby as Kiss reshuffles deck
World.content:
The 1,000th Wallaby is poised to be capped in Townsville after hulking prop Massimo De Lutiis was named on the bench to face Japan.

Les Kiss, in his second game in charge, has also recalled fly half Carter Gordon at Declan Meredith's expense.

With Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii injured, he has given Isaac Henry a starting debut at outside centre a week after he earned his first minutes in a tight Osaka defeat of Eddie Jones's side.

Lukhan Salakaia-Loto's Test return has also been secured, the Queensland Reds firebrand set to partner Lachlan Shaw — in his starting debut — in the second row, with Jeremy Williams on the bench and Josh Canham rested.

The Kiss era has begun, and new coach Les is seeking the 'Wallaby way' The new Wallabies era under Les Kiss began with a win in tough conditions against an improving nation, but coach Les Kiss wants more than just wins to be the legacy of his tenure.

Kiss has also shaken up the back row, with Charlie Cale and Carlo Tizzano to partner skipper Harry Wilson, leaving Fraser McReight on the bench and Rob Valetini out of the 23.

Brandon Paenga-Amosa will get his chance under Kiss as replacement hooker while Filipo Daugunu has also been included on the bench as backline cover.

Angus Bell and Taniela Tupou also return to the starting side after stirring second-half cameos in Osaka, while the back three are unchanged and Tate McDermott and Ben Donaldson again provide play-making options on the bench.

It continues the theme of Kiss's tenure, with the new coach keen to assess his options before a long run of Tests ahead of next year's Rugby World Cup in Australia.

"The coaches have looked to find some balance in the selection after what was a physically taxing Test week in the heat in Japan," Kiss said.

"The whole group has worked hard this week and we know where we need to improve.

"This Saturday in Townsville gives us an opportunity to grow and strengthen our game on home soil in front of our supporters."

Gordon impressed at fly half against Ireland, before missing the next two Tests with a calf injury.

Meredith started in the past three Tests alongside Brumbies clubmate Ryan Lonergan, who has been retained the starting scrum half role.

World.title: Cunningham's trans stance opens WNBA up to its latest hijacking atempt
World.content:
Pre-game press conferences are usually a bit of a nothingburger in the WNBA.

Coaches will answer questions about their starting line-ups, address recent trends and it is all very smooth and easy.

However, when Indiana Fever coach Stephanie White arrived at the podium prior to her team's clash against the New York Liberty this week, the mood was different.

White didn't let the journalists ask questions first, as is usually the case in these settings. Her press conference began and ended with a passionate two-minute address.

"The hate, the fear-mongering, the divisiveness, the stuff that's trying to hijack our league will not win. It won't win. We are united. We are connected. We will not be divided," White said in part.

"Every day, these women put their ass on the line … I stand by them. I will always stand by them. Everybody else can go to hell."

White's statement comes after another week where WNBA headlines have had very little to do with the on-court product.

It is sadly old news for a league that is undoubtedly growing but continues to be hijacked by different agendas, whether they be political, racial or financial.

WNBA player claims 'white privilege' saw her ejected after foul Chicago's DiJonai Carrington was ejected for a foul on Indiana Fever's Sophie Cunningham, but stormed off only to post "white privilege" on social media minutes later.

Racial tensions in the WNBA were heightened earlier this week when Chicago Sky defender DiJonai Carrington tweeted "WHITE PRIVILEGE" and tagged the Fever account after being ejected from a game against the Fever due to a hard foul on Fever guard Sophie Cunningham.

Cunningham believed the foul was "absolutely" intentional, adding that Carrington probably had some "pent-up stuff".

White, Cunningham's coach on the Fever, did not think Carrington intended to hurt Cunningham, and was criticised by some for not supporting her players. It was a criticism that left the Fever coach seething.

Cunningham is the WNBA's latest main character, and it is hardly her first time in the limelight.

Sophie Cunningham (right) first went viral after becoming Caitlin Clark's unofficial bodyguard on the court for the Fever. (Getty Images: Jess Rapfogel)

The 29-year-old isn't one of the WNBA's best players, but she is one of its most marketable.

A combination of a suite of endorsement deals, a Sports Illustrated Swimsuit cover, a guest UFC referee spot and an unofficial role as star teammate Caitlin Clark's bodyguard has all combined to net her 3.8 million Instagram followers.

For comparison, the WNBA's consensus best player and four-time league MVP A'ja Wilson has just 1.5 million followers.

Cunningham was the subject of an ESPN feature last month where she spoke out against the participation of transgender women in women's sports, saying "young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men".

Sophie Cunningham has no problems being the villain on her Fever team. (Melissa Tamez/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

When pressed about her comments a few days later, Cunningham did not back down, saying her stance is simply "common sense".

"I think I'll always believe in that," she said.

"I think it's really important to protect children, and that's little girls who are also involved in that category. I stand on what I said."

Cunningham has always presented her views on transgender athletes under the guise of protecting the sanctity of women's sport, and while she may be well-intentioned, the views are problematic in a league that prides itself on diversity and being a safe space for the trans community and other minorities.

Cheryl Reeve has shown her support to the transgender community in the wake of Sophie Cunningham's comments. (Jerry Holt/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images)

Her comments were met with a wave of support for the transgender community from within the WNBA.

Cheryl Reeve, the head coach and president of the Minnesota Lynx, wore a T-shirt reading "Trans Kids Belong" when her team faced Cunningham's Fever.

"I come from a space of inclusion," she said.

"The narrative that I think is problematic is to suggest that transgender athletes are the biggest problem in women's sports."

The WNBA's Player's Association also denounced "hate abuse and demonisation of the transgender community" in a statement.

While Cunningham cares about the league and its future, her views opened the door to people outside the WNBA to gatecrash and use it as a vehicle to push their agendas,an all too familiar a tale for the league.

Unsurprisingly, US President Donald Trump and his vice-president JD Vance wasted little time jumping on the Cunningham train, with Vance labelling her "inspiring".

Riley Gaines, a vocal campaigner against the participation of transgender women in women's sports, also took a sudden interest in Cunningham and the WNBA.

Two former NBA players, Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White, have taken the jig a step further by declaring their intentions to enter the 2027 WNBA draft, more as an attack on the league's current eligibility guidelines and gender inclusivity as a whole rather than a genuine attempt to commence women's basketball careers.

It is a shameless publicity stunt that will ultimately fail. Sadly, it is coming at the cost of both the transgender community and women's sport as a whole.

White has done multiple interviews in a long-haired wig since declaring his draft eligibility and has claimed he is in his "feminine era".

Like Gaines, neither Kanter nor White have previously displayed much public interest in the WNBA.

Perhaps realising the firestorm her comments caused, Cunningham took aim at media covering the WNBA, accusing reporters of covering "everything except basketball" in the days following her ESPN interview.

The irony of it is that Cunningham's comments regarding transgender women in the WNBA came despite there being no transgender players in the league currently, or none about to enter the draft.

She was the one who drove the conversation away from the league's on-court product.

There should be headlines about the 2027 draft class. USC's Juju Watkins is one of the most exciting draft prospects in WNBA history. Her teammate Jazzy Davidson is another star in the making and could also declare.

Instead, we're all here talking about Kanter, a player who spent 11 seasons in the NBA, and White, a former first-round NBA draft pick, threatening to finagle their way into the league while pretending to care about the women's game.

Republican party's bid to claim Clark

Caitlin Clark's arrival in the WNBA has seen the league's popularity skyrocket over the past two seasons. (Getty Images: Michael Hickey)

Clark's arrival in the WNBA as the top pick in 2024 supercharged the interest in the league.

While her sensational long-range shooting and playmaking have endeared her to basketball fans, a different set of traits — being a catholic white woman from Iowa — made her the top target of the Republican Party.

Being the Republican representative of the WNBA is not a role Clark has ever asked for.

That hasn't stopped the Republican Party from attempting to use Clark as a weapon to wield in order to try and stoke race wars within the league, given the majority of its players are of colour.

Last month, eleven Republican politicians wrote to the WNBA asking the league to protect Clark from fouls that they deemed to be "attacks" on her because she is white.

The politicians claimed they were worried that "attacks against Clark may be racially motivated".

The Fever said they were unaware of the Republican letter and added that neither "our organisation nor Caitlin has had any interaction with anyone in this congressional group".

Ironically, while the Republicans complained over so-called attacks on Clark, it was a black player who fouled her, Alyssa Thomas, who was subjected to racist attacks on social media. Thomas was suspended for one game for her collision with Clark.

As Cunningham's teammate, Clark has also been involuntarily dragged into the transgender debate and has said it wasn't a topic of discussion within the Fever locker room.

Clark was asked for her thoughts on the matter in a post-game press conference and said: "It's for leagues and governing bodies to work with their athletes to find solutions".

Conservatives are unimpressed that, unlike Cunningham, Clark has not publicly denounced the participation of transgender athletes in women's sport.

A bizarre sex toy invasion

The WNBA has also been used for financial gain, infamously for the betting company Polymarket.

Last season, multiple games were forced into stoppages after green coloured sex toys were thrown onto the court.

The toys were aimed at the court and towards the players, and one accidentally hit a man watching a game in the stands.

Eventually, members of a meme-coin group, Green Dildo Coin, took responsibility for the bizarre acts, claiming they were simply promotional stunts to promote the launch of their meme-coin.

Polymarket is a company that allows you to bet on pretty much anything, and as it turned out, people were betting on what games sex toys would be thrown on and what colour the toys would be, and then winning the money themselves by throwing the toys into the court.

One of the toys thrown came close to hitting Cunningham, and she denounced the actions on her podcast.

"Everyone's trying to make sure the W is not a joke and it's taken seriously, and then that happens," she said.

Reeve, as she did on the transgender topic, spoke out again, calling the sex toy saga the league's latest "distraction".

"The sexualisation of women. This is the latest version of that," she said.

"It's not funny and it should not be the butt of jokes on radio shows, or in print or any comments."

Loading...

The WNBA is now in its 30th season and continues to go from strength to strength, whether its detractors like it or not.

A host of brilliant young players, headlined by Clark, are bending the realms of what was previously thought possible in the women's game.

Sport and politics are always more intertwined than people think, or like to admit, and unfortunately sport will always be wielded as a political tool by bad-faith operators for as long as it exists.

That is not a good enough excuse for the WNBA to be treated the way it so regularly is.

Cunningham may be passionate about defending women's sport, but has to know that she opened the door for the latest attack on her own league.

World.title: Sexual favours scandal rocks South Korea football association
World.content:
The Korean Football Association (KFA), the governing body of soccer in South Korea, has issued a public apology for "various controversies", including an allegation that payments were made for sexual favours for foreign referees.

South Korean broadcaster JTBC reported last Thursday, local time, that the KFA had provided such services to foreign referees on multiple occasions in 2011 and 2012, including when the referees were in the country for qualifying matches for the 2014 World Cup and the 2012 London Olympics.

In its news report, JTBC cited a 2016 sports ministry investigation that found the KFA had provided inappropriate entertainment to foreign referees on seven occasions between March 2011 and March 2012, including trips to massage parlours where the fees included the costs of sexual services.

South Korea qualified for the 2012 Olympic Games and the 2014 World Cup.

On social media, the KFA issued a public apology for several controversies, including the team's poor results at this year's World Cup and "media reports regarding events from over a decade ago that even many of our own staff members were unaware of".

"However, we wish to clearly state that such inappropriate conduct or misuse of corporate cards is absolutely not occurring at the association at present," the KFA said, as reported by BBC.

"Our association, which ought to bring joy and exhilaration to football fans through the fierce pursuit of goals and the fair sportsmanship that emerges in the process, has recently lost sight of its fundamental purpose and finds itself in a truly dire situation."

The allegations add to scrutiny of the association over a separate issue involving the appointment of former national team coach Hong Myung-bo.

Hong Myung-bo resigned after the 2026 FIFA World Cup. (Getty Images: Chung Sung-Jun)

Hong and KFA president Chung Mong-gyu both resigned following the World Cup.

Seoul police raided the KFA's offices on Thursday as part of an investigation related to Hong's appointment, police told Reuters.

Hong returned as national team coach in 2024 after a previous spell in charge from 2013 to 2014. His appointment drew scrutiny after the KFA abandoned a months-long search involving foreign candidates and selected Hong following a brief meeting.

The controversy resurfaced after South Korea's disappointing World Cup campaign ended in a group-stage exit.

World.title: How a 1mm error had Supercars champ driving a slower car all season
World.content:
Supercars and Triple Eight Race Engineering have both responded after the revelation that 2024 champion Will Brown has been driving with an engine airflow restrictor that is 1 millimetre undersized all season.

Throughout 25 races in 2026, Brown has achieved one pole position and two podiums, while teammate Broc Feeney has five wins in what should be similar machinery.

But on Tuesday night, following a poor outing for Brown in Perth two weekends ago, Red Bull Triple Eight Race Engineering found Brown's Ford Mustang has been underpowered all season.

"After Perth we promised Will, his crew and all stakeholders associated with Car #888, which includes our beloved fans, that we would leave no stone unturned and find reasons why Car #888 has not been fighting for race wins recently," team principal Jamie Whincup said.

"At 7pm [Tuesday] night we found a significant issue on Car #888.

"Since the start of this season, Car #888 has been running with an undersized engine airflow restrictor. This part manages the airflow into the engine and has a significant negative impact on engine performance, and therefore lap time.

"This is not a part we, Triple Eight or Red Bull Ampol Racing, manufacture. This is a supplied part from Supercars expected to be the same for all 11 Ford Mustangs, distributed at the start of the season and expected to be run for the whole season."

Will Brown has just two podiums from 25 races this season. (Getty Images: Daniel Kalisz)

Whincup said the undersized part was costing Brown 0.15 seconds per lap, explaining why the Red Bull Triple Eight Race Engineering driver has struggled for pace often this year.

"We as a team are taking responsibility and want to deeply apologise to everyone involved for allowing this to happen," Whincup said.

"While this error has cost our team a considerable amount of resource, sport is an emotional game and these types of things have knock-on effects bigger than the average 1.5 tenths a lap.

"We will be taking up with Supercars why they have supplied us with what is a controlled component out of specification, which has negatively impacted the performance of Car #888 this season to date.

"We will continue to roll out our new chassis for Car #888 at Queensland Raceway and look forward to measuring our capability now we are competing with the same horsepower as the rest of the field."

On Wednesday, Supercars acknowledged the revelation that Will Brown's car had been fitted with an air restrictor, provided by them, that was 1mm too small.

However, Supercars said the undersized restrictor was only supposed to be used for demonstration purposes only, provided for the team to do a launch in Geelong in February.

"The component was loaned by Supercars to Triple Eight Race Engineering (T8RE) for demonstration purposes only at the team's launch in February.

"The air restrictor subsequently remained fitted to Car 888 through the Perth Super 440. Neither party identified the discrepancy until it was discovered by T8RE during preparations for next weekend's event in Ipswich.

"Throughout the Supercars season, routine scrutineering and compliance checks are carried out at random by Supercars' technical department, covering a vast range of components and systems. As of the Perth event, the air restrictor fitted to Car 888 had not been selected for inspection during those checks.

"Supercars is reviewing the circumstances surrounding this matter and will evaluate opportunities to strengthen its technical and operational procedures moving forward.

"Supercars acknowledges and appreciates T8RE's identifying and prompt reporting of the matter to Supercars."

Brown will now be driving with an engine on parity with the other Mustangs during the next round at Queensland Raceway in Ipswich on August 21-23.

World.title: Jonas Brothers confirmed as half-time entertainment for historic MCG clash
World.content:
The Jonas Brothers will perform at half-time of the NFL's season opener between the San Francisco 49ers and the Los Angeles Rams at the MCG.

The NFL announced the headliners for the half-time show overnight. The game will air on Netflix in Australia on the morning of Friday, September 11. The Jonas Brothers will be part of the entertainment line-up for the league's international schedule this season involving seven countries and four continents.

"We couldn't be more excited to perform at half-time during the NFL's first-ever regular season game in Australia," the Jonas Brothers said in a statement.

"Playing at the iconic Melbourne Cricket Ground in front of such passionate Australian fans is an incredible honour."

The Jonas Brothers — featuring Nick, Joe and Kevin — have sold more than 20 million albums and recently landed a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.

Tim Tubito, the NFL's senior director of global game presentation and entertainment, said the league's first regular season game in Australia is a landmark for the NFL.

NFL confirms historic MCG game to be played on AFL semifinal weekend The first-ever regular-season NFL game played in Australia has had its date confirmed, with the Melbourne Cricket Ground to host the historic match in the middle of the AFL finals series.

"The Jonas Brothers are global entertainers whose music connects across generations, making them the ideal artists to help us celebrate this historic game in Melbourne," Tubito said.

"We look forward to delivering a memorable half-time performance for our fans in Australia and those watching around the world."

The NFL game is set to clash with the AFL's semifinal weekend when the two losing teams of the qualifying finals will host matches.

That could cause headaches for the AFL if those two teams are Victorian clubs, with Hawthorn likely to finish top four and Melbourne and Geelong still in the hunt.
